articles.title: TRADES' UNIONS AND POLITICS.
articles.text:
TRADES' UNIONS AND
POLITICS.

"Trades Unions and Politics !" Tile asso-
ciation of these words will make the hair of
many well-meaning friends belonging to trade
societies stana on end; they recoil from the
association with terror and dislike, believing,
or affecting to believe, it means the destruc-
tion of their cherished unions. As a public
writer, however, in the true interests of the
working classes, it becomes my duty not to
pander to the prejudices of timid or unthinking
men, but boldly to proclaim what I deem best
for their interests, however unpalatable or un-
welcome those truths may be. I have, there-
fore no hesitation. in affirming it as my belief
that trades' unions and politics must be
combined, if ever those unions are to become,
what all desire them to be, the means whereby
their members may be raised to their proper
position in the social scale. The unnatural
and extraordinary dislike entertained by so
many members of trades' unions to associate
them with politics, arises from a false estimate
of the meaning attached to the word. They
do not take the word on its broad principle,
but confound it with those measures adopfed by
faction or party to advance its own particular
views or interests. Politics is simply a name
for principles which regulates, or ought to
regulate, the action of government to ensure
the greatest happiness of the greatest number
of the body politic; and it is the perversion of
those principles to the purposes of parties and
factions that has made politics an object of so
much dislike to those who will not take the
trouble to look below the surface, and induces
trades' unions to echo the senseless cry of" No
politics." . _ _ _ _ _

- The formation of a trades' unioni is in itself
a political act, and every movement taken to
advance the interests of its members is based
on that principle. What are the main objects
of a trades' union? The protection and
advancement of the social rights of its mem-
bers, by regulating the scale of wages, and the
hours of labour;b and they cannot take one
single step in the defence or attainment of those
rights without coming. into contact with one of
the most important of all political principles,—
that of political economy. Whence arises the
necessity for trades' unions? The answer is
plain. From the acts—the political acts—of
the legislature, in which the employing class
have political power, and from which the
working classes—the members of trades'
unions—are, as a body, excluded. Trades'
unions are formed to protect social rights,
endangered by political actions, and, therefore,
it is politics that bring them into being.
Why is it that trades' unions frequently fail
in. carrying out their objects, or when success-
flu only at a cost that makes a seeming victory
a real defeat ?- Because they do not fight on
equal terms with their antagonists; forgetful
of their origin they only oppose their social
organisation,—and that too often an imperfect
one,—to the combined and therefore power-
ful social and political organisation of
the capitalist employers. Thus it has hitherto
been, and thus it will continue to be, until
trades' unions discard the foolish and slavish
cry of" No politics," and obtain possession of
the same weapons as those parties to whom
they are opposed.

To those unacquainted with the strong con-
servative -feeling -pervading-the majority of
trades' unions, and the tenacity with which
working men cling to early habits and pre-
judices, it is a matter of much astonishment
that the repeated attacks which have been made
on these unions, through the political action
of the Government, have not long since aroused
them to a sense of their comparatively helpless
condition, by their thus unwisely ignoring poli-
tics; by in eetin g,to speak figuratively, the political
tomahawk with the social penknife. Two flag-
rant cases have occured within the last sixteen
months. The aid afforded to the master builders
by a political body connected with the Govern-
ment—the War Office—in lending the services
of the sappers to erect the Chelsea barracks,
during the dispute on :the hour system, was
direct political action in opposition to the
unions of the building trades. And yet these
unions, or most of them, can go on repeating
"We have nothing to do with politics." Polities
however, replies, "We have a great deal to do
with • you, and when we think proper
can help your employers to defeat your de-
mands." I may here be met with the remark,
"But the unions, by the representations of their
delegates, got these sappers withdrawn."
Granted. But this tardy withdrawal was owing
to political action; by some of the more ad-
vanced unions, discarding for the time, their
"No politics" cry, and ,directly meeting the
political representative of that department of
the Government. By taking political action
the delegates were successful, and proved my
case. Again look at the conduct pursued by the
Government in the case of the iron ship build-
ers at Chatham dockyard. No sooner had these
men acted upon the rules of their union than
they were discharged. So far it was a simple
question between employer and employed, but
what followed? The influence of a powerful
political section of the Government in the
Board of Admiralty' was at once brought
to bear against the men. Orders were
sent round by the Board of Admiralty
to all the government dockyards, that
none of these men were on any account ever
again to be employed in those ytirds. Was not
this bringing political power to bear against the
ship builders' And yet I am afraid this
union will still go on repeating, "We have
nothing to do with politics ! " althoufth
politics did its best to deprive 100 of its memb -
hers of employment, and throwttheru a burdV
on its fund.

I would, then, in the face of all that has
transpired, and what is likely to ensue in the
coming session of Parliament, seriously ask
trades' unionists whether they mean to go on
in the present humdrum style, or whether they
are prepared to strike out a bolder path, and
take the "bull by the horns ? " They may.
still go on with their "no politics" policy.;
"'lt how will that policy serve them if, as is
probable an attempt be made by Parliament to
curtail the social action of their unions, so
far as the
regulation of trade matters is con-
cerned,
and reduce them simply to friendly
societies? They will theii, when too late, be
forced into aan abandonment of their suicidal
policy, and nave to
main-
tain their present fight desperately to main-
ground. One half the energy,
Organisation, and amount of money that will
'
-to
then be required fight the enemies of labour,
atid labour's rights, would, if now brought
into the field, gain for them the franchise
right, by-the possession of which, and by which
alone, they can hope to obtain a sufficient
.leverage for their unions to raise themselves
permanently in the social scale.
Since the above lines were penned, I have
had placed in my hands "An Address to the
1
Trades' Unionists of the United Kingdom" on
the above subject. This address appears in
another column; and I strongly commend it 1
to the serious and thoughtful perusal of my)

THE ." BEE-HIVE" AND THE "BRITISH
MINER."
PEOPLE are often angry at falsehoods being told,
but, they are invariably 'very angry when the truth
tells against them. It is thus we account for a
very angry article upon the BEE-lIIVE in the
seventh number of the British Miner, of Saturday,
the 25th nit. On the 11th of September we glanced
at the tendency of the leading article in number one
of that journal, shewinp; first, that it, essentially
supported the false philosophy which originates,
causes, and maintains, the whole
,of the evils which
it freely sets forth, and which it professed to exist
and to remove; and second, it ignores, discounten-
ances, and denounces, the only means by which the
miners of Britain, or at present can help them-
selves :—viz., to strike either against wrong, or
to obtain their rights.
We renew again the two charges—lst, that the
British Miner is an organ teaching and defending
the present relations of capital and labour, and which
has originated and caused all the evils of the labour-
ing classes, and of miners especially; and, 2nd,
that it denounces all strikes collectively, and teaches
that they never did, and never can, do anybody any
good. In proof of our first charge we will give
quotations in the closest order of sequence we can
command, and then show the bearing of our objec-
tions :—" The rate of wages is governed by natural
laws, of which the operation is in the long run
inevitable; and which, in a primiEve state of things,
will be, as recompense, exactly .the whole produce
of his toil, but in a complex state of society, when the
whole surface of the land has become appropriated,
the more skilful or industrious accumulate more pro-
duce than they immediately require, and these
become the landowners and capitalists. Population
increasing, necessitates those who have neither land
,nor produce to labour for those who have; and thus
they become dependent for the means of both life and
labour. The capitalist is desirous of still increasing
his store, hires the labourer upon the condition of
receiving a sufficient portion of the produce to enable
him to do this; or in other words, the labourer sells
himself for as much as he can get from the results
of his labour. Putting aside differences of rate of
wages, as depending upon. skill, endurance, &c., it
May be affirmed, that the average rate of wages de-
pends upon the proportion of capital disposable by
the capitalist, and the number of labourers seeking
work. The accumulation of eapital tends to increase
the demand for labour, and to raise wages, conse-
quently, while the increase of population tends to
increase the competition for labour, and thus to
diminish wages; population and capital are also
striving which shall increase fastest, and hence a
perpetual necessity for adjustment. Capital seeks
employment, and labour does the same, and upon
.bargaining, the result in the long run depends just
upon the amount of capital there is compared with
the number of labourers, the tendency being for capi-
tal to divide itself evenly among the whole of the
labourers, and the more labourers the less there will
be for each. There is a natural tendency in both
parties to combine to maintain their own iuterests ;
in the past, the employers by law prevented combi-
nations among workmen; but at present, both exer-
cise their liberty to do so frequently ; so that it may
be considered that both sides are in a permanent
organisation of strife; the masters generally having
the advantage from the command of capital. The
payment of wages is however governed by natural
laws, which do not admit of being transgressed, as
the labourer must receive sufficient necessaries of
life to live by his work; and there is a limit beyond
which the capitalist would pay away his capital.
Arbitrary laws for a just regulation are found incom-
patible with a vigorous growth rilf society, and
Jegislators find it best to let the question settle itself,
'in faith that the prudence and sagacity of the Reople
has been found to be the best course. The power
of preventing wages from falling unreasonably and
disastrously low, so far as it exists, lies mainly with
the people themselves; by the cultivation of habits
of forethought, and in the determination not to leave
their offspring worse off than themselves; which,
according to Mr. M'Culloch, are powerful enough to
imnackreeaste in theheprogrmesesanos f subsistence."
fof population subordinate to the
We have thus, at considerable length, con-
densed honestly the whole bearing of the article,
upon which our comments have given such strong
offence. It was not necessary for our purpose to
have gone to this length, but really the editor has
put together so admirably the dogmas of the day-
departing, that by the way of registering the philoso-
phy before our readers, we have thus reproduced it.
There are in it views and tendencies removed so
far from the common considerations, and even
opportunities of thought, of British miners, that we
shouid fail, just as the editor has done in command-
ing attention, in rebutting a philosophy beyond their
reach; but there will be no mistake upon the broad
fact, that this teaching is the exact doctrine of the
capitalists, and that the editor is the teacher and
defender of it.
No doubt there is law governing even what is
chance to us, and historically, we admit the editor
gives fairly the tendency of the actions of capital and
labour upon each other, both in the past, and present.
But before we go into the examination of particulars,
we should like to agree Arst, what should be con-
sidered the object a law to attain. What should

it do? for it is necessary- to understand that, before
we can defend law as such. No doubt that the laws
of God are just absolutely—not so the laws of man.
Now the laws of the relation of capital and labour
are at present, so far as man is concerned, conven-
tional.
.They are not laws of nature. Nature never
gave to. one man a right of so many manors—and of
all surface, and, of
,all mineral beneath. But human
laws -having. done so, can only be defended on the
consideration "that they are for the greatest good
of the greatest number." If, then, the laws of the
relation-of capital -and labour are to be tested by the
greatest -good of the -greatest number? and the
Editor affirms to the natural inevitability of what he
has" Stated--; what, is his object? Is it to alter the
inevitable ? The British miner has truly obtained
a strange advocate! Does the Editor think the
British miners—some 300,000—have obtained the
greatest good that the -present selations of capital
admit of? And yet- the said 'Editor teaches and
defends the said relations, as both natural and in-
evitable ! The truck system, tommy shops, and
gambling associations, are doubtless evils, but they
are mere trifles to the fundamental question of
just; and right, of wages. Either the miner has
or has not
.‘‘ a fair day's wage for a fair day's work;"
and we Nyould put it -directly to the Editor to say at
once, and openly before his readers, whether
thinks they have received or not their just equivalent.
of wages in proportion to production ; in other
words, ought wages to receive a proportion propor-
tionate to production? . .

Perhaps the question of the right of proportion,
or even its ratio, never came before the Editor. It
has, unfortunately, baen deeply engraven on our
minds, and circumstances have as unfortunately
compelled an investigation and preof of the facts,
which we shall be
_glad to furnish, that for the last
50 years population has increased at the rate of
say SO per cent; and production has increased in
the ratio of more than 500 per cent. It is clear,
then, that capital has far exceeded in. 'increase
the proportion of labour to the wage fund.
Our next position is, that, as a whole, the la-
bouring classes engaged in production have not re-
ceived more than 25 per cent in wages; and apart
from the advantages of a reduced price , of articles,
and increased price of rentals, and :of other neces-
saries, we again affirm that the advantages of pro-
duction, the improvements of art, science, and civil-
ization, have not been adequately shared in by the
operative classes in general. This is not a singular
or novel doctrine-.—all our great statesmen proclaim
it. Sir. Robert. Peel and Lord John Russell, Dis-
raeli and Gladstone, are here all agreed.
We think' the Editor of the British Miner will
not dispute this—but what, then, does he propose
for a remedy ? In few words, where lies the evil ?
According to the British Miner, it is all in private
or individual. faults; and all his advice for remedy
is thus tending. Now we see, besides this, the
general fault of a false philosophy, in which capital
is placed before humanity, and the increase of wealth
before the suffering of man. We see this philo-
sophy held .up nnd defended by the Editor of the
British .Miner, and hence we see, as previously
indicated, a strange inconsistency betwixt profes—
sions. and means—betwixt objects and doctrines.
We are not angry with the childish names of
"wretched production;" "Solomon in print' "waspish
drone, striving to live on the earnings of industrious
bees,"or even of "originator, a fosterer of discontent,'
&c., &e., with which the Editor has so profusely
bespattered us. They are neither new, nor true,
and it only promotes a smile of contempt; after this,
to be called "virulent, scurrilous, and impudent."
We called the British Miner no names; nor d d
we impute motives;. but we did, do now, and will
amain, defend the interests and welfare of the
British miner against the errors of their self-
assumed friends (F) - We did this before the British
Miner was in existence, and perhaps may after it
has ceased to live; in the meantime, we wish it a
better temper, and better views, towards which it
Will be our endeavour, earnestly, for the cause's sake,
to direct attention, and to aim at correction, without
malice, fear, or favour.

THE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

EA.ST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL EXECUTIVE.

(REPORTED SPECIALLY FOR THE BEEHIVE.)
. The usual weekly meeting of the executive took
place on Monday, at the Committee • Rooms, Speak-
buildings, Pad i ham. Present: The. Rev. E. A. Verity,
Rector of Ilabergham (president) ; James Heap, John
Howarth, James Denbigh, Lawrence Shackleton (vice
president), James Crompton, David 'Walton (Burnley),
James Hartley, Henry Whitehead, George Hargreaves
(Habergham), W. Wilkinson (treasurer), Joseph Pea-
cock (secretary). . •

The minutes'of the last meeting were read and con-
firmed. The Secretary gavein his report; after which
the deputation to Lee& delivered an account of their
journey and reception by the trades of that town. The
thanks of the meeting were voted to Alr: Geo. Potter
for a remittance of £l5 from the BEEHIVE newspaper;
and to the men of Bristol for the gift of £l.O. The
deputation to Bacup and Great Harwood delivered in
their report. A resolution was passed that a deputa-
tion proceed to Birmingham to visit the trades in that
town, and lay the truth before them respecting the
claims of the Central upon the working classes. 500
.collecting bills were ordered to be printed and sent to
the British -Miner, with the best thanks of the executive
to Mr. Maitland. The working zuen of Leeds sent a
small instalment of what they intended to do.- Mr.
Shackleton said he believed the hearts of the Leeds
men beat warm towards our Central, but they had,
as in Birmingham, been entrapped into a middle-class
committee formed by Mr. Baines and others in that
town. •

The Chairman thought it disgraceful for the
wealthier classes to bolster up' their sickly subscrip-
tions with the gifts of the working classes. Let each
class support.its own Central, and then there will be no
discord between them.

The deputies from Burnley,
,Habergls'am, and Padi-
ham gave in their accounts. The distre'ss is fearfully
increasing. The poor are even pledging the clothing
given by middle class committees, because they are not
sufficiently relieved. The usual grants were made to
these districts.

Mr. Wilkinson said that unless the `London trades
were to raise £5,000 as a.loan fund for the Bacup Co-
operators, he teared the progress Of—this movement
would ho stopped in that locality for years to come.
The Chairman said the matter would be shortly sub-
mitted to the London men.

The Secretary announced the arrival of a parcel of
clothing fromla clergyman in Lincolnshire. He wished
some kind friend would present them with some
blankets.

The following letter has been sent to us for publica-
tion : _ 13.1istol, Nov. 12, 1862.
-

DEAR SIR —I forward you a post-office order for
£lO, which please acknowledge, and pay into the East
Lancashire Central Operatives' Relief Fund, as coming
fm the Working Men's Committee, Colston's Hall,
Bristol. I trust the working men all through the
country will do more than they have hitherto done for
the support of those of their own class who are now so
terribly destitute. I find a few generous spirits among
them; but the great mass are too selfish to render the
least aid to their suffering fellow-countrymen. I cannot
help feeling very strongly on this matter. I hold that
every man in regular employment should contribute a
small sum weekly towards the relief fund so long as
the necessity lasts. The great industrial community
who subsist on weekly wages never had so grand an
opp3rtunity of mAnifesting to the world the true
nature of the sympathy they have for their own class.
This sad calamity will have an end. Those who now
suffer will again see prosperity. Let the working men
now do their duty to each other, and, with the return
of better times, they will find themselves on a higher
moral elevation, and in a better position to obtain every
right, social and political.

YOUTEI very truly, WM. BUTCHER.
To the Rev. A. Verity, Padiham.

MEETING OF WORKING MEN AT NOTTING
HILL.

• On Tuesday evening a public meeting of the work-
ing men resident ' a Notting-hill, Bayswater, and
Kensington, was held in the Horbury School-room,
Notting-hill, for the purpose of taking into considera-
tion the distress now existing amongst the Lancashire
cotton operatives, and to adopt measures for aiding the
fund now collecting on their behalf. The meeting
was well attended, and great enthusiasm prevailed.
Mr. Joseph Pacey having been voted to the chair,
said that several preliminary meetings had been held
amongst the working men in these districts in order
to see what steps they could take to aid in relieving
the sufferings of their follow-wmkmen, and the result
had been the convening of this general meeting. The
operatives of Lancashire were now in that state that
must excite the sympathy of every working man in
England. Working men were not in receipt of larger
wages than they required for their own wants, but the
present was a time when all should be willing to make
a sacrifice to alleviate the sufferings of their brethren.
There had never, in his recallection, so great a calamity
fallen on such large masses of their fellow-countrymen,
and therefore he hoped they would endeavour to do all
in their power to alleviate the suffering caused by this
calamity.. (Hear.)
Mr. Henry White then moved the following reso-
lution :---‘ That we the working men of Notting-hill,
Bayswater, and Kensington deeply sympathise with
our brethren in Lancashire in their present unparalleled
privations and distress, caused by the lamentable civil
war in America, and that in pledging ourselves to
render them all the pecuniary aid in our power, this
meeting most emphatically condemns the application
of the labour test to those men as disgraceful alike to
the Poor-law and its administrators, as such a test
should only be applied to habitual paupers, and not
to respectable artisans thrown out of employment by
no fault of their own.' The speaker read several ex-
tracts from the last report of Mr. Farnall, to show the
state of the existing distress. In London, when any
great calamity fell upon a large body of working men,
there were generally enough left in steady employ-
ment to prevent their brethren. falling into a state of
pauperism, but in Lancashire all were involved in on( ,
common ruin.

Mr. John Osborne seconded the resolution, strongly
-
enforcing on the working men present the duty of tb Air
contributing, to the utmost of their power, to the r( )lief
of their brethren.

The resolution was unanimously adopted..
Mr. Kingston moved the second resolution :
the following working men form a committee to receive
subscriptions, and to apply the same to the relief of
the operatives through one of the General Cr Imulittera
in Lancashire, formed for that purpose, vi' h., Messrs.
Smith, Anderson, Holyfield, Osborne, Chad, lock, Pacy,=
Elton, White, Hingston, Clarke, She Wool-
ford, Heath, Flood, Nieus, and Page. That
nd that the
secretary, treasurer, and chairman air
Saturday evening at Mr. Talbot's coffee house, in the
Mall, from seven till nine, to receive monies and to
give any information respecting the ex penditure of the
same, to persons applying for it.'
Mr. Smith seconded the resoluticr Al it every

agreed to.

Skin Dlieases and their Cure by Diath,etical Treatment.
With Cases. By Ed win Payne, M.D., &c. London:
Henry Renshaw.
In this little book we find a rational method of
treating those most distressing complaints, diseases of
the skin. :Dr. Payne, educated in the modern and more
enlightened school of medicine advocates, their treat,
raent upon constitutional principles instead of dealing
with them by name. In these few pages there is a
multum in parvo and for the encturagement of those
who suffer we find the questions—' is this eruption
curable?' 'Will it be long before I get well?' Can
this disease be cured without injury to my health?'
all answered satisfactorily. We cordially recommend
its perusal to the multitude of desparing sufferers.

A NEGRO LYNCHED AND BURNED.—The Baltimore
American of the 3rd November has a letter from
Dalton, Caroline county, giving an account of the
lynching of a negro, under arrest for the outrage and
murder of a little girl, daughter of Edgar Plummer.
A large number of excited people came into town, en-
rounded the gaol, forced open the doors, took the
prisoner, and hung him. While suspended, fifteen
bullets perforated his body. He was cut down and his
throat cut by the infuriated mob. The body was
dragged through the streets and finally taken in
front of the negro church, where it was cut to pieces
and burned. • t

articles.title: GREAT FIRE IN WHITEFRIARS.
articles.text:
GREAT FIRE IN WHITEFRIARS.

On Thursday evening, at five o'clock, a fire, accom-
panied by a great destruction of property, broke out
in the extensive oil and tallow warehouses, belonging
to Messrs. Price and Co., Tudor-street, Whitefriars.
In consequence of the extensive stock on the premises
of Messrs. Price, and its contiguity to the City Gas
Works, the greateat alarm existed in • the neighbour-
hood. Fortunately, however, the wind blew in a
southerly direction, and the flames were diverted from
the gas works. • For
.up wards of six: hours the flames
retained possession of Messrs. Price's warehouses, the
lower portion of which, with the whole of their con-
tents, were entirely destroyed.
Four barges lying alongside the wharf, loaded with
cargoes of oil and turpentine, were also burnt. The
flames likewise attacked the coal depot of Messrs.
Capel, which speedily fell a prey to the flames. The
hack portion of the premises in Chatham-place, Black-
friars, belonging to the Royal Hotel, were also much
burned and damaged by water. A large number. of
the Brigade engines were in attendance with the new
steam-engine of Mr. Hodge, the distiller, and the two
floating engines; but there was an unaccountably short
supply of water for the land engines in the early part
of the fire, and the tide being low, the floating engines
were some time before they could be brought into play.
The fire was not got under until twelve o'clock at
night. Its cause could not be ascertained.

articles.title: AN ANTICIPATED RIOT IN
articles.text:
AN ANTICIPATED RIOT IN

TVOLVERILIMPTON.

Gavazzi lectured on Wednesday night in Wolver-
hampton on Victor Emmanuel, Garibaldi, and the
Pope; Italy, her present and her future.' Remembering
the excesses that have been occasioned in other towns,
and especially in Birkenhead, by Irish mobs, the
mayor and magistrates took steps to ascertain if there
was any reason to expect that such proceedings would
Ibe repeated in Wolverhampton. They received infor-
mation to the effect that a riot might be feared on the
1 part of the Irish, and they ascertained that the returned
convictkat large in the district were being organised by
a ringleader of their number, to avail themselves of the
occasion to 'make a foray upon the most vulnerable
parts of the town, and that the respective depots of the
arms of the volunteer companies in the town would be
sacked. The mayor and,the magistrates. supported by
the leading ratepayers, thereupon determined to take
prompt steps to summarily suppress any violence if it
should be attempted. They forwarded a request to
Birmingham for a troop of dragoons, instructed Cap-
tain Thorneycroft to be in realiness with his troop
of yeomanry, and desired the assistance of Colonel
Hogg, the chief constable of the countv, and a
body of his men, removed the arms of the volun-
teers into safe custody, and swore in a body of
special constables to secure the safe keeping of the arms.
On Tueday afternoon the dragoons rode into the
town ; subsequently a force or 126 of the county con-
stabulary, headed by Colonel Hogg, Major M‘linight
(the deputy chief constable), and Chief Superinten-
dent Sweeting, and flanked by three superintendents,
all upon horseback, entered the town, and were met
by the stipendiary of the district, also mounted. All
the constables wore their sabres,- but their weapons
were hidden by the long cloaks which the men wore.
Captain Segrave, the chief constable of the town, had
his own force ready, and placed them in piequets in
different peas of the town, so that if any attempt
should be made to disturb the peace elsewhere than at
the place of the na.eeting he might be prepared to quell
it. These preparations have secured peace. A vast
number of roughs assembled, but were ketrt moving.
Gavazzi had an enthusiastic reception, and the mayor
was cheered.

FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—ESCAPE OF SIX MEN.—
On Tuesday morning, between 8 and 9 o'clock, a
colliery accident, unhappily fatal in its results, took
place in a pit now being sunk in Park-lane, near
Wigan, by Messrs. Mercer and Evans. It appears
that eight n:en were engaged as usual, two, named
Goulding and Catterall, being at work ramming a shot,
when, by some means, a spark reached the powder they
were using, and an explosion took place, the full force
of which had to be borne by the two workmen above-
named, one of whom (Goulding) received fatal inju-
ries, and the other (Catterall) was so much hurt that
his life was despaired of. Strange to say, of the re-
maining six men who were at work p.t the time of the
accident, not one is serionsly injured, though the place
in which they were working was necessarily very
small. The body of Goulding has been removed to
the Red Lion Inn, near the colliery, to await the in-
quest.

ATTEMPTED Munnint.—On Tuesday morning, be-
tween two and three o'clock, Captain John Peter
Sweden, a Norwegian, and Peter Lawson, mate of a
vessel in the London Docks, and also a Norwegian,
who had been to Deptford on business, were returning;
home, and when near a low beershop by the Comtner-
cial Docks, stopped to listen to what three Dutchmen
were quarrelling about. The latter suddenly pulled
out their long knives and attacked the two unfortunate
men. A police-constable and a sailor, hearing the
cries of Murder' and proceeded to the spot
from whence the cries came, and found the two
unfortunate sufferers in a pool of blood. Without loss
of time they were conveyed to the hospital, where it
was found that the captain had three very deep stabs
in the back, one in the cheat and several in the face.
Lawson had been stabbed through the jugular vein
and in tha region of the heart and chest. Both
now remain, in a very dangerous condition. Up to
the present time the assassins have not been appre-
hended.

Tr in SUICIDE OF A YOUNG WOMAN AT WESTMINSTER
BRY.DRR—On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Bedford con-
elrlded, at Westminster Hospital, the investigation
ir Ao the death of a female unknown, who committed
r suicide by drowning herself in the Thames at West-
minster Bridge. The deceased was an unfortunate;
and, on the morning of Friday week, she and another
of the same class, Elizabeth Harwood, left the Hay-
market, and, while proceeding down Parliament-street,
proposed that they should both commit suicide by
tying their arms together and jumping. into the river.
On arriving at the steps by Westminster Bridge, Hu-
wood suggested that the handkerchief should be untied,
so that they should go in one at a time, saying that she
would follow deceased. Their proceedings were ob-
served, and a policeman followed them and called out,
but before he got within fifty yards of deceased she
slipped between the railings into the water. Other
assistance was called, but upon the deceased being got
out and taken to Westminster Hospital life was found
to be extinct. Christina Walsh, describing herself as a
waistcoat maker, living in Dean. street, Soho, identified
the body as that of Mary Anne Hollands, aged 19
years. Deceased bad no parents and was of no
occupation. She had frequently talked of committing
suicide, and on one occasion she sharpened a knife and
attempted to cut her throat. She often said that she
was tired of her course of life. She had a young man
who frequently quarrelled with awl ill-treated her.
The jury returned a verdict TiDtt deceased drowned,
herself while in a state of temporary insanity,'

articles.title: TRADES' UNION POLITICAL UNION.
articles.text:
TRADES' UNION POLITICAL UNION.

TO THE vorroa OF THE BEEHIVE.
SIR —Several numerously attended meetings of
members of the London Trade Societies have recently
been held at the Brown Bear, Broad-street, Blooms-
bury, for the purpose of organising the Trades So-
cieties of the United Kingdom on behalf of the question
of Political Reform. At an adjourned meeting, held
on Tuesday last, Mr. Facey, painter, in the chair, an
acting sub-committee was appointed, the following
resolutions were passed, the accompanying address
drawn up and agreed to, and it was unanimously re-
solved, that the address and resolutions should be
forwarded to the edttors of the liberal, daily, and
weekly newspapers for the favour of insertion.

Mos. GRAN-1
P-A-C;;; Secretary.

REsoLunoNs.

That this Association is established for the purpose
of obtainisig registered manhood suffrage, and voting
by ballot; and is entitled The Trades Unionists'
Manhood Suffrage and Vote by Ballot Association.'
That we base our demands on the natural and God-
given rights of every man to equal political rights.
That all persons becoming inembera of this Associa-
tion shall be furnished with a card of membership, for
which they shall pay one penny; but that all other
expenses of this Association, such as public meetings,
petitions, printing, stationery, &c., shall be defrayed
by voluntary contributions.

- That all daces shall he filled gratuitously.
That societies, and members of societies, be invited
to form branches of this Association, and send repre-
sentatives for the purpose of forming a political council
to work out its objects; and. that the trade societies in
the provinces be also invited to form themselves into
branches and co-operate with the central committee.
That moral agitation alone be employed, such as
meetings, petitions, circular; addresses, and deputa-
tions, and requesting to be heard at the bar of the
House of Commons in favour of the principles of this
Association.

That meetings be held fortnightly to receive reports
of proceedings, and for discussing such political and
social questions as affect the interests of the working
classes, and that the branches in the provinces be
recommended to pursue the same course.
That the Council shall issue an address, and a report
of progress monthly.
That this Association co •operate with other associa-
tions having the same objects in view.

ADDRESS TO THE TRADES' UNIONISTS OF
- THE UNITED KINGDOM.
FELLOW WOBEMEN,—Our numbers, and our posi-
tion, as the skilled artisans of this country, give us
an influence, which, if wisely directed, would greatly
advance the interests of the toiling masses of our
fellow countrymen in every direction. Heretofore our
efforts have been directed to the removal of one evil
only, forgetting, or only partially remembering, that
all the evils under which we suffer have a qommon
origin, namely, an excess of political power in )e hands
of those holding a higher social position. edo not
.1/3
wish you to relax one iota of your efforts n reference
to the amelioration of our social condition. Our advice
is, be more than ever united for the purpose of reducing
the hours of labour, and for advancing its price. Nor
do we wish to turn our trade societies into political
organisations to divert them from their social objects;
but we must not forget tnat we are citizens, and, as
such, should have citizens' rights. Recollect also,- that
by obtaining these rights, we Mien be able more
effectually to secure our legitimate demands as unionists.
Our object is, therefore, to create an organisation for
the purpose of securing our rights as citizens; or, in
other words, our just share of political power. We
know that our unions contain large numbers of
intelligent and progressive men, that many of these
meit are active and earnest supporters of every other
movement having for its object the impr,ovement of
our condition, politically and intellectually, as well as
socially, and we desire to see these men brought into
closer contact with each other, and their present
isolated efforts concentrated on one great object, so as
to make it successful. The objects sought to be ob-
tained by the present agitation are precise and definite,
viz.: Registered manhood suffrage, and the protection
of that suffrage by the ballot. Upon these two great
principles, we take our stand and invite the whole of
the trades unionists of the United Kingdom to co-
operate with us until our agitation is crowned with
success. We have no desire to dictate to the trades
the manner in which they shellac ton this great question;
they may do so as societies, if their members think
proper; or individual members may meet among them-
selves, and so form a committee to carry out these
plans in aid of the association. The expenses of the
association are to be defrayed entirely by voluntary
contributions ; and all offices are to be filled gratui-
tously. You will, therefore, see that the promoters of
this agitation have no other interests in its success than
the common interest of all working men who are now
deprived of their rights as citizens of this great country.
And now, fellow-workmen, let us exhort you to enter
earnestly into this great work. It will not be the work
of a day; it may be of years; but its ultimate success
will amply repay us for all our struggles to obtain it.
In this agitation we deprecate all violent measures,
and all violent language likewise. Let our advocacy
be firm, intelligent, and persistent; not a sowing of
the seeds of discord, but a promotion of the growth of
union; not an exciting of class against class, but an
endeavour to promote the welfare of all; by modera-
tion in our demands, forbearance to our opponents, and
while earnestly contending for our own rights, by the
sacred maintenance of the rights of others. Rally
around us, then, fellow-countrymen—' The field is
wide, there is work enough for all.' Hold your meet-
ings throughout the length and breadth of the land;.
pour in your petitions by thousands; but let them be
well authenticated in their signatures. Let us work I
work! work! unitedly, consistently, and persistently,
and our voice shall be heard within the walls of Pan.
liament. The friends of Progress there will support
our demands, and both Sovereign and people will, at no.
distant day, celebrate our victory.
(Signed)
W. CREMER,
G. HOWELL,
R. APPLEGARTH,
B. RICHARDS,
J. GRAHAM,
J. CASSIDY,
J. EGLINGTON,
GEo. ODGERS, Chairman.

I remain, Sir, years, &c.,

articles.title: EXECUTION OFROBERT,COOPER.
articles.text:
EXECUTION OFROBERT,COOPER.

;Theixeciition of Robert Cooper, who was convicted
at the last session of the Central Criminal Court of the
murder of a young woman named Anne Jane Barnham,
by shooting her with a pistol, took place on the 17th at
eight o'clock at Newgate.
The circumstances under which the crime was com-
mitted will be fresh in the recollectien of the public.
The prisoner had cohabited with the deceased for a con-
siderable time, the ceremony of marriage having been
previously gone through between them, but upon her
discovering that the culprit had a wife living, she re-
fused to reside with him any longer, and in a fit
of desperation and passion he shot her, and for
this act he forfeited his life. Notwithstanding the fact
of his having destroyed her life, there appears to be no
doubt that he entertained the deepest affection for the
unhappy young woman, and he has never ceased to ex-
press his deep remorse at the crime, and he accounts for
his conduct by saying that he was driven almost to
frenzy, and that he did not know what he was doing at
the time he committed the offence. He, however, de-
clared on several occasions that it was not true as stated
by one of the witnesses at the trial, that he had shown
three pistol bullets to her a considerable time before
the murder was committed, and that he at the same
time said that he only purchased the pistol on the day
before the act was consummated, in the Westminster-road,
and that on the same day he bought the bullets and
powder at another shop in Fleet-street, and that he had I
no bullet in his possession until this time, and that he
committed the offenVe under a sudden impulse.
The prisoner, it has been already stated, served in two
cavalry regiments, and, as he was a man of some educa-
tion, and, in particular, a very good penman, he speedily
obtained the rank of corporal, and was for some time at
the military school to be trained as an army school-
master, but it appeared that he did not conduct himself
properly, and he deserted, and was branded as such with
the letter D, and after he was dismissed from the army,
he obtained a livelihood by his trade, which was that of
a painter and grainer, and at which, it is said, he was
very expert, and able to earn good wages. Since his
conviction he has conducted himself in a most becoming
manner, and was constantly engaged in apparently most
fervent prayer, and he paid the most earnest attention to
the exhortations of the Rev. Mr. Davis' the chaplain of
the gaol. During his confinement he has been visited
by one of his brothers, the only relative he has in
London, and on Friday his child by the unhappy deceased
also was brought to the gaol by her grandmother, and it
is rather a singular coincidence that she attained her
second year on the very day her unhappy parent died on
the scaffold.

The culprit went to bed on Sunday night about ten
o'clock, and it appears that he then slept soundly until
past four, when he got up and dressed, and engaged
himself in reading the Bible until he was visited by the
Rev. Mr. Davis, wtth whom he continued in prayer for
a considerable time, and he acknowledged the justice of
his sentence and expressed his readiness to meet his
fate. For a con.iderable time after his conviction the
culprit exhibited a great deal of despondency, but as the
fatal moment drew nearer his confidence and firmness
appeared to increase, and he endured the fearful ordeal
he had to pass through with becoming fortitude.
Mr. Alderman and Sheriff Lawrence, and Mr. Sheriff
Jones, arrived at the gaol shortly before eight o'clock,
and they at once proceeded to the pressroom, accompa-
nied by Mr. Jonas, the governor of Newgate, and other
officials. After the culprit had been pinioned, he prayed
for a short time in a loud firm voice, and uttered a
fervent request to the Almighty that he might be par-
doned for the sins he had committed, and particularly for
the henious crime for which he was to suffer. He had
previously handed a written paper to Mr. Sheriff Law-
rence; but it appeared to be composed merely of
religious matters, and it was not considered advisable
that it should be made public. Just before eight
o'clock, the mournful procession passed from the
press-room to the Scaffold, and just as the culprit was
about to go up the steps he turned round and shook
hands with the sher. ffs, and thanked them for their
kindness to him, and he then walked on to the scaffold
with a firm step. The moment he was seen by the
crowd, there was a loud shout, and several persons were
heard to call out, 'Where's the sweep allusion to
the man Gardner, who had been respited, and a good
many persons, at the same time, expressed their opinion
that the greater criminal of the two had escaped.
When the bolt was drawn, the culprit appeared to
struggle convulsively for a few seconds, and then all
was over.

After hanging the usual time, the body was cut down
and placed in a shell, and in the course of the day it
was buried in one of the passages of the gaol by the side
of Catherine Wilson, the poisoner.
The number of persons present at the execution was
not considerable, but there were a larger number of
women among them than usual.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

When the intelligence was spread that Gardner's life
was to be spared, it was supposed that the gathering
would not be so great as on the occasion of Mrs. Wilson's
execution. Happily this expectation was fully realise I.
The crowd, we should think, did not contain more than
eight or ten thousand persons. A good many of the
windows commanding a view of the scaffold were
without tenants. We noticed that several well-
dressed women were at some of the windows
that were occupied, and that the opera glasses
were as usual in requisition, but certainly much less
educated or genteel curiosity touching Cal&aft's mani-
pulations and their results was manifested than Irr-id
been displayed a month ago. It was said that £4 were
asked for a room with three windows on the Ludgate-
hill side of the gallows. We wonder if the landlords of
the houses near the scaffold claim any additional rent on
the ground of the very peculiar advantages which their
tenants enjoy. At midnight at least a hundred persons
had taken up their position near the gallows with the
view of remaining till all was over. It would not,
we think, be any great libel on them to say that they
chiefly belonged to the classes who resided in the
fetid court pointed out to Alton Locke by Sandy
Mackay—' thieves, prostitutes, or worse.' Between
seven and eight the crowd was very noisy. A band of
preachers had tatz en up their stand on the Smithfield
side of the scaffold, and in a style which resembled that
of Mr. Richard Weaver loudly exhorted all within
hearing to instant repentance. One of the body gave
out for the text—John, 3rd chapter, 14th verse, 'As
Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness,' &c. The
preacher, with a rud- el, .quence, drew a contrast between
the man who was about to suffer for his own crime and
the Saviour who had suffered for the sins of mankind.
Let us hope that the seed which was cast on a truly
stony soil was not altogether lost.
The crowd as a whole behaved neither better nos
worse than other crowds of the same description had
done before.

ZOIITHERN WAY OF CLINCHTNG AN ARGUMENT.—
Under this heading a paragraph was given in the Daily
News a few days ago, describing a scene in a railway
carriage, where one of the passengers was from the
Southern States of America, and the other was a Man-
chester man, and where an argument on-slavery ended
in the former seizing his antagonist by the throat. The
paragraph was copied into a Manchester paper, and has
called forth a letter from the friend of the Southerner,
in which he professes to give a fairer version of the affair.
In substance his letter corroborates all that was stated
in the Daily News, except that it alleges further, as the
cause of the assault, that the Manchester gentleman, in
defending the conduct of General Butler, cast an impu-
tation upon the conduct of the women of the South.
The letter then goes on to say :--` The Southerner then
did take him by the throat. Afterwards, knowing he
had done wrong, under any provocation, to commit such
an assault in this country, he at once offered as repara-
tion £lO, to be given to the Lancashire Relief Fund;
but the gentlemen in the same carriage, who knew the
provocation, very properly would not admit of such a
proceeding, and there the matter ended.'
FATHER THAMES AND THE SESSlON.—Parliamentary
notices have been given for next Session for private
Bills for new bridges to be built apposite the Tower,
opposite St. Paun, opposite the Temple steamboat pier,
opposite Cheyne-walk, Chelsea, and at Wandsworth,
Hampton, Walton, and Shepperton.. The Metropolitan
Board of Works have given notice for continuing the
embankment on the north side of the river to Queen-
hithe, on the westernside of Southwark-bridge, and for a
new street from that point to the Mansion-house, and also
for an embankment on the Surrey side from the foot of
Chelsea suspension-bridge to near London-bridge.
The christening. of the -son of Prince Napoleon and
the Princess Clothllde is to take place in the course of the
month.

DEATH OF A CAVALRY VETERAN.—Died, en the 9th
instant, at the Cavalry Barracks, Cahir, Crimean
Bob,' the oldest troop horse in the British cavalry.
This veteran commenced his career in the 15th Hussars,
and on their embarkation for India was transferred to
the 14th Light Dragoons, and from that regiment to
the 11th Hussars in like manner, when the 14th were
ordered on foreign service. He first joined the army
on the 2nd October, 1E33, making a total of military
service of nearly thirty years, during which period he
was all through the Crimean campaign, and was ridden
in the Memorable charge of Balaklava, and at the
battles of Alma and Inkerman, by the present farrier-
major of the regiment, and during the whole of the
campaign was never once struck off duty through
sickness. On the return of the regiment to England
he was shown to his Royal Highness the General
Coramtnding-in-Chief, who would not allow him to be
Cast; but ordered him to be retained in the regiment
until his death, which occurred on Sunday morning,
from ad age and general decay, to the sincere regret
of all ranks of the regiment, from the old Col. down to
the youngest recruit. • -

articles.title: SMITHFIELD CLUB CATTLE SHOW.
articles.text:
SMITHFIELD CLUB CATTLE SHOW.

It is not long since the majority of our country cousins
left London, and soon, to the delight of theatrical lessees,
music hall proprietors, and lodging-house keepers, they
will be amongst us ones more. The great Cattle Show of
the Smithfield Club will be opened on the Bth of Decem-
cer ; and there can be no doubt that the agriculturists
who used to come in swarms to Baker-street will find
their way to the New Agricultural Hall, Islington.
Several excursion trains will be started by the direc-
tors of the Great Western, Great Northern, and other
railways; and a special omnibus service, to and from
all parts of the nsetropolis is being arranged. The
building in which the show is to be held is thrice
as large as the former premeiss of the club, and
is, indeed, one of the noblest halls in London.
The area embraced by it will be nearly three
acres, and the arrangements that are now in rapid pro-
gress will turn the whole of this space to the best
account. After glancing at the exterior of the building,
at its Italian facade, and its two towers, the visitor
who enters from the Liverpool-road will find himself in
the main hall, which is no less than 384 feet in length,
by 217 in breadth. The glass roof, which is 76 feet in
height, has a central span of 125 feet; and the hall is
Eurrounded by galleries, which are 36 feet wide; and
to which access is obtained by means of five sets of
double staircases. Passing onwards to the other end
of the building, a spacious apartment, known as
the Minor Hall,' is reached. It is a hundred feet
square, and is intended entirely for the reception
of the pigs. Some idea of the dimensions of the
building may be afforded by the mention of the
facts that about a thousand tons of iron have been
used in its construction ; that nine miles of iron
sash-bar have been required; that there are an acre of
glass and two acres of slating in the roof; and that the
gallery space exceeds an acre. The roof, which is light
and graceful for its size, will help to ensure abundant
light during the day, and at night the place will be lit
by 14 large central gaseliers, each containing 48 lights,
and 60 smaller ones with 24 lights each. The towers
have been constructed with a special regard to the
requirements of ventilation, and the hollow iron pillars
serve as drains from the roof to the basement. In case
of fire, a reservoir capable of containing 50,000 gallons
of water is at hand. Profiting by the experience
of the Exhibition, the proprietors have bestowed
unusual care in providing minor but still impor-
tant conveniences and facilities for the visitors—
such, for instance, as dressing-rooms, reading-rooms,
writing•rooms, and the like; and the refreshment
department has been entrusted to the caterer for
the Grand Stand at Epsom and for the recent Agri-
cultural Show at Battersea. The awards of prizes will
be made on Saturday, December 6, and on the opening
day, Monday, the Bth, the charge for admission will be
five shillings. On the four other days of the show it
will only be a shilling. The building is now a scene of
bustle and animation. Much has been done already,
but much still remains to do. The light and elegant
iron stalls for the reception of the sheep and cattle are
being placed in position, and the galleries are already
in a fit state to receive the implements that will be
exhibited there. The most will doubtless be made of
the three weeks that still remain ror preparations, and,
with the energy that is now being displayed, the time
will be amply sufficient for the work. The prizes to be
given will amount to £2,000, and the entries of cattle
are nearly double those of the previous show.
The cattle will be divided into twenty-nine classes,
to which, in the aggregate, no less a sum than £1,155 in

The Paris Ifoniteur publishes the following:—
'The London Gazette publishes the text of the dispatch
addressed by Lord Russell to Lord Cowley, her Bri-
tannic Majesty's Ambassador at Paris, in reply to the
dispatch of M. Droun de Lhuys on American affairs.
The correspondence from St. Petersburg also gives u,
the substance of the reply of Prince Gortschakoff. Da,
English dispatch renders full homage to the sentiments
which dictated the step taken by the Emperor's
Government. It shows, on the part of the English
Government, a lively desire to act in concert with
France. While declining at present the co-operation
offered to it, it is exclusively occupied with the chances
more or less favourable, which the proposal of the
French Government might meet with in the United
States. It is not a refusal; it is an adjournment.
'A similar judgment may be passed upon the Russian
dispatch. It renders full justice to the idea of con-
ciliation and of humanity which has inspired the
Government of the Emperor, and, if necessary, pro-
mises the moral support of Russia to any measure
attempted at Washington. At St. Petersburg, as at
London, it is the internal condition of the United
States which postpones any resolution in the sense of
the French proposition.
In fact, the manner in which an cffer of good ser-
vices may be taken into account in America deserves
great consideration; but, if our information is correct,
the hesitations of the Cabinets of London and of St.
Petersburg are likely soon to terminate. A feeling
prevails in America, in the North as well as in the
South, desirous of peace, and that feeling gains ground
daily. The elections now taking place in the Northern
States are a proof of the progress of that feeling, the
supporters of which are obtaining great advantage,
and it will probably have a majority in the next Con-
gress.'

articles.title: BC.RGL.d.R SHOT BY A LADY.
articles.text:
A BC.RGL.d.R SHOT BY A LADY.

A very extraordinary case occurred in Derbyehireon
the 12th instant. Mr. Fox received a report from
Superintendent Shaw, of a burglary having been com-
mitted at the house of Mr. Norman, of Howich End,
Whaley Bridge, Derbyshire. The entrance was effected
through the house shutters, which were opened with a
'jemmy,' and three men, armed and masked, ob-
tained unmolested admission to the dining-room.
At half-past three Mrs. Norman was disturbed by a
strange noise, and having listened for a few seconds
determined to leave her bed and discover the cause.
She therefore partially dressed herself, and, armed with
a revolver, went down stairs, and upon reaching the
front room she found a man using a lighted candle and
wearing a mask. Mrs. Norman maintained her com-
posure with wonderful nerve; and, taking a good aim,
fired and hit the burglar in the breast. The shot
served as an alarm, and instantly the wounded
burglar was dragged through the window (bleeding
and groaning) by his alarmed companions who were
on the watch. The effect of the shot was such that
the wounded man was observed by Mrs. Norman
to fall against the wall of the room, and it is suspected
by the police that the wound may have proved fatal.
Mr. Fax has left Derby to take the superintendence of
the chase of the wounded burglars, and there are ,
strong hopes that the offenders may be discovered. It
will be remembered that in February, 1857, a burglary
was committed at the house of the Rev. J. Nodder, in
this county, and that the rev. gentleman (a very old
man) shot at and wounded severely a man named
Wootton, alias 'Shog,' who was apprehended at Bir-
mingham with considerable skill and courage by the
present chief constable of Birmingham, Mr. George
Glossop, and subsequently transported for twenty-five
years.

The Turin correspondent of the Times sends news
of an extraordinary victory by a strong band of
brigands:— _

very painful sensation has been caused throughout
the country by the tidings of the massacre of• a detach-
ment of 40 infantry men of the royal army by a band
of 200 brigands near St. Severo, in the province of
Capitanata. The unlucky soldiers had been led into
an ambush by a spy, who informed them that ten
brigands were lurking in a wood called 11 Bosco della
Grotta, between Santa Croce di Magliano and Maglianico.
Surrounded by a force five times their own number, in
the thick of the forest, the brave men endeavoured
to cut their way through the midst of them. Twenty-
one of them were shot or cut down on the spot,
thirteen were taken prisoners and burnt alive at no
great distance in a straw loft. Among the latter was
the officer in command of the detachment, Captain
Rota, a Garibaldian, who was one of the famous
Thousand of Marsala. It seems that no less than 800
brigands, all mounted, are at this present moment in-
festing the open plains of Puglia, and especially the
province of Capitanata. It never happens, however,
that these ruffians obtain any success over the royal
troops, or even await an encounter with them. The
troops, nevertheless, are worn out and disgusted, if not
dispirited, and the population so utterly demoralised
by the incredible sufferings to which the continuance
of the scourge of brigandage exposes them, that no
less than one-fourth of the lands of the provinces are
out of cultivation.

articles.title: CROWDED STATE OF TURIN.
articles.text:
THE CROWDED STATE OF TURIN.

If any reason, or string of reasons, were wanting—
writes the Turin correspondent of The Times—to excuse
Italian anxiety on the subject of that most abominable
Roman question, sufficient, I believe, might be drawn
from the condition of the present Italian capital. The
town of Turin has been most uncomfortably out-
grown by its population. It is not merely that apart-
ments, furnished or unfurnished, are let out at
a rent eight and ten times higher than it was
only four or five years ago—the real grievance is
that no accommodotion whatever is to be had for love
or money. Those who have a suite of a few wretched
holes, or 'members' as they call them, to let, not
only put forth exorbitant demands as to prices, but
insist on long leases of nine, or twice and thrice nine,
and, at all events, no less than three years. Turin is
revelling in its unexpected, unbounded, but, as many
anticipate, transient and. fleeting prosperity. Its
citizens are eating, drinking, and merry-making, for
to-morrow they die P Carnival is the season for
selling masks, and hay must be made while the sun
shines. To-day all Italy is thronging upon Turin;
next week, or next month, or next year, Government
will shut up shop and move oft to another city. The
subjects of Victor Emmanuel will come by their own,
Parliament will meet on the Capitol, the Court be
lodged. in the Quirinal, and grass grow in the streets
of Turin, as it does in those of Ferrar.

Mr. Marsh, the American Minister, an accom-
plished and amiable gentleman, after running the
round of the few vacant lodgings in the city, is off to
Pegli, or some other place in the neighbourhood of
Genoa, in the utter impossibility of conveniently
houseing his family near the Government to which he
is accredited. Sir James Hudson, the highly respected
and universally beloved English Minister, has been
compelled to give up his splendid residence at the Palazzo
Sangiorgio, in Ambassadors'-street, because his laiy.ilord
O k
wanted to pin him down to a nine years' lease, he
sanguine friend of Italy thinks he may have to ' up
and be off to some mansion in the Corso long bete e one
ninth of that period is out. A third diplomatic gentle-
man is too happy to rusticate at a villa near Alpignano,
at an hour's railway distance from his office, because
the inhospitable town has not a roof to offer him to
shelter his head. And now winter is closing in, Par-
liament is to be re-opened, and more than 400 deputies
with above 200 senators, are wandering about the
streets, carpet bag in hand, some of them with wife and
children at their heels, aryi lucky are those who can
get a third floor at 1,00011. (40) a month, and who are
able to afford it!

articles.title: ANOTHER SHOCKING ATTEMPT TO
articles.text:
ANOTHER SHOCKING ATTEMPT TO

MURDER A WIFE.

A rather short slender man, well dressed, named.
James Wadden, age twenty-nine, and who gave his
address as of 42, Salisbury-place, Lock's-fields, and who
described himself as a hairdresser, was brought to the
Marylebone Police-court on the 17th, in the custody of
Mr. Charles Burrows inspector D division, Marlin 267,
and Wilkins 244 D, Charged with cutting the throat of
his wife with intent to murder her, at No. 3, New
Church-street, Edgware-road, the same being a coffee-
show kept by a Mr. Cololey.
The court and its precincts were so crowded that an
extra body of police had to be sent from Marylebone-
lane station to keep the passages clear. It may be as
vrell to state here that the prisoner and his wife went
into the coffee-shop the previous night, and after a little
while went up to bed to a room on the second floor back.
After they had been up there about an hour Mr. Cobley
was disturbed by loud screams, and on going up and
entering the room he saw the prisoner and his wife, and
at a short distance off an open razor and a small bag
capable of holding such an instrument. On his (Mr.
Cobley's) asking who had done it, alluding to the cut in
her throat, prisoner said his wife had done it herself.
The wife, from whose wound the blood was flowing
copiously, smiled, and with a perfect look of reason,
shook her head, as she could not speak, to indicate
No.' The police were instantly summoned, and
Inspector Burrows at once called in Dr. Graves of
Newcastle-place, Edgware-road, and Dr. Kirby, of 77,
Connaught-terrace, Hyde Park, who promptly attended,
and whilst they were attending the poor unfortunate
woman expressed silently to the inspector that they
considered it a hopeless case, and recommended the
magistrate's attendance to take her deposition. Mr.
Burrows at once went and summoned Mr. Yardley, who
attended by the side of the bed, about a quarter to one
in the morning, and took the following deposition from
the woman :
On the question being put as to whether she could
speak she gave a slight shake of the head, significant
of No.' Appearing calm and rational she was asked
if she could write, when, with a nod of her head, not
without evident pain, she signified Yes.' Mr. Yardley
then asked her if she was able to answer through the
means of the pencil any Questions which might be put
to her. With a painful nod of the head she answered
in the affirmative.
Her depositions in reply to his Worship's questions
were then as follows :—My name is Maria Colchester
Harriet Wadden. On my oath I live at the Pitt's Head,
High-street, Portland Town, with my father. Last
night he took a razor out of a bag, and I did not think
the prisoner meant to touch me. Ie drew it across ray
throat. He said nothing at all at the time. The bag
produced is what he took the razor from. He has before
threatened to do it.
Prisoner was here informed that he might put any
questions to his wife.
Prisoner then asked her it he had done it? '

The Wife replied that he had.
Prisoner: I did not do it, so help me God. He then
asked her if she had not upon one occasion cut her own
throat?

The Wife (through the medium of the pencil) : I did
cut my throat twelve months ago.
This being the whole of the statement of the wife
taken upon that occasion, the magistrate returned home,
and the prisoner was conveyed; to the station-house,
from whence he was removed on Monday morning to
the court.

During the sitting of the Court further intimation
was given to Mr. Yardley that his presence was re-
quired to attend upon the female, and in company with
Mr. Phillips, chief clerk, and the two medical gentle-
men, he proceeded to where the poor woman was lying.
On the prisoner's arrival at the house in custody, all
parties proceeded to the second-floor back room. On
the bed lay the prisoner's wife, slightly lifting herself
on her left side, appearing quite collected, with bandages
round her throat, and her hair dishevelled, and blood
over her night-dress. As each one entered the room
she kept her gaze upon them, and when her gaze met
that of her husband she averted her head, and he (the
husband) clasped his hands together, and pulled a white
cambric handkerchief from corner to corner.

Mr. Graves and Mr. Kirby took their positions on
each side of the bed and administered stimulants to the
wife, when, in reply to the following questions she
wrote, lying on her left side, upon the desposition paper,
and which had been placed on a piece of board, kindly
upheld by Mr. Phillips. The answers were written in
a firm, clear, and expeditious hand.
Mr. Yardley: Has he ill-used you before?
Wife: My father can tellyou how he has ill-used me.
Mr. Yardley: Did he ever ill-treat you before?
Wife: Yes.

Mr. Yardley: Say when and where?
Wife: By giving me black eyes soon after our mar-
riage, and has done so repeatedly since, which is three
years next month.
(Stimulants, owing to the prostrate condition of the
wife, had here to be administered and her face sponged.)
She again continued: Within a week of my marriage-
day he gave me a black eye, which is three years ago
the third of next month.

Mr. Yardley: Did he ever attempt to cut your throat
before; if 80, say when?
Wife: About two years ago, as I was leaving my
father, he took a penknife from his pocket and said he
would be the death of me. At that time I separated from
him, and went and lived with my father for six weeks.
Mr. Yardley (to prisoner) : Do you wish to ask your
wife any question?
Pisoner (looking towards the bed where his wife was
lying, and from whom he had withheld his face) mut-
tered something incoherently, and
His worship again repeated the question, when
Prisoner said she was tipsy last night.
Mr. Yardley asked the wife if she was tipsy last
night.
Wife wrote: I was not tipsy last night.

-
Mr. Yardley: Is there any other question which you
would like to put to your wife?
-•,.
Prisoner: She knows I did not do it.
Mr. Yardley: You misunderstand me. Have you
any other question?
Prisoner: She knows I did not do it. I have none.
(Sobbing, "Oh dear, oh dear.")
After he had become somewhat calm, prisoner said:
Some time ago my wife became acquainted with another
gentleman, and she said the first time she could she
would put me out of the way. Time after time she has
said this.

Mr. Yardley: I will ask her that.
In reply to his warship the wife said, through the
same medium, that she bad never said such words.
Prisoner: Oh, you know you have. You said that
last night in the street. Hundreds of times you have
said that. (Crying and wringing his hands.) Have
not you and Esther said the same thing? Oh, do tell
the truth.

In reply to Mr. Yardley, she (the wife) again said
she had never used such words.

Prisoner: Your father and you have told me you
would have me put away, and your father has told his
customers so.

The examination was here deemed to have gone on
long enough, and the poor creature signed her name to
the depositions, and sne was left again in quiet.
Prisoner was then conveyed in a cab back to the
police-court, from whence he was remanded for a week.

articles.title: NEW ZEALAND CHIEFS.
articles.text:
THE NEW ZEALAND CHIEFS.

The following address has been forwarded by Gover-
nor Sir George Grey to the Duke of Newcastle for
transmission to Her Majesty :
Oh, Victoria, our Mother !—We greet you! You,
who are all that now remains to recall to our recollec-
tion Albert, the Prince Consort, who can never again be
gazed upon by the people.
We, your Maori chiliren, are now sighing in sorrow
together with you, even with a sorrow like to yours.
All we can now do is to weep together with you. Oh,
our good mother, who hart nourished us, your ignorant
children of this island, even to this day!
We have just heard the crash of the huge-headed
forest tree which has untimely Ulan, ere it had attained
its full growth of greatness.

Oh, good lady-, pray look with favour on our love.
Although we may have been perverse children, we
have ever loved you.
This is our lament.
Great is the pain which preys on me for the loss of
ray beloved.
Ah, you will now lie buried among the other de-
parted Kings!

They Will leave you with the other departed heroes
of the land.
With the dead of the tribes of the multitude of 'Ti
Mani.

'Go fearless then, 0 Pango, my beloved, in the path
of death; for no evil slanders can follow you.
Oh, my very heart! Thou didst shelter me from
the sorrows and ills of life.
Oh, my pet bird, whose sweet voice welcomed my
glad guests!
Oh, my noble pet bird, caught in the forests of
Rapaura !
Let, then, the body of my beloved be covered with
Royal purple robes!
'Let it be covered with all-rare robes!
The great Rewa, my beloved, shall himself 'bind
these round thee.

And my ear-ring of precious jasper shall be hung in
thy ear.
'For, oh! my most precious jewel, thou art now lost
to me.

Yes, thou, the pillar that Clidst support my palace,
haat been borne to the skies.

Oh, my beloved! you used to stand in the very prow
of the war-canoe, inciting all others to noble deeds.
Yes, in thy lifetime thou wast great.
'And no w thou hast departed to the place where even
all the mighty must at last go.
Where, oh physicians, was the power of your
remedies?
What, oh priests, availed your prayers?
For I have lost my love; no more can he revisit
this world.

articles.title: ITALIAN BRIGANDAGE.
articles.text:
ITALIAN BRIGANDAGE.

If you are not tired of brigand stories I will give
you another, the scene of which was also near Ebo
There were labourers engaged in some kind of occupa-
tion not far from a large fountain in that neighbour-
hood, who filled up the intervals between work and
their devotions to the Madonna with a little brigand-
age on their own account. When a carriage appeared
the zappa or the trowel was abandoned, and then
muskets were taken up from under the sod. The
travellers were rifled, a horse or a man shot, as the
case might require, and then these industrious fellows
resumed their ordinary labours. This had gone on for
' some time, and no one could trace out the guilty parties.
As for the padrone, he could answer for his men
as being always occupied. One of the band, how-
ever, who divided the affections of a woman with
another man who was not of the band, murdered his
rival one fine evening, and the woman was arrested.
Under menace of being shot if she did not reveal the
names of the murderer and his accomplices, she betrayed
six of the latter. A week after she was again arrested,
and then sentenced to be shot if she did not also betray
he capo. Agreed. In the dark of the evening she
goes to her trysting place, followed by Carabineers,
mounts a tree, and gives a whistle. Immediately the
ground rises not far off, and the capo emerges from his
subterranean hiding. place, which had been ingeni-
ously covered over with boughs of trees, leaves and
sods. The woman descends, and it is unne•
cessary to say that the ardour of their embraces
was cooled down by the rush of the Carabineers, who
arrested both. These are true stories, and a hundred
others might be repeated which would beat Mrs. Rad-
cliffe out of the field; but the moral of them is this,
that, thanks to the Bourbons, society is completely
disorganised in Southern Italy. There is no public or
private morality; the labourer in the country districts
is half workman, half brigand, and if there be any
difference between him and the employe or the galantu-
omo of the towns, it is that while the former uses
violence the latter resort to the refined arts of lying
and cunning. It is a wise resolution of the Govern-
ment to send more cavalry into the provinces, and the
fine regiment called Saluzzo,' which was reviewed by
La Marmora last week, is to leave for Puglia.—Times
Correspondent.

articles.title: MURDER OF BRITISH SEAMEN.
articles.text:
MURDER OF BRITISH SEAMEN.

In September, 1859, the Kitty, of Newcastle, was
lost in Hudson's Straits, by being nipped in the ice.
Five of her crew, who got into a small boat, after en-
during great suffering by exposure to the cold, suc-
ceeded in reaching a Moravian missionary station,
where they were hospitably entertained, and three of
them sent to their homes in England next summer.
But of the fate of the master of this vessel, Mr. Ellis,
and the remainder of the crew, who left the ship in a
longboat, nothing has been heard until the arrival of
the vessels from the Hudson Bay stations this autumn,
when the sad intelligence has been brought that the 11
poor fellows fell into the hands of unfriendly Esqui-
maux, and were murdered for the sake of their
blankets. The missionaries at Okak, writing to the
widow of the master of the vessel in August last, say
—‘ It is with grief, madam, we must inform you
that it is, alas, only too true that the long-
boat, with her master and crew, arrived at Ungava
Bay, but that none of the men survive. Last winter
Esquimaux from Ungava Bay visited our northern-
most settlement, Hebron, who related that in the
winter of 1859 60, several Europeans in a boat landed
at the island called Akpatok, in Ungava Bay. They
lived with the Esquimaux until about January, upon
what the latter could provide for them; but then,
most likely when their provisions became short, the
Esquimaux attacked them when they were asleep
and killed them, stabbing them with their knives.
There is no doubt of these really being the
men from the Kitty, btcause the Esquimaux knew
there had been another boat with five men belonging
to them, whom they deemed lost. They said one man
of the murdered company had very frost-bitten feet,
and him the Lquimaux would not kill by stabbing,
but showed him a kind of heathen mercy, as they put
him into the open air until he was dead by severe
cold.' It seems that these unfortunate men had been
murdered for the sake of the blankets they had with
them. It would appear that one of the Esquimaux
wanted to save the three Europeans who lodged with
him, but they met the same fate as !heir companions.
The tribe who have committed this murder do not
appear to have been brought in contact with the Euro-
pean missions; and the friendly tribe who brought the
information in to Hebron further informed the Mora-
vian missionaries at that place that a little further
north from Ungava Bay a.whole crew, consisting in all
of about 40 men, were enticed on shore and then killed
by the Esquimaux.
