Oarittits,

Garibaldi said, Rome cannot be save,ll second time
by the "Cackling of geese.''
It is said that next session there will be some pro-
posal to modify the law of capital punishment, which
at present is in a very unsatisfactory site.
There is no truth (says the Observer) in the rumoured
retirement of Lord Elgin from the government of
India. Lady Elgin left town on Saturday for Pdartesilles
en routs for India, to join her husband, the Governor-
General.
The Birmingham Chamber of Commerce has had it
in contemplation to invite the Chancellor of the Ex-
chequer to pay a visit to the town.
We understand that the gay and impudent anony-
mous horsewoman who made a boast of her powers of
fascinating a married man, and luring him to quit a
happy home and young wife, has left the victim at
Naples, and returned to England. The pourquoi was
that the cash was all spent.
The Society of Painters in Water Colours will
shortly open a winter exhibition at their Gallery in
Pall-mall East. It is expected that this will comprise
sketches and studies from nature, first thoughts and
compositions for pictures, &c.
An unlooked-for supply of cotton has suggested itself
to the spinners at Rouen in promoting a general battue
among the owners el mattresses and bedding stuffed
with that article, in almost every household. Immense
stores of the welcome material have come to market
from these hidden recesses.
George 11. being informed that an impwient printer
was to be punished for publishing a spurious Royal
speech, answered, that he hoped the man's punishment
would be of the mildest sort, because, so far as he ,under-
stood either of them, he liked the spurious specch much
better than his own.
The most extraordinary rumours have been heard
as to the health and condition of the Sultan. That his
Majesty is ill there is no doubt, but it is only a clever
trick to complicate matters by the addenda we have
heard, and which it is only respectful and fair not to
quote.
During the past week the Conncil of the Duehy of
Cornwall made up the financial accounts previous to the
Prince of Wales taking personal possession, and found
the sum total derived from the Duchy amounts to about
£500,000.
It is believed in Paris—not in Gr,el; circles but in
other quarters—that the Due de Leuchtenberg will be
elected to the throne of Otho. It is said the King and.
Queen have left behind them some compromising papers
relative to the Crimean war.
A Prussian citizen has recently had his son brought
before the legal authorities, and compelled the erasure
of his name to a political address which w,-s not in
accordance with the parental views. The son was not
quite twenty-one' and consequently an infant. This
was performing the part of governor rather auto-
cratically.
Upon the first signal of a row at Athens, some
Italian volunteers wanted to leave for the scene of ac-
tion; but their ardour was quickly silenced by an
intimation that their company was not wanted, and that
Greeks for Greece sufficed.

An .order has been received from the War Office that
commanding officers of Volunteers are not to allow the
subscriptions of Volunteers to stand over beyond six
months from the time when first applied for, but are to
take prompt legal steps for the recovery of the same.
A paintinc, is on view at present in Brussels, said to
be the work of Raffaelle • it represents the death of St.
Joseph, and is about eighteen inches kn.- by sixteen
wide. The Abbe Nicolle has the merit of having dis-
covered this work of art at Rome during the month of
May in the present year.
Mr. Gambart has given two important commissions
to the great Belgian artists, MM. Leys and Gallait. To
the former he is to pay £B,OOO for the preliminary pic-
tures he has painted for the frescoes which he is about
to paint at the Hotel de Ville, at Antwerp. To M.
Gallait he is to pay £4,000.f0r a large picture on 'The
Plague of Touraay.

Captain Jay, at the dinner of the Honourabb3
Artillery Company, on Monday, expressed a hope that
the Prince of Wales would, ere long, by her Majesty's
authority, be enrolled in the same record, and hold the
same rank in the Honourable Artillery Company, which
his Royal father had held before; also King George,
when Prince of Wales, the Duke of Sussex, and
William IV.

The International glories of art are gone; during their
reign they eclipsed the neighbouring show of the South
Kensington Museum, which had its great merit: it may
be almost said—in a real art sense—had greater merits.
It is not too late, we believe, to make the anzende to the
neglected one, and to reap a great deal of instruction
and entertainment. Walk over the way, ladies and
gentlemen—lose no time—will shortly close ; ' and then
you will regret that you have not seen what you might
have seen.

Accounts received from the cotton-ma.nufacturing
districts state that several manufacturers who had
continued to work notwithstanding the high price of the.
raw material, finding that their produce has not risen
in proportion, have closed their mills, having calculated
that it would be mere beneficial to sell the raw cotton on
hand than to manufacture it. [We thought the tempta-
tion would be too great.]
His Royal Highness Prince Louis of Hesse and the
Princess Alice's stay in England will be for about two
months. Prince Louis recently bought the Botanical
Gardens at Darmstadt, with a view of building a grand
palace on the site, which will be immediately com-
menced, and finished towards the end of next year.
Princess Alice is said to have acquired, by her affability,
and grace, the affection and sympathy of the whole popu-
lation of Darmstadt, notwithstanding that her residence
among them dates but from a recent period.
Professor Ansted, the eminent mineralogist, reports
the discovery at St. Cuthbert's, in the Mendip Hills,
about three miles from Wells, in Somersetshire' of a.
deposit of lead-producing debris of old mines and lead-
washings of ancient miners, filling up the bed of a
stream that flowed in former ages. This metallic lime,
of exceeding richness, amounts, he says, to 600,000 tons,
extends over twenty-five acres to the depth of thirty
feet, and is computed to be worth half-a-million of money
for the lead which it contains.

House rent is higher this season at Nice than it has
been known for many years, and house room very
scarce, so much so that the people who flock there every

articles.title: IVEG.RO RIOTS IN ST. VINCENT.
articles.text:
IVEG.RO RIOTS IN ST. VINCENT.

The following letter from St. Vincent, West Indies,
received by the last mail, brings news of a riot which at
one time assumea very alarming proportions. The
writer, who is a gentleman of position in the colony,
bore no inconsiderable part in the events he de-
scribes :

St. Vincent, Oct. 24.
You will be sorry to hear that a very serious dis-
turbance has occurred here, which has not been quelled
without difficulty and loss of life. For some time past it
has been the custom oa several estates here to issue to
the labourers employed on them rum, sugar, &c., in ad-
dition to their regular wages, and the withholding of these
allowances was the apparent cause of the first outbreak,
which took place about four weeks ago upon an estate on
the windward side of the island. The Labourers on that
property struck work, assembled ix large bodies, and
assaulted the overseer. A warrant for the apprehension of
the ringleader having been obtained, the police who
attempted to execute it were resisted and beaten. A
reinforcement of police was therefore marched to the
scene of the disturbance, but the mob, which consisted
of several hundred infuriated labourers of both sexes,
armed with cutlasses, fire-arms, and bludgeons, sur-
rounded the mansion-house on the estate in which the
police were posted, and where the attorney and his
family had taken refuge, and commenced yelling and
shouting and blowing conch shells, cuttiog the canes,
firing houses and cane fields, and, in short-, behaving
like madmen. The officer in command of the police,
feeling that his small force of twenty-four men was
unable to cope with such overwhelming numbers, com-
municated the state of affairs to Lieutenant Governor
Musgrave, who visited the estate in company with the
Attorney-General, the Hon. C. D. Stewart, and ad-
dressed the rioters, promising an inquiry into their
alleged grievances, upon which they dispersed appa-
rently satisfied.
A few days after a large body of labourers, among
whom were those who had committed the riot at Mount
Bentincls, collected, and visited several estates nearer
Kingstown, beating the managers and their families and
destroying the furniture and contents of their dwellings.
The colony being without any organized force, and the
persons in charge of estates being unable to rely upon the
assistance of the better disposed labourers, who were
forced by the rioters to join in their lawless proceedings,
it was impossible to oppose any resistance to the mob,
which had greatly increas4d, and was marching towards
Kingstown; destroying the houses and property of the
owners and managers of estates, and ill-treating every
one who came in its way. Every hour fugitives arrived
in the town, some severely injured, and many deprived
of all their property.
The danger became so imminent that Lieutenant-
Governor Musgrave at once placed the colony under
martial law, and a force of mounted and foot volun-
teers with some artillery and two small field-pieces,
about 150 in all, were, under the command of the Hon.
C. D. Stewart, posted about a mile from the town, so
as to check any advance of the rebels, who, it was un-
derstood, had planned the attack of Kingstown, where
there were a large number of ill-disposed persons ready
to rise and assist in the work of plunder and destruc-
tion. On Wednesday, the 2nd instant, the mounted
volunteers, in number about 20, were detached, under
the command of Major Van Heyningen, and proceeded
to an estate some six miles from Kingstown, where it
was understood the rioters were committing serious de-
predations. This small body of horsemen met a mob
of about 800 who were armed, and who drew up to
Roceive the volunteers; a charge was made, which the
rioters resisted for a few minutes, but then breaking
into disorder fled to a steep place where horses could
not follow them. Some of their number were left dead
on the spot, and several others were mortally wounded.
The police and moulted volunteers were subsequently
moved forward as far as Georgetown, about 20 miles
from Kingstown, but the rioters disappeared before them
and retired into the thick woods in the interior of the
island. This advance had the satisfactory effect of dis-
couraging some thousand laboureas who had procured
arms and were threatening the firing and plunder of
Georgetown, and in their progress the force took several
prisoners.
The Lieutenant-Governor had sent to Trinidad for a
man-of-war, and accordingly Her Majesty's ship Chal-
lenger, 22, Captain Kennedy, C. 8., arrived, and landed
her complement of Marines. Her launch was subse-
quently sent to visit the leeward coast, where, although
the labouring population were comparatively quiet and
orderly, several of the principal rioters were stated to be
concealed. The presence of the Challenger in the bay
had a very sedative effect on the malcontents in the town,
which had been guarded night and day by a large body
of special constables.
A detachment of her Majesty's 21st Regt. arrived
on the 12th from Barbadoes The rioters heir's.' thus
dispersed, and the ringleaders and their followers to the
number of 200 having been taken, martial law was
abolished on the 20th, and business and the cultivation
of estates are being resumed
From the confessions already made by some of the
prisoners, there remains no doubt that, while the first
outbreak arose apparently on account of the disconti-
nuance of the practice of issuing rum and sugar to the
labourers, it was taken advantage of to carry into exe-
cution a plot which has for some existed among the
lower classes of the black population, the object of
which was to seize and appropriate the several estates
in the island, and to dispose of the white and coloured
inhabitants; while it is also stated that a worse fate
awaited the female members of their families, some of
whom had actually, in anticipation of success, been
•allotted to the ringleaders of these scoundrels.
Much praise is due to the Lieutenant-Governor and
those acting under him for the decisive steps taken; and
the Legislature, which met yesterday, while passing
measures rendered necessary by this unforturate affair,
did not forget to acknowledge the exertions of his Excel-
lency, and those who have been mainly instrumental in
quelling this serious insurrection—the most serious this
Island has experienced in the present century.
It is estimated that it will have cost the colony not
less than £4,000, while the loss to the unhappy
planters, some of whom have lost their all, and some
have been injured for life, is most serious; added to
which, the suspension of business and of cultivation,
and the feeling of insecurity which must naturally
follow such an outbreak, are productive of great injury
to the colony.

articles.title: BLOW AT TIM AF_RICAY SLAVE
articles.text:
A BLOW AT TIM AF_RICAY SLAVE

TRADE.

(From the New York Times, Nov._l.)

Another important blow at the slave trade was dealt
yesterday in the United States Circuit Court in this
City, in the conviction of Albert Horn for lit ting out
the steamer City of Norfolk for that traffic. The evi.
deuce, as [given in court, showed that the case was a
most flagrant one. It showed that Horn bought the
vessel, paying 25,000 dols. for her; that she was run
on one voyage to Havana and back, and then was sent
to St. Thomas, having had some 25,000 dols. more of
repairs and, outfit put on board of her. At St. Thomas
the transfer, which is an almost universal accom-
paniment of these cases, took place, and the vessel,
after running th Barcelona (Venezuela), to get water
enough, sailed for the African coast, and on arriving
in the Bight of Benin took in eight hundred negroes
in broad daylight and sailed for Cuba, where she
arrived with them. Having discharged them into
boats the steamer was abandoned by her crew, but was
shortly afterwards captured by a Spanish man-of-war,
which also captured most of the negroes. Horn's de-
fence, of course, was that he had nothing to do with

LARGE DEER HORNS AND DEER.

Captain Horatio Ross writes as follows in answer to a
correspondent in the Field There is an old. castle
called Moritzburgh, about twenty miles from Dresden, in
which there is the most perfect collection of heads that
I have ever seen. Moritzburgh is an old bunting
chateau of the reigning family of Saxony. I visited it
about twenty-five years ago. In the great banqueting-
hall there are three tiers of heads; the lowest row has
twenty-five points, the next thirty-six, and the upper
row forty-two points. The horns have the colossal
proportions of the wapiti, and the points are very fine.
At one end of the room there is a head with either fifty
or sixty points, but I did not admire it so much as some
of the thirty-six pointers—they were the best; the points
of the head I allude to were small. In another room
there were elks' beads, and in a third a vast collection
of monstrosities—stags who had died fighting with their
horns locked together, &c. The old woman who had
charge of the chateau could not give me any informa-
tion as to when the deer had been killed, but she could
say positively that for fifty years no head had been
killed in the forest good enough to be hung up, as she
had been there for half a century. I think, however,
that we may infer from some pictures in the chateau
that the chasses where these deer were killed took place
a long time ago. The deer appear to have been col-
lected and surrounded by a high fence covered with
canvas; a stage was erected, whcre the great man sat,
with a band of music behind him; the deer were driven
past, while he shot them with bolts shot from a steel
cross-bow • there were bowers erected in various parts
of the enclosure, in which ladies were sitting, each at-
tended by cavaliers, and the ladies were represented
shooting the deer with small cross-bows. These pic-
tures give one a vivid and curious insight to the 'deer-
stalking' of the olden times. I should prefer the grey
mountains of Scotland, a good rifle in my hand, and one
of Alexander Ross's telescopes slung on my shoulders.
There are, however—or, at all events, there were five-
and-twenty years ago—some colossal stags still alive in
the forests of Germany and Hungary. About the period
I allude to I had the extraordinary good fortune to find
myself, pro tempore, lord and master of the fined !leer-
forest on the Continent: Prince Esterhazy, long the
Austrian Minister in this country, placed his forest in
Hungary at my disposal. I had it all to myself. I be-
lieve it was 120,000 acres in extent, and I had sixty jagers
at my command. I need not say how much I enjoyed iny-
self during the fortnight I spent in that glorious forest.
was not lucky enough to kill any of the monsters of the
forest—it was difficult to find them in a wiped of such
vast extent; but I shot many large deer, and one that
weighed thirty-six stone as be fell; he had an immense
head of fourteen points, with brow antlers fifteen inches
long. I saw on the walls of the shooting lodge heads
with twenty-five to thirty points, which were very little
inferior to the Moritzburgh heads, and which had been
shot a few years. The forest-master gave me a return
of deer killed in the last great chasse (about eight years
before I was there) : 1,008 deer were shot in five days,
one of which weighed 7001bs. A German pound is ten
per cent. heavier than the English pound, so that this
monarch of the forest weighed as he fell 770 English
pounds, or 55 stone. Great deer are also found in the
Carpathian mountains. I have never been there, but I
have seen heads which have been killed in these forests,
and they were enormous. This is all I know about
Continental deer.'

articles.title: LAW AS TO HIGH SHERIFFS.
articles.text:
THE LAW AS TO HIGH SHERIFFS.

A curious question has arisen about the privileges of
the Queen's Household in respect to the liability of the
officials to serve as High Sheriffs. At the nomination
before the Lords of the Privy Council, on Wednesday,
in the Court of Exchequer, Mr. Burnaby, who was
chosen for tie county of Leicester, sought to be excused
on the ground that he was one of the Gentlemen of her
Majesty's Privy Chamber, and, as such, was not liable
to serve, unless there was no other gentleman in the
county eligible for the office. Mr. Burnaby also
claimed, if retained on the list, to be excused serving
next year. As it was absurd to think there was no one
else eligible in the county of Leicester, the point raised
by Mr. Burnaby was a puzzler for my Lords,' who
evinced great reluctance to admit the claim of exemp-
tion, and so confirm and establish a privilege which,
perhaps, at present, is very doubtful, at least as far as
Officers of the Household of Mr. Burnaby's rank are
concerned. The matter ended for this time in a com-
promise. Mr. Burnaby stands excused for the present
—that is, from service next year; and before the next
nomination the Privy Council will be enabled to consult
authorities and precedents, and make up their minds
about the question at issue. There were some other
claims for exemption mad( at this nomination rather
curious in their way. One gentleman asked to be ex-
cused on the ground that he had only 2,000/. a-year,
which seemed to be fruitful of amusement to their lord-
ships. Another claimed exemption on the ground that
the estate was his wife's; but this the Lord Chancellor
overruled at once. A learned judge made a grave
mistake in making a presentment for a Welsh county;
for when he gave in three names it was found that one
of the gentlemen had been permanently excused from
serving the office, and the whole nomination became
incomplete. The Chancellor of the Exchequer kindly
came to the rescue by a suggestion that before the list
was submitted to the Queen the learned judge should
furnish the name of another gentleman for selection.—
Court Journal.

articles.title: IffP.ERIAL SPORT.
articles.text:
IffP.ERIAL SPORT.

A letter from Compiegne, dated Nov. 14, has the
following :—A stag hunt took place three days ago in
the forest of Laigue, where it was thought better sport
might be met with than here. The Emperor, who pre-
ceded the guests, drove in a light four-wheeled car-
riage direct to the Puits d'Orieans, where a number of
persons had assembled. His Majesty alighted and
walked about for some time among the crowd, talking
to several persons, particularly to M. Arachequesne,
Mayor of Compiegne. Just when the deer started, his
Majesty, who was in plain clothes, re-entered his car-
riage, while the Empress, the Princess Anna Mutat, and
Prince Joachim Murat, who were on horseback, fol-
lowed the hounds. After a rapid chase the stag threw
itself ints the Aisne, but being alarmed by the cries of
the persons assembled on the opposite bank, returned
to land and again took to the forest. The dogs were
for a time thrown off the scent, but afterwards re•
covered it, and the stag was at length come up with on
the banks of the river. It again plunged, but, unfor-
tunately, was killed by a shot from a rifle, and disap-
peared in the water. The body was not found until
the next day, when the curve took place as usual by
torchlight in the courtyard of the palace. Their
Majesties and most of the guests witnessed the scene
from the balcony. The next day the Emperor took a
walk through the town of Compeigne, accompanied by
General Fleury and MM. de Saulcv and Viollet-Leduc.
After going through a number -of the streets, and
visiting the Place de Motel de Ville, the Emperor
returned to the palace.

We are happy to announce the formation of another
company for the cultivation of cotton in this island.
The company is a Glasgow one, with a capital of £50,000
already subscribed. A large abandoned sugar estate has
been purchased in the lower part of the parish of Cla-
rendon, and operations have been already commenced in
the clearing of lands, &c.—Jamaica Guardian.
A Copenhagen journal states that at the last sitting
of the council of state the King of Denmark decided
on granting a local government to Holstein. It will
enter on its functions in the beginning of December,
and will be located in tho Duchy of Holstein, after
arrangements shall have been made for its transference
from Copenhagen. Count do Moltke will be president
of the Holstein government.
REGISTRAR-GENERAL OP SEA3IEN.—On the 11th
Captain Brown, R.N., C. 8., retired from his duties as
Registrar-General of Seamen—a post which he has filled
during the last 27 years with much benefit to the
mercantile community and to the country at large. To
this gallant officer, one of the now very few survivors of
the battle of Trafalgar, is entirely due the merit of
originating and establishing in all its details the great
scheme of the Naval Reserve, and in overcoming those
prejudices of the merchant seamen which so long kept
them from joining in the movement. How successful
these efforts have been is proved by the fact that the
Naval Reserve now numbers 15,000 picked able seamen,
—or, in other words, the best parts of the crews of 50
line-of-battle ships-__a larger force of able seamen than
England possessed at the close of her long war with
Napoleon. Captain Brown's retirement is deeply
regretted by all who have served under him, anti who,
before he finally quitted his arduous duties, took leave
of him with every mark of affectionate respect. The
vacant office of Registrar has been conferred by Mr.
Milner Gibson, on Mr. J. J. Mayo, assistant-accountant
at the Board of Trade, and one of the ablest subordinate
members of that department. Mr. Mayo was entrusted
in 1849 with organising and carrying out most of the
difficult details of the Merchant Shipping Act of the
previous year, and in doing so introduced the important
improvement of the Seamen's Savings-banks, which has
worked with such beneficial results at all our ports. The
details of this scheme were considered so admirable, and
so perfect in their chicks on fraud, that Mr. Gladstone
unhesitatingly adopted its provisions in his plan for the
Post-office Savings-banks, which, taken collectively, are
fast becoming one of the most important of our recent
institutions. Mr. Mayo was afterwards intimately
connected with the Naval Reserve, drawing up its forms
and regulations, &C., in which duty he showed such a
perfect acquaintance with the whole of this difficult
subject as to at once point him out to Mr. Gibson as the
most fitting successor he could choose to Capt. Brown,
whose retirement wee then talked 04

articles.title: METROPOLITAN TABERNACLE.
articles.text:
METROPOLITAN TABERNACLE.

On Sunday at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, the Rev.
C. H. Spurpeon announced that the additional subscrip-
tions received during the week in aid of the distress in
Lancashire had raised the amount of the collections
made at that place of worship on the previous Sabbath
to £735. He proposed to Keep it open for the receipt
of additional subscriptions during the whole of the
present week, and to give an account shortly of the
manner in which it had been disposed of. He further
announced that in about six weeks hence another
collection at morning and evening service, for the same
object, would be made at the tabernacle, when he hoped
the congregation would raise a sum equal in amount to
that they had now contributed.
CHRIST CHURCH, NORTH BRIXTON.

The Rev. James M'Connell liusey, the incumbeat of
this church, has made a very earnest and eloquent
appeal to his congregation in behalf of the distressed
Lancashire operatives, which resulted in the collection
of the liberal sum of £l4B 18s. id.

articles.title: MANCHESTER.
articles.text:
MANCHESTER.

The donations received on Saturday at the offices of
the Executive Committee of the Central Relief Fund
included one of 250 rabbits and 100 pheasants from the

articles.title: PRESTON.
articles.text:
PRESTON.

More extensive preparations for the relief of the poor
distressed operatives of Preston have to be made as their
poverty and destitution increase. A weekly, instead of
a fortnightly, distribution of coals has been found neces-
sary, and seven yards have just been engaged—one for
each ward and two for St. Peter's, where exists the most
distress. The dispensation of bedding and clothing
commenced on Saturday, and will now go on weekly for
some time on a large scale. A large number of applica-
tions for wearing apparel have already been received by
the Relief Committee, and the district visitors in the
various wards have been inquiring into the urgency or
otherwise of the cases presented to their notice. They
describe the urgency as very great, and, to hasten the
supply of the great want now experienced by the poor,
nine tailors, 62 seamstresses, and several shoemenders
have been engaged to repair the articles presented by
the benevolent. A costly present of clothing was on
Friday received at the Crooked-lane establishment from
Lady Talbot Clifton. Owing to the distribution of coals,
bedding, and clothing the weekly cost henceforth cannot
be less than £1,500. There has been added a depositary
for chaff and new beds, and some joiners have been
engacred making bedsteads.
The report of the Relief Committee, issued on Satur-
day mornino., shows another increase in the number of
cases relieved. The increase of cases is this week 416,
comprising 1,575 persons; and of the cost or value of
relief afforded, £79 10s. 4d. The total number of per-
sons relieved is upwards of 35,000, and the expenditure
for the week, including the sick kitchen and a small
portion of bedding and clothing, is £1,082. The bread
distributed is 31,540 loaves, of nearly 41b. each, weighing
altogether 56 tons 6cwt. lqr., 211 b. At the two soup-
kitchens in Crooked-lane and Walker-street 31,412
quarts of soup, 5,286 of `scouse,' or potato hash, and
1,335 quarts of coffee have been dispensed, including
what is sold as well as that given away by tickets. The
donations to the relief fund during the week have
amounted altogether to £2,600.
The overseers of the township of Preston are preparing
for the levying of a poor-rate for the half- year which
commenced on the Ist ult. Although the amount is not
yet definitively confirmed, it is to be the same as the last
rate-35., in the pound, making Os. for the year, which is
higher than was ever levied in Preston for a single year.

articles.title: WIGAN.
articles.text:
WIGAN.

The returns of the number of persons relieved this
week by boards of guardians and by Relief Committees
show that the worst stage of distress in Wigan has not
yet been reached. The officers and board on Friday re-
ported that there were 4,789 persons receiving outdoor
relief, an increase of 147 on the week, and one of 2,472
on the corresponding week of last year. The expenditure
had been £339 7s. 6d., or £2B more than last week, and
£212 10s. more than in the same week of 1861. In tha
town of Wigan alone 3,103 persons were in receipt of
relief, an increase of 129 since the last return, and 1,930
more than in 1861. The increased cost in the borough
has been £173 2s. 7d. In the workhouse there are 481
persons, and 59 vagrants were relieved last week. Adding
the number of paupers to the number assisted by the Relief
Committee, a total is obtained of 16,253 persons wholly or
partially dependant upon one of the two bodies. This
is an increase of 688 during the last seven days. The
guardians had on Friday again to consider the state of
their finances. The balance at the bank was low, and
would probably be exhausted this week. The clerk
stated that certain townships had not paid the first in-
stalment of a call due in October, and unless they did
so before the next meeting he should have to ask the
board for instructions to summon the overseers. This
must be done, for money must be had. The guardians
next considered the requests made by the labourers in
their employ to a member of the board, as reported in
the Times of Saturday. They resolved to reduce the
hours of labour, and to pay the men wages as usual for
the days upon which it was too frosty to work. They
objected to make any alteration in the other arrange-
ments, which they considered to be much better for all
concerned than those proposed in place of them.

articles.title: BLACKBURN.
articles.text:
BLACKBURN.

A joint meeting of deputations from the Poor Law
Guardians and the Relief Committee met in the Town-
hall on Thursday evening, to consider the pi °position
expounded by Mr. Commissioner Farnall at the meeting
of the guardians on the Bth inst. to conduce to the better
relief of the needy. A long discussion ensued as to what
would be the best course to adopt. The Relief Com-
mittee suggested that they would take the entire charge
of 20,000 persons, and leave the rest to the care of the
guardians, undertaking also to give clothing to the
necessitous indiscriminately as to which board they
were relieved by. This proposition was cordially
approved by the deputation of guardians, and the
matter is left for settlement to the constituted bodies.
It is the intention of the Relief Committee during
the winter to make up eainings and distribute relief to
the extent of is. 6d. per head per week, exclusive of
fuel, clothing, and bedding, which they this week
intend to commence distributing. During the past week
they have extended aid to about 24,000 persons, many
of whom are also relieva d by the guardians with about
46,0001 b. of bread, and a like quantity of meal. The
returns of cut relief presented to the Board of Guardians
at their meeting on Saturday showed that during the
week 21,994 persons had been relieved in the union with
£1,158 is. id., against 3,123 with £l5l 12s. 4d. in the
corresponding week of last year. Of the 21,994 relieved,
no fewer than 17,375 belonged to the Blackburn relief
district, and they were relieved with £938 6s. 6d.,
or scarcely is. id. per head, a sum utterly insufficient to
maintain life and health. It was, however, gratifying
on Saturday to find that the guardians extended this
scale of relief to new applicants and in cases of renewal.

articles.title: STOCKPORT
articles.text:
STOCKPORT

Notwithstanding the wide spread distress already pre-
vailing in this town, we have to report a serious in-
crease in the number of persons receiving relief during
the week, the number of applicants at the various Relief
Committees having increased upwards of 800, and those
in receipt of p iroebial relief more than 300. The re-
turns of all the mills in the borough have been collected
during last week by the police, and from one corrected
up to the latest dates we find that out of the 19,567
hands employed in the 88 mills in the district, only
2,006 are still working full time; 224 are working four
and a half days per week; 540 are working four days;
464 three and a half days; 3,329 are labouring three
days; 2,379 two days; 385 only one day; and 10,210,
cr considerably more than one half of the whole, are
entirely out of employment; the number working short
time, varying from four and a half to one day per week,
being 6,321. The above figures, however, do not repre-
sent the whole number of people out of employment in
the town, for, making moderate allowance for other
trades than those immediately connected with the cotton
manufacture, but which are more or less effected by the
existing depression, there are not less than 12,000 per-
sons now entirely without the means of subsistence, while
the large number who are working short time are only
just a degree above the worst off.

articles.title: CHORLEY.
articles.text:
CHORLEY.

Since our last there has been a further serious in-
crease in the distress in this town. During the week
ending on Saturday there was an increase of 106 heads
of families who applied to the Relief Committee for
support. The sum of £385 was received from the
Manchester Committee for the purpose of providing
more clothing for the poor operatives. - -

BURNLEY.
The weekly meeting of the Relief Committee was
held in the Council-room last Thursday, under the pre-
sidency of the Mayor.
The grant of £6OO from the Manchester Central
Committee was acknowledged as a gift for clothing, and
a resolution was adopted to raise the scale of relief to
2s. per head per week, and a further scale was adopted
to vary the rrlief according to the number of family.
The clothing committee recommended that the
clothing and bedding should be distributed as loans on a
scale of 3s. per head, each article being stamped to pre-
vent its sale. The recommendation was carried. It
was reperted that 842 blankets bad been purchased for
£344 3s. 2d., and that tenders had been received for a,
supply of don.
Tne district of Briercliffe was added to Burnley, and
the committee adiourned.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.
articles.text:
AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.

This week opened with a very wet day, and as there
were showers on Monday for a short period about mid.
day, no fieldwork could then be proceeded with. A
sharp white frost was however experienced at night,
with the wind from the westward.

Tuesday was cold, with the thermometer down to 39.
On that day our advices from Lincolnshire state : The
weather since our last has been variable, but, upon the
whole, favourable for the time of year. Wind west.'
From Northumberland it was remarked on the same day:
The weather has bees fine and frosty since yesterday,
wind south-west.' From Yorkshire it was written :
The weather was wild all last week, but since the
beginning of this it has turned frosty.'
Wednesday proved cold, after another white and
severe frost. Our advices from Worcestershire on that
day state that the farmers are busy in wheat sowing;
and the few frosts having pulverized the land, it works
well. In all the late districts this has been the case,
and good progress has been made for two days, the far-
mers being anxious to take advantage of every oppor-
tunity to push on this most important work.'
Thursday was a thick foggy day after another sharp
white frost. In many parts of the country the sun
shone out brightly, and a considerable breadth of land
was completed with wheat sowing, although late, in very
good order. We heard of one farmer that with every
care he had taken fourteen days to complete nine acres,
the previous heavy rains having so saturated his heavy
soil at intervals as to prevent a finish, although his first
sowing was early in October, when he got in Hallett's
Pedigree' and Kessingland ' in fine order. He has
now a fine plant of both, strong and healthy to stand the
winter's severity, while the present week's frosts will
have given it a nice check.
On Friday the wind was round to the north-east after
the fourth white frost. Usually it is considered three
white frosts bring rain, but this has counted up to four
before a change has even been approached. Many
farmers must have finished wheat sowing at this late
and protracted period. No doubt they are glad they
have got it in the ground, where it may be considered
safe in a good bed, and soon ready to germinate from the
excellent quality of the seed.
Although Saturday was cold, yet there had been
no frost during the previous night, wind northerly,
barometer high—up to 30.20, thermometer 40 degrees
at midday. A change took place in the afternoon,
slight rain having fallen at 4 p.m., and the night appeared
threatening. When frost sets in during the month of No-
vember, it is seldom lasting, and such has now proved to
be the case. Much good has been done to the land, all
sorts having worked well with this sharp weather, and
wheat thrashing may have gone on better than of late,
although farmers are tired of bringing this grain to
market, whilst the trade is so bad, owing to soft condi-
tion and a superabundance of foreign imports, amount-
ing in October to 1,164,299 qrs. Many have turned
their attention to barley thrashing, as they cai. obtain
fair prices for all useful and good malting qualities, and
with increased deliveries, the greater number of malt-
sters now at work take off the article as fast as it is
brought forward. The imports of foreign in no way in-
terfere with the sale of home-grown, as only 15,981 qrs.
were received during the month of October, a very
trivial amount compared with wheat.—November 18.

articles.title: NORTH AND SOUTH.
articles.text:
NORTH AND SOUTH.

The following letter has been addressed to the
Times :

Sir,—The thanks of all Wessex men are due to you
for your article on Friday, contrasting the Poor-rates of
Wessex with those of Lancashire.

Time was when we had many and grievous faults
(not quite extinct yet) ; and you told us of them sharply.
and honestly. You have now brought forward a re-
deeming point in our conduct, and we thank you for it.
The world will now know that though there has beei a
great deal of foul linen' in Wessex, yet we washed it
at home.'

Whatever our Dorsetshire Squires did, they never
asked Queen Victoria to open her private purse in
order to take their cottagers' blankets out of the
pawnshop. Whatever the Andover Guardians did,
they never informed England that Andover would
do her duty in time ; but that till they considered
that the time was come England must do their duty
for them. It pleased us in Wessex to keep our land
ill-cultivated and our labourers depressed; but we
paid for our hobby ourselves, and sunk in it, as you say,
no less than £8,000,000 in the last 17 years. And now
we are asked in addition to our own Poor-rates to con-
tribute to the Poor-rates of Lancashire—for all gifts and
subscriptions of ours will be nothing else than contribu-
tions to Poor-rates. We shall do it; but 'grudgingly
and of necessity,' I an 2 sorry to say, and in anything
but the spirit of a cheerful giver,' as far as the rate-
payers are concerned.: How can it be otherwise? I know
a clergyman who has a living (actual gross, not rateable
value) worth £6OO a year. Out of that £6OO he has
been paying for the last 20 years more than £lOO in
Poor-rates, that is, he has sunk in the relief of the poor
more £2,000, besides his subscriptions and private
charities. His parishioners have, of course, been
paying Poor-rates at nearly the same ratio of 3s. 4d.
in the pound. And now,' he says, lam asked to
contribute, and to persuade my parishioners to contri-
bute, to the aid of a county which it appears has been
paying Poor-rates at less than half that ratio; and which
now, if it chose to tax itself by one such a " One-and-
threepenny rate," as we have often three times in a year,
might furnish for its poor £40,000 a week for the next
three months. lam asked, too, to contribute clothes
and bedding to a district where every pawnbroker's
shop is already teeming with clothes and bedding
(pawned, of course, at far less than their real value,
and therefore all the more easily redeemable),
and thereby to enable the Lancashire pawn-
brokers to make their fortunes out of the glut. 1
shall do it, of course, but under false pretences.
I dare not tell my people the facts of the case. I
should rouse their indignation. I should button up
their pockets. I should make my honest farmers
say, "Well, then, all that we used to hear of the
ways of these Manchester cotton-spinners, 40 years ago,
is true after all. You used to tell us that they were
altered, civilised, grown generous and pubiic-spirited,
and setting us an example as to how we should behave
to our labourers. Perhaps some of them may, but, for
the mass of Lancashire men, let their Poor-rates be
judge between them and us. Meanwhile they may
take care of their poor, and we shall take care of
ours."' So says the clergyman, and so will the
farmers say. But they will, I verily believe, give
largely nevertheless. Nothing can be more masterly
than the game which the Lancashire Boards of Guar-
dians seem to be playing. They count correctly on
John Bull's impatient generosity. They know that we
cannot compel them (at least at present) to tax them-
selves as highly as they ought. They know that we
cannot wait to see their paupers starve. Their
move is perfectly successful. Let them have full credit
for it.

And, meanwhile, let those who see school children
robbed of their little savings, and delicate ladies starving
themselves into illness, to save here a shilling and there
a shilling for the Lancashire folk; and who know that,
in the ch4in of cause and effect, the actual fate of that
hard-wrung shilling will to be enable some rich man of
Lancashire to escape the giving up some paltry luxury;
let them, I beg, exercise the Englishman's right to give;
but while he gives, to grumble—and remember that
these Lancashire men have directly helped to cause the
present distress and the present war by their determin.9.-
tion to use exclusively slave-grown cotton, developing
thereby alike slavery itself and the political power of
the slaveowners.

We are authorised to state that the account given under
the head of Condemned Prisoners,' in Monday morn-
ing's papers, of what took place with reference to the
convict Samuel Gardner is incorrect in many particulars.
Sir George Grey had no personal interview with the
counsel for the prisoner, and the alleged conversations
between him and Mr. Ribton are wholly without founda-
tion. After the answer that had been sent early last
week to the prisoner's solicitors, Sir George Grey received
several communications from medical gentlemen with
reference to the matezial point in the evidence, as to the
time which had elapsed between the commission and the
discovery of the murder. These communications, to-
gether with some others relating to trio case, were
referred ic the Lord Chief Baron, with whom Sir George
Grey had several personal conferences, after which he
informed the prisoner's solicitors in writing of the ground
on which the reprieve was granted.—Globe.
NATIVE INDIAN LADIES.— Lady Frere is making
effoits in Bombay to induce the wives of the native
gentry to meet her in public. Bombay is a better place
for such an experiment than Calcutta or Madras, the
native community being much more public spirited and
enlightened. The Indu lb akash, translated in a Bombay
paper, remarks on the plan—' The great drawback is
that Rindoo ladies are not educated. They do not
know how to sit or behave in a durbar. Native ladies
will only stare at each other and sit silent. The case
is different with European ladies. They are clever and
intelligent, skilled in dancing, music, and the fine arts.
When such opposite natures are mixed together, it is not
possible that mutual sympathy should awaken in each
other. The zenana system, according to which, in
Calcutta, English ladies visit Hindoo families and teach
them, succeeds in Calcutta; but it requires on the part
of such ladies a knowledge of the vernacular, which
few (says the Friend of India) witk film cares of married
life can afford to acquit*.

TEE ISIOOSE.—The chief fact of a mooselfi person is
that pair of strange excrescences, his horns. Like
trends of tree-fern, like great corals or sea-fans, these
great palmated plates of bone lift themselves from his
,ad, grand, useless, clumsy. A pair of moose-horns
overlooks me as I write; they weigh twenty pounds,
are nearly five feet in spread, on the right horn are
nine developed, and two undeveloped antlers, the
plates are sixteen inches broad—s doughty head-piece.
Every year the great, slow-witted animal must renew
his head-gear. He must lose his deformity, his pride,
and cultivate another. Iu spring, when the first ane-
mone trembles to the vernal breeze, the moose nods
welcome to the wind, and as he nods feels something
rattle on his skull. He nods again, as Homer some-
times did. Lo! something drops. A horn has dropped,
and he stands a bewildered unicorn. For a few days
he steers wild; in his ill-balanced course his lone horn
strikes every tree on this side, as he dodges from that
side. The unhappy creature is staggered, body and
mind. In what Jericho of the forest can he hide his
diminished head? He flies frantic. He runs amuck
through the woods. Days pass by in gloom, and then
comes despair; another horn falls, and he becomes
defenceless; and not till autumn does his brow bear
again its full honours.—The Atlantic Monthly.
EFFECT OF I FLOWER ON A PRISONER—I have a
remembrance of looking through the 'inspection' of a
cell some years ago, and perceiving a prisoner, with
her elbows on the table, staring at a common daisy,
which she had plucked from the central patch of grass
during her rounds—one of those rude, repulsive, yet
not only bad prisoners, from whom no display of sen-
timent was anticipated. Yet the wistful look of that
woman at her stolen prize was a gleam of as true sen-
timent as ever breathed in a poet's line. Six months
afterwards I saw the flower pressed between the
leaves of her Bible—a little treasure I should not have
had the heart to take away, had there been any laws
of confiscation concerning dasies in 'the books.'—
Female Lfe in Prison, by a Female Matron.
PUOFESSOR WILSON A PEDESTRIAN.—His pedestrian
fiats were marvellous. On one occasion, having been
absent a day or two, we asked him, on his return to
the common-room, Oxford, where he had been. He
said, in London. When did you return ?—This morn-
ing. How did you come ?—On foot. As we all ex-
pressed surprise, he said—' Why, the fact is, I dined
yesterday with a friend in Grosvenor (I think it was)
square, and as I quitted the house a fell w who was
passing was impertinent and insulted me, upon which
knocked him down; and as I did not choose to have
myself called in question for a street row, I at once
started, as I was, in my dinner dress, and never
stopped until I got to the College gate this morning,
as it was being opened.' Now this was a walk o t
fifty-eight miles at least: which he must have got over
in eight or nine hours at most, supposing him to have
left the dinner party at nine in the evening.—Chris-
topher .North; a Memoir of John Wilson, late Professor
of Moral Philosophy in the University of Edinburgh.

THE GLOW •-wolot.—We all know it well. We have
all admired it silently shining on the fresh greensward
of the country, and we all value this insect for the
agreeable souvenirs which it calls forth as we contem-
plate its soft light. These little shining beings remind
us of our younger days. They were shown to us in
our early childhood, and we have been taught t look
upon them as something mysterious. Those sparks in
the grass, what are they? Insects. But the light 1 '
How often have we not heard such questions. Or this,
again :—' Tell me then,—you, a philosopher,—what is
it, definitely, that produces the light of the glow-
worm ? "ro which we can only reply, Those spttri.s
in the grass which have excited the inquisitiveness cif
philosophers, no less than the curiosity of children; but
that which is a mystery to the latter is still a secret, cr
nearly so, for the others.'—.Plez:pson on Phosphorescciae.

RECOLLECTIONS OF Iturruns.—l have sat near that
young man at a public dinner, and beheld him in a
gilded uniform. But yesterday he lived in splendour,
had long hair, a flowing beard, a jewel at his neck, and
a smart surtout. So attired he stood but yesterday in
court; and to-day he sits over a bowl of prison cocoa,
with a shaved head, and in a felon's jerkin. That
beard and head shaved, that gaudy deputy-lieutenant's
coat exchanged for felon uniform, and your daily
bottle of champagne for prison cocoa, my poor Rupilius,
what a comfort it must be to have the business brought
to an end! Champagne was the hon. gentleman's
drink in the House of Commons dining-room, as I am
informed. What uncommonly dry champagne that
must have been! When we saw him outwardly happy,
how miserable he must have been! When we thought
him prosperous, how dismally poor! When the great
Mr. Harker, at the public dinners, called out—' Gen-
tlemen, charge your glasses, and, please, silence for
the honourable member for Lambeth 1' How that
honourable member must have writhed inwardly
One day, when there was a talk of a gentleman's
honour being questioned, Rupilius. said, 'lf any man
doubted mine, I would knock him down.' But that
speech was in the way of business. The Spartan boy,
who stole the fox, smiled while the beast was gnawing
him under his cloak. I promise you Rupilius had some
sharp fangs gnashing under his. We have sate at the
same feast, I say; we have paid our contribution to
the same charity. Ah ! when I ask this day for my
daily bied, I pray not to be led into temptation, and
to be delivered from evil.—' Roundabout Papers,' in
Cornhillelfagazine for November.
THE LAND'S-END.—You will see, very near the End,
the deep marks of a horse's hoofs in the turf, within
two feet of the verge. A stupid and blustering idiot
()Ice made a bet that he vould ride on horseback to
the Land's-end; meaning to the very extremity of
the little rocky headland. He forced his horse down
the steep and rugged descent from the heathery
plateau above, and upon the neck of the turf. covered
rock that joins the headland to the shore. But when
the horse reached the slippery neck, he testified how
much more sense he had than the blustering idiot who
rode him, by refusing to go any farther. The bluster-
ing idiot goaded him with whip and spur: and
slipping upon the short turf, the poor creature fell, and
clung by his fore-feet in the marks you see, before
making the awful plunge below. The fall was not in
the water, but upon the sharp rocks, and the poor
horse miserably perished. I lamented the horse's late,
and I could not but conclude that had his master
been smashed instead of himself, the nobler creature of
the two would have been saved, and the loss to man-
kind would have been inappreciably small. It is fifty-
five years since the horse's hoofs clung to the last
hope, but the deep marks have been uiligently kept
clear, and they remain as when the horse was wickedly
killed, serving as a monument of his sad fate, and of
what a brainless fool his master was. After standing
on the rocky table which is emphatically styled the
End, you will clamber down a rough path, and lie
down at all your length on a very ovethanging crag.
Here your head -will project much over the sea, and
the intelligent old man will keep a tight hold of your
feet. And now, looking away to the right, you will
discern the reason why you were brought to this pre-
carious position. You will see that the rocky neck
joining the End to the shore is penetrated clean through
by a lofty Gothic arch, through which the waves fret
in foam. You will be told of another lesser arch,
which you cannot see. These have been worn in the
lapse of ages; and some day, if the world stands, the
superincumbent rock will fall, and the Land's-end will
become a little rocky islet.—Good Words.

CANDOUR AND COURTESY. We cannot borrow
climate from our southern friends, but we rely with
benefit borrow from them something of their social
courtesy, their liberal spirit, and their ease of manner.
For your true-born Briton, on either side of the Tweed,
is too apt to hide himself in his nutshell, caring nothing
for those without, nor for what they think of him.
His house is his castle, no doubt, but he is too apt to
have the guns pointed at all corners, feeling that for
some unaecountable reason he and the world are on
bad terms, and that he should never be unprepared for
desperate resistance. Something of this defiant air
prevails in all our intercourse with strangers, and
although it may offend our national pride to say
it, it betrays provincialism and want of ease. We
might copy from the Continent with great advantage
in this repect. The easy courtesy and considerate
deference of the Parisian simply argue better breeding,
and more knowledge of the world than our half-surly
half-shy manners to those we do not know. Sitting
at the door of the cafe may be a poor substitute for
home; but there the bourgeois rubs his ideas against
those of his neighbour, and learns not to think too
much of his little excellences, or too slightingly of
those of others. Above all, he learns the true secret of
courtesy, to consider what is pleasant to his consort,
Instead of what is agreeable to himself. It is said all
this is on tho surface, while British roughness covers a
warm and honest heart. Suppose it be so, why should
a man be disagreeable because his heart is warm and
his conscience honest ? The good manners of the
foreigner may be a mock, or may be a reality, but the
manners are unquestionably good. But the truth is, it
is not warmth or honesty which prompts the uncour-
thous or cold address for which we are distinguished.
it is that we have not learned, by mixing with all con-
ditions of men, to think of others and forget ourselves.'
--The lord Advocate at _Dunfermline.

SPRUNG FROM THE PLOUGIT.-Lord Cranworth, at
the Orpington Agricultural meeting the other day, told
the guests a striking fact :—Many years ago he had the
great pleasure of being to some extent acquainted with
one of our most distinguished artists—he meant the
celebrated Mr. Chantler. He had also the pleasure of
being acquainted with a very great agriculturist, ths
late Lord Leicester, who had very large lands in his
occupation, which he raised from a rental of
is. 6d. an acre to. 305., and was therefere acquainted
with the subject in every point. Chantler was once
staying at his house, associating with peers and princes,
and one day looking at a field, he said to Mr. Cooke (for
he was not then Lord Leicester), I don't think the
fellow has ploughed that as he ought.' Mr. Cooke
replied, That's a far more difficult thing than you
think for.' On this, Chantler took off his coat and
ploughed better than any of the men. 'How can you
do it?' asked Lord Leicester. Chantler replied, Now,
I have the pleasure of moving in high society, but I
began ray life as a ploughman.' It was gratifying to
think of men rising from such an humble origin; but
with a firm determination there was no position in life
to which they might not rise.

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1862.

SUMMARY.

4,
