FOREIGN.

Greece appears to want Prince Alfred as King
at Athens, and may become a pressing suitor
to the young gentleman; although like courting
in another department of life, the applicant in
this case may have more love for the dowry
than the person. The Greeks have not seen
much of the Prince, but they see, or fancy that
thef see his dowry in the Jordan islands, which
since 1815 have been under ourprotection. All the
'intinental Powers would oppose the estab-
t of a British Prince on the Grecian
9 a transference of the East practically
vereignty. Domestic alliances are.
1
ilosophers to be unproductive of
suits, but diplomatists regard

them in a different light, or from some nearer
point of view.
The French Ambassador to this Court, the
Count de Flauhalt, retires at his own request,
; and is succeeded by Baron Gros, who was
engaged with the Earl of Elgin in the recent
negociations at Pekin. The Count de Flauhalt
is in his seventy-seventh year, and has been
occupied in public life almost from the date of
the French Revolution.
Assassinations—in the last instance, the
Chief Commissioner of Police—have been
followed by excessive stringency at Warsaw.
The Poles are kept down by superior force, but
the political embers of a great political fire
linger in Poland.
Notwithstanding large exportations of corn
from the Baltic, yet famine exists in Finland,
and presses hard upon the population.
The refusals of the British and Russian Go-
vernments to join the proposal of France and
invite the Confederates and Federals to adopt
an armistice, as already explained, have not
caused that irritation in France which might
have been anticipated; and the French Court
apparently agrees in the propriety cf post-
poning any interference between the dispu-
tants in the present stage of the quarrel.
The French reply to the request of Italy for
Rome has been published, and the Emperor
Napoleon alleges the impossibility of his army
abandoning Rme,withoutobtaining guarantees
for the safety of the Pontiff. Napoleon demands
bail from the King of Italy for his good beha-
viour to the Pope, and as the amount and the
nature of the security must be satisfactory to
the Emperor, it is not likely ever to be fouucl.
He should at once say that he requires twenty
four years notice,
The elections on the 4th current in Illinois,
New Jersey, and New York, went against
President Lincoln, his administration, and the
Republican party, giving decided majorities to
the democratic party who oppose the policy of
the Government, and the President's procla-
mation regarding slavery. The majority of the
representatives in Congress are now said to be
Democrats, and the President's proclamation
being "unconstitutional," will be called null
and void.
The elections may have no immediate results,
although they indicate a condition of popular
feeling, in which no reliance can be placed on
any documents respecting the negroes, that are
not regularly passed through the Northern
Congress, and even the latter might be repealed.
The New Governor, of the State of New York,
will not enter on office until the lstiJanuary next.
and the members of Congreso now elected may
not assemble for business until a much later
period of next year.
Mexico has sent little intelligence for some
time, but now that the French and the Mexi-
cans have passed Through the dangerous period
of the season, they may beg,n to fight. The
French have been largely reinforced, and will
attempt to reach the city of Mexico.
New Granada has been nearly all pacified
by the success of the Liberal party in strategic
movements, followed by a decisive victory;
but particulars of these battles in the North
American States do not reach us. A history
of South American wars would pirtially explain
the fact that a great division of the earth, rich
in minerals, fertile in soil, easy of access
intersected by the greatest internal navigation
on the earth, still presents the peculiarity of a
scanty population in a flowery well-watered
wilderness.

Chinese papers say that the Taeping
Wangites again threaten some of the places
that had been taken from their grasp by our
fleets and soldiers, acting in conjunction with
the French and with native pirates and robbers.
A great portion-of the latter division of this re-
spectable " trefederacy " abandoned the allied
company and the Imperial standard, and joined
the "revolution," probably having first taken
into consideration, the possibility of Taeping
being a better paymaster than the Tartar, or
giving a higher rate of wages.
That curious chief offers no opposition to
commerce. Perhaps President Lincoln might
advantageously sit for lessons in political eco-
nomy at the feet of the Taeping, who supplies
his foes with silks an teas in exchange for
goods or money, so long as they please to
purchase.

- No interference probably occurs on the part
of the revolutionary Government. They may
charge a tax in transit. Far,ther than that
small piece of custom house business, they do
not meddle with trading matters. As they do not
interfere with commercial dealings, it must be
at least equally obvious that they do not pre-
vent cultivation. Some of our speculative
merchants believed our sub-Foreign secretary,
the member for Southwark; Captain Osborne
and all the other authorities who spread scandal
regarding the Christian, or even semi-Christian
revolutionaries of China. 3 3
All the enormous lying of the Times was
accepted as truth by silly and rich persons on
'Change. They backed with their drafts the
saying of the Times that the Taeping Wangites
Were figurative locusts, who found the
heathen land a garden and left it a desert;
and accordingly they accompanied their money
sent to the extreme East with orders to buy
silks and teas. Agents in Hong Kong, in
Shanghae, and other towns, literally followed
their instructions, and the quantities of. silks
and teas sent to this country accordingly ex-
ceed, for the period of the season, and very
largely exceed, the experience of former years.
Many of the speculators will be bitten to the
bone for believing Mr. LAYARD, and putting
t
faith in the Times.
The shipment of teas to the dale of the last
letter had reached fifty-two millions of pounds,
and those of silks were over four millions

sterling, in value, while half as many more
bales had be en sent to the ports. The Taeping
Wangites have given the best reply to the
charges that they make deserts out of gardens,
as silks and teas are chiefly produced in the
regions under their rule. I A
COLONIAL.
/
The oil-tradb of Canada rises into great im—
portance, and a second public company has
been proposed in London to conduct the busi-
ness. The public companies centreing in
London, and engaged in the colonial and
Indian trades, have a capital employed of more
than two hundred millions, and obtain returns
of twelve to fourteen millions annually from
their investments.

A large increase had been made, before the
departure of the last mail, to the Canadian

,
subscriptions for relief of the distress existing
in Lancashire; and at the date of the last

Australian mail the receipts to this fund had
reached £50,000.
The deputations from the North American
colonies respecting the Inter-colonial Railway,
will soon arrive here, with the view of com-
pleting their negotiations of the line to unite
the ocean and Quebec. This work would give
activity to our iron trade for a time, find farms
_

at a comparatively short distance for several
hundred thousand families of agricultural
labourers, and half complete the line across
the American Continent, which will be the

rue north-western passage, and bring ou

communications with the Australian colonies
"within the month."

The cotton accounts from India are quite
cheerful. It is calculated that 1,600,000 to
, 1,700,000 bales of Cotton may arrive here
from India in 1863; and as the West Indies,
Africa, even Australia, certainly Western
Asia, and Egypt, will increase their supply,
the trade may have two million bales to work
upon, even if the Confederate States
.should
remain closed for next year.
Wool at the current sales has advanced by
one penny to twopence per pound, on good
colonial fleeces. ' Flax is plentiful, and along
with its kindred hemp and jute, especially the
latter, it recedes in value. Silks come west-
ward in large quantities, and may be cheaper,
for at the present prices the importations cf
the year will not be under ten millions sterling.
The metal trades are rather duller, and the
iron trade is slightly affected by the discharge
of many workmen from Woolwich, and the
public building yards.
The exportation of bullion by the Indian
steamer of last week exceeded one million, and
the quantity to be forwarded by tke steamer
of this week will exceed one-third of a
million, while the last steamer from New York
has Onlya little less than one hundred thousand
pounds; and the "Great Britain" steamer,
with a half million in gold Etom Australia, is
over due.

DOMESTIC.

Consols and money maintain the rates of
last week. Cotton is cheaper by id. to 2d.
per lb. Wheat is lower by is. to 2s. per
quarter, but we repeat the notice that flour in
retail is a fixture. It never gets any cheaper.
Flour never falls apparently, or is never to fall
again in comnion stores. What do the co-
operative store keepers say to that determina-
tion.

0 8 6
0 6 10

WHO ARE TO BLAME?

TIIE extent and intensity of the Lancashire
distress is not easily represented. It has re-
duced one sixth of a population of nearly two
millions; to relief from the parochial rates,
stringently administered, and many thousands
--nears- one hundred thousand persons share
benevolent funds, while not as yet, obtaining
help from the parish. Although these figures
imply a pressure of great severity, yet they
misrepresent the nature of this terrible crisis.
The cotton districts might tide through their
troubles, if all the inhabitants not yet seeking
public assistance were still in receipt of their
ordinary means; but the Earl of DERBY writes
that,five-sixths of the ratepayers in the places
chiefly supported by the cotton trade are dis-
tressed and embarrassed; and he cannot expect
a better state of matters for some time.
Mr. GLADSTONE, Mr. KINGSLEY, and other
eminent men charge a large portion of the
cotton-trade with selfish negligence of the
operatives. The BEE HIVE mentioned this
characteristic of the cottonocracy several
weeks ago, and it is now forcing itself offen-
sively on the public. Mr. GLA.DSTorrE has
accurately classified the parties who have
become rich by the cotton-trade into land-
owners, merchants, spinners, and weavers.
The landowners have drifted into wealth
without the slightest exertion on their part.
Rents flowed in upon them; but probably,
money lightly got was lightly spent, and the
landowners of the district have been liberal
contributors to the benevolent fund of the
different towns. One nobleman, in addition
to public subscriptions and rates, gave
privately one thousand pounds, and forty
pounds weekly to a special fund. Another
has added to general subscriptions two hun-
dred pounds weekly to one fund. The public
men of this class must have already made
acrifices for their neighbours, and they must
make more before Lancashire can pass without
great loss of life through the winter. The
mercantile class include brokers and speculators
who have been enriched, not only. by the cotton
business generally, but by this particular
catastrophe; the landed interest have gained
nothing by the calamity in cotton; on the
contrary, they must be heavy losers by this
event. Their property has been gradually en-
hanced in value duriu,„.o. the rise and progress
of this manufacture; and their income must be
temporarily affected by this check to its pros-
perity, from which they could neither directly
nor indirectly have derived anything.
The manufacturers, in at least that capacity,
have a current and great loss, by the suspen-
sion of their works. A Spinning or weaving
factory that has cost £BO,OOO in building, and
machinery involves an annual cost of five per
cent., or 0E4,000 for interest; and even while
the business is stopped the deterioration and
expense of "looking after," will not be less
than ten per cent., or £8,000; and so idleness
costs the manufacturer, with machinery and
premises, on this scale £l,OOO by the month,
or £12,000 by the year. Manufacturers on
any scale, are exposed to the same per centage
of loss. Fifteen per cent, upon the value of
their plant, including deterioration, current
expenses and interest, will not do more than
cover the annual loss of the manufacturer from
the suspension of the trade.
Many manufacturers have also been mer-
chants, dealing in cotton rot requisite for their
own premises, and in goods not produced at
their own works; but the losses of the first
branch of their business are not affected by
gains on the second, except in relation to
their individual solvency or wealth. Mer-
chants and speculators have made extreme
fortunes by the Lancashire ruin. Like dealers
in old material, who are enriched by a fire or
a storm, they have extracted wealth from the
wreck. Ruin to others has been riches to
them. A colonist who finds himself suddenly
independent by the discovery of a gold-field
in his vicinity, or even an oil well, shares only
the prosperity of his neighbours; but cotton-
brokers, importers, merchants, and speculators
have sprung into unexpected means by the
strokes that have ground to pieces the ma-
jority of their customers, and their operatives.
These distinctions are inadequately considered
or put forward in apportioning the moral
responsibility of the persons interested in this
trade.

The landowners, as landowners, have ex-
perienced a reduction of their incomes, as yet,
probably, very slight, and some addition to
their rates from this crisis. The manufacturers,
as manufacturers, have met a complete cessa-
tion of their income; for it is not said that
any person can spin and weave cotton at
present prices of materials and productions
with profit; and they also suffer a loss of
fifteen per cent. on the capital involved on
plant; and while those old firms who have
paid all their plant merely lose income from
this cause, others who have borrowed money
on the security of buildings or machinery must
sustain direct pressure. Merchants and spe-
culators, in that capacity, having sustained no
loss on rates or rent by tear or wear have
amassed almost incredible fortunes. Forty
millions sterling have been named as the gains
on cotton and its productions during the last
twelve or eighteen months. Indian cotton,
sold in ordinary seasons at fourpenee to

sixpence per pound, has sold during the
last summer at One shilling and four .pence to
one shilling and eightpence per pound. The
difference on a bale of cotton is twenty pounds;
on the first million bales of cotton imported
from India after the outbreak of the American
war, this increase would be twenty millions
sterling, but the stock on hand two years ago
was Over half a million of bales; and nearly a
half million of. bales have been received since
the blockade of the American cotton ports
from other sources, in addition to the Indian
supply, while the immense stocks of cotton
goods and yarns on hand in this country, and
in other countries on consignment from our
merchants, have been shielded from sales at
ruinous rates and have acquired a greatly
enhanced value, so that the estimate of FORTY
MILLioNs ofprofits made out of this ruin, great
and strange as it may Appear, is probably not
an exaggeration.

For ;lir object, it matters nothing whether the
profits be estimated a little over the reality at
forty millions; or much under the truth at
twenty millions, for from the smaller reckon-
ing waere is the five per cent, or the tithe, or
the fifth, of an honest heart, or the half of
a generous, liberal spirit, that should have been
cheerfully and thankfully given to save families
from starvation, by the calamity which accumu-
lated this wealth? Landowners have been
enriched by the gradual growth of the cotton
trade, and they should remember in this dis-
tress the men who quadrupled the value of
their soil. Manufacturers have rapidly built
fortunes in this business, and should spend part of
them to sustain the operatives, whose labours
have raised the " cottonocracy" to stations of
consideration and influence in the State. A
third-class have incurred a moral debt with
ample means for its discharge; and the diffi-
culty experienced in reaching the million
required by Mr. COBDEN is a reproach to these
men. They shelter themselves in No. 26, or
N 0.126 of some square or street, while the land-
owner is identified with his estate, or the man-
facturer with his mill; and thus the former
escape observation, but the mercantile cupidity
of this class is an utter disgrace to their order,
for unless their hearts were hard as nether
mill-stones, the Lancashire distress would.
be easily met. The gains of such men are their
shame in the circumstances, and they are not
ashamed of their money and its meaning. They
appear in society, talking of having cleared
some enormous amount, by a hit which they
never expected. One man says that he has
made £250,000 in the cotton crisis. We should
see his name down for 225,000 or £50,000 to
the fund, not for relieving, but for supporting
the idle operatives at the present time; and
we have not the smallest reason for supposing
that he has given 25,000 pence for the pur-
pose.

- One mercantile firm has been saved almost
from prostration by the crisis, for it was, being
smothered in cottons, here, there, everywhere,
having gone into them with a reckless forget-
fulness of the laws regarding demand and
supply. it has been saved from its folly,
enriched by its commercial stupidity, and has
added immensely to its means by less than a
windfall. This firm should be generously
grateful, munificently thant.dul—saved from
ruin, raised to wealth; these commercial facts
might bring out £20,000, and leave £200,000
or £300,000 over—and one partner has given
£250, and others may have sent. equal sums,
and been pleased with the sacrifice which they
have made! We are entitled while urging every-
one who can spare pence or shillings to aid in
rescuing their countrymen and countrywomen
from famine, and fever to follow on famine,
and death—we are entitled while discharging
that duty to examine the mercantile morality
Of this crisis, and denouuce the selfishness of
those flinty hearts that worship in the plain of
Dura and yet aspire to rule our state. The
highest subscription from a manufacturer of
Rochdale is said in the Daily Hews, no mean
authority on Rochdale affairs, to be one hundred
and twenty pounds! That is a damaging confes-
sion ; for firms in Rochdale might give ten to
twelve thousand pounds without being ma-
terially straitened; but the disgrace is com-
paratively limited, as the sin, is small, when
compared with the mercantile or speculative
cupidity brought out in the narratives of the
cotton trade for the year.

articles.title: NOVEMBER PROMISES.
articles.text:
NOVEMBER PROMISES.

NOVEMBER has come, and is nearly gone—
with its fogs, and frosts, and sufferings, ac-
cording to custom, but its movements in
favour of a new reform bill, with a complete
and perfect suffrage, have not come. That
promise has been deferred until a more con- 1
venient opportunity. Good words, and even 1
good deeds, in one department are abundant.
Sympathy with sorrow is expressed in personal
sacrifices. Calamity itself is enriching the
country in drawing closer its many classes. A
great cloud has darkened the cotton land, but
it shows the. operatives, there, bright stars of
benevolence, charity, friendship, from unknown
and distant colonies—from remote counties—
from all parts of the empire—from all classes
in the empire—from the scanty pay of regi-
ments in distant stations—from the wages of
seamen far away, as they get into port for a,
time—from the lonely shepherd in the Aus-
tralian bush—from the hardy foresters in the
Canadian wilds—from .the grazier and the
miner, and the planters in all colonies—and
from classes as far distant in social, as
are all these colonists in geographical position.
We knoW that the stars shine although the sun
be not set, and yet we know of them better
after he has sunk in the west. So we did not
need this grief to know that any suffering class
in the empire would be surrounded with sym-
pathy. We knew the fact as a theory, but
perhaps it has become better known as a great
practical realised truth. This belt of good
deeds and loving kindness strengthens our
system. It should not be always visible, yet
we are not worse of the knowledge that it can
never be eclipsed. Commercial prosperity and
the successes of trade do not come between us
and this voluntary community of means, but
only renders activity needless for a time. It
is the reserved light, but this reserve never
fails. Individuals save their money, classes
shrink from duty, but the people generally,
rich and poor, will be found on the right side,
both as hearers and doers on all emergencies
of this nature. That fact is a substratum of
good will under all agitations and differences;
but it does not require the concealment of
opinions. We may entertain gratitude without
ceasing to claim justice. Even the cry of the
hour is for better legislation. A million of
aged and young persons in our land are depen-
dent on others for daily bread and clothes,
because the legislature carelessly omitted duties
that once done would have averted these
straits. We do not call the neglect criminal.
It was an oversight. It originated in ignorance.
It may have been rooted in stiff adherence to
antiquated principles of political economy. It
may have proceeded from some of those good
intentioias, that hi their turn proceed down-
wards to a very great depth, and remain there.

We make no pretensions to analyse the parts
of a.glaring fact that the million starve who
should have been would have been, with good
management, in Plenty.
Let us not quarrel with the past. Let us
not then refer to these graves of time, save to
pull from them experiences for the future. All
classes have committed errors. All classes
may have meant well. And however they
meant, even if they were selfish, let charity
fulfil its duty, and soften the memory of evil;
if conversion cover the multitude of sins. But
no excuse for apathy is to be found in forgive-
ness; and the call of duty sounds in the cry
of suffering. The material of employment
abounds under the British flag. We ask not
for bread, but the means of earning and grow-
lo in, bread. We ask not enfranchisement to
gratify pride, or to confer a right, but to
oppose a wrong. And the unenfranchisad
classes of this country may rest assured that
no class can care for their business better than
themselves. If they think that the November
now going out: is not that November in which
they should band together to achieve their
emancipation in full, this gentle serfship of
theirs must last another year, as it will
last all the years, until a generation of
men arise who, weary of a negative slavery,
will intimate their purpose to be free, aud they
will be freed; exactly as the present genera-
tion may secure their liberty and bring into
use all the resources of a mighty empire; the
mightiest ever formed on earth to avert from
them and theirs a repetition of the season's
wants, and to so widen out our home as to
gain time from toil and fair wages for all who
are willing to do fair work.

articles.title: PRESENT DUTY.
articles.text:
THE PRESENT DUTY.

May no word written in anger, and an in-
telligible irritation with the conduct of some
persons enriched in cotton, cause any other
persons to delay Vie assistance that they may
have been half disposed to send into the cotton
towns, even for an hour.

Our responsibilities are our own. We cannot
shift them on others, or shirk them under the
excuse of bad examples. One man's duty
cannot be neglected prudently because
another man declines . his duty; and the
following extracts from a letter which reached
our office last night will show our readers that
"speed" is almost everything is this case, at
this season.

"Now is the time to be of use to the opera-
tives, just to prepare them for the cold weather.
You will see shortly that a pestilence will fol-
low all this starvation. As a medical .man
have always noticed a pestilence to follow in
the wake of a famine, and war after a pesti-
lence. The Lord only knows where it will end.
One thing I do know, the people are not half-
fed."

We share the fears of this correspondent
that famine will precede pestilence; and few
words are necessary for those who seek to save
life. May all that can be accomplished be
done quickly to restore pledged day and night
clothes, and to find food for that lar go section
of the operative classes who are ready to
perish.

articles.title: CORR,ESPONDENCE.
articles.text:
CORR,ESPONDENCE.

THE BIRMINGHAM WORKING- MEN'S RELIEF
COMMITTEE AND MR. PEACOCK.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
SlR,—The chairman of the Birmingham Working
Men's Committee appears to feel very keenly the
assertion made in my first letter, that it was merely
a sham to decoy the working classes into subscribing
towards the Mayor's Fund.' This truth, like truths in
general, has only done what it is ever intended that
truth should accomplish, excite a pang of suffering
in the offender. Mr. Bishop cannot but be conscious
of the position in. which he stands, and feels that
public notice, once directed fully upon him, will detect
the imposition sought to be imposed on the working
classes of Birmingham. Two Central Relief Committees
are applying to Mr. Bishop for the funds which he pro-
fesses to collect for the distressed in Lancashire; one is a
middle-class, the other a Working Man's Central. Now,
it is obvious that justice v 4 ould require that the sub-
scriptions of the working classes ought to go to the
Working Men's Central, and those of the middle classes
of Birmingham to the Manchester Central. Why is
this division not approved of? Simply because it
would expose the small amount collected from the
middle classes; who, without the admirable mode
adopted ingeniously by Mr. Bishop, would be found
to subscribe a miserable pittance, considering the
wealth of the town. Mr. Bishop stands, therefore, as
the connecting link between the workmen and the
employers in the use of this stratagem. The issue
gained is, that the whole amount of the funds is trans-
mitted to the Mayor, who sends it to the Manchester
employers, and not to the Lancashire workmen.
Now it is no palliation of the offence for Mr. Bishop to
say it is done elsewhere. I know it is done elsewhere;
but what I mean to maintain is, that wherever the
sham is practised it is disgraceful, if the parties are
aware of a Working Man's Central being in existence.
Mr. Bishop is aware of this, and yet persists in sending
'working men's subscriptions to swell employers'
funds. The man that does this is no true working
man; and the committee who sanction it (whatev( r
name they may choose to purloin) is not a bona fide
working man's committee. Will Mr. Bishop under-
take to deny that the man who represents upon his
committee the workshop where he collects is not some
foreman chosen. by the employer, and that the collec-
tion is not to a certain extent enforced by the authori-
ties in the workshop? A committee composed of such
men is not a bona fide working man's committee;
and I am not at all surprised that an application com-
ing from our Central should be rejected in preference
to that of the Manchester employers. Mr. Bishop
accuses me of throwing the apple of discord' among
his flock. If breaking up such an unnatural alliance
were the result, I should rejoice to be the honoured
instrument. All shams are detestable, and there are
plenty of them in Birmingham, without teaching the
honest working man the art of dissimulation. Mr.
Bishop's scheme will last so long as he can keep his
system in darkness, concealed from the men whom he
is deceiving, but no longer. It will be my duty to en-
lighten them. I shall, therefore, allow Mr. Eishop to
take his course, and I shall take mine. It will be for
my fellow-workmen of Birmingham to decide which
Central they will support,

BREAD OR BLOOD.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
Snt,—ln years gone by, when commercial depression
deprived the working class of employment and of food,
it was nothing unusual for great numbers of working
men to meet in Mobs and raise the cry of 'Bread or
blood,' and in numerous instances have they been
known to carry it into practice; but to the credit of the
working men of England be it said, the spirit, of
Ludditism is almost, if not entirely become extinct;
for if ever there was a time within the memory of man
when such means might be resorted to with any show
of justice, the present crisis in Lancashire is the time
above all others; and having been an eye-witaess of
the poverty and destitution in some parts of Lanca-
shire enables me to judge of the manner in which the
unfortunate factory operatives bear their trials. There ,
are no mob meetings, no acts of violence, no threaten-
ing letters; their complaints are made in sorrow, not
in anger. Men may be seen walking the streets,
shadows of their former selves. Misery and starvation
are depicted in almost every face. Mothers, oft with
infants in their arms, with scarce sufficient clothes to
cover their own nakedness, vainly attempting to shield
the innocent babe at their breasts from the keen Novem-
ber blast, and casting a glance at the passers by which
would melt the heart of a stone. Young women, from
whose cheeks the bloom of health has departed, who
twelve months ago possessed an amount of pride and
dignity which is essential to true womanhood, now
saunter miserable and dejected through the streets
pale, wan features turned
and occasionally you see the
towards you, and in a low, timid tone you hear the
words, Con yo help us a bit?' I ask, will the work-
ing men of London allow this state of misery and
destitution to exist, when the remedy is in their hands?
for if every working man in London would contribute
6d. per week, it would purchase a sufficiency of food
for several of the towns that are the most depressed.
If such a course were adopted, an atnnunt of suffering
in the aggregate almost incredible would be alle-
viated. LIUMANITY.

NEW YORK, Nov. 10.
GeneralllPClellan has been relieved of the command.
of the army of the Potomac. General Burnside has
been appointed his successor. General 111`01ellan has
virtually retired from active service. A correspon—
dence between General HaHeck and the Secretary of
War has been published, in which the former states
that he issued peremptory orders to Gen. 14PClellan on
the 6th of October to cross the Potomac and give
battle to the enemy, or drive him south. General
IVlTlellan failed to obey this order, on the ground that
he was short of supplies. General Haneck, however,
states that General 11PClellan's requisitions were
promptly supplied, and Ultra was nothing to prevent
him from advancing. General M'Clellan's removal
has caused considerable excitement in the army, and
among the •people generally. All the republican
journals endorse the President's action.

.Confederates
under General Breckenridge, 28,000 strong, have
attacked Nashville on two sides. They were repulsed
on one side, but the result of the attack on the other"
is not known.

IMPOR7'A2TT TO CABMEN.

•
Francis Nash was brought up yesterday at Bow-
street Police-office, on a 'warrant charging him that on
the 16th of Jun.ci he, having applied for a licence to
act as driver of Metropolitan Hackney carriages, and
having signed a requisition to that effect, the said
requisition contained certain false representations.
Upon application for licences by cabmen, they are
called upon to sign a certain forth of requisition con-
taining various statements, such as whether they
have been previously licensed or refused licences
whether they have ever been charged With any
offence, and if so, whether convicted, and the
_like.
Any misstatement on these points, or as to thek
name or address of the applicant, _renders him-riable
to a penalty of £5, or two months' imprisonment.
It appeared that the prisoner had applied for the re-
quisition, giving the name of Frederick-Nash, and de-
claring in the requisition that he had never before held
a licence, that he had never applied for a licence and
been refused, and that he had never been charged. with
any offence. It was ascertained that he had twice held
a licence, viz., in 1859 and in 1861; that he applied for
a licence in the earlier part of that month (June) which
was refused; and that when holding a licence 'he had
been :cur times convicted of drunkenness and other
misconduct.

The magistrate said there were deliberate false state-
ments as to having had the licence and having been
convicted. He must pay the full penalty of £5, or be
imprisoned six weeks. Inspector Martin hoped
publicity would be given to the case, as a warning to
other cabmen, this offence being of frequent
currence.

THE BOILER EXPLOSION AT PADDINGTON.—The
inquest on the bodies of the men who were killed by
the explosion of the locomotive engine Perseus at the
Paddington station was resumed yesterday. Captain
Tyler, the Government inspector, said the accident had
been caused by the corrosion of one of the rings of the
barrel at the bottom of the boiler. He was of opinion
that such boilers should be examined at least every
three years. A verdict of accidental death was
returned.

—Yesterday morning, on the arrival of the up train.

extinct. From documents found on the deceased, who

TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

THE CHELSEA SHOEMAKERS.

We have received the following letter from the
Secretary of the Chelsea Shoemakers' Society

TO THE BDITOR Or THE BEEHIVE.

Stn,—lt is nearly fifteen months since Mr. Yapp,
boot maker, of Sloane-street, Chelsea, locked his
workmen out upon the plea that they were society
men, and informed them that he should not employ
them any longer unless they left their trade society.
At the same time he printed a statement of the wages
he intended to pay for the future, being nearly ten per
cent. reduction. From that period to this, only two
of the men out of the 69 so locked out (much to their
credit) have worked for him, his work having been
made b.ythose dirty fellows called, in our trade scabs.
It was thought by some of the men as the shop had
been of above twelve months, that Mr. Yapp may bare
forgotten his prejudices towards society men and that
he would allow them the privilege of at lease thinking;
for themselves. The consequence was, that a deputa-
tion was appointed to wait upon him for the purpose
of informinc, him that the trade was willing to accept
the wages he is supposed to be paying, but instead of
listening to the deputation, they were sent away with
as little ceremony as an imperial tyrant would dismiss
his serfs pleading for the privilege of freedom.
The shop is still blocked.
Yours, &c.,
11, Lower North-street.

IRON V. WOOD; OR, BLACK WALL V.
POPLAR.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

SIR,—In reading your paper of the 16th I felt very
glad to see there was one wooden man among those
*who call themselves respectable unionists bold enough
to come out and answer my letter of the Bth. But,
Sir, I hope he will confine himself to the truth when
he writes again. In the first place, he says Messrs.
Wig,ram are not defeated by the iron shipbuilders
keeping away from their yard. What would he call
it when they have plenty of machinery and room to do
it, which they had not in the case of the ship he
mentions—viz., the Ripen? The keel of that ship
they did put out, for they then had not the conveni-
ence to make it, which they have now to make the
one that they have sent to Messrs. Westwood and Co.
to do for them, and to be made by iron shipbuilders.
In the Itext place, he wants to know, Can the iron
shipbuilders build a ship by themselves? Mark the
word, by themselves. I say yes; and they have done
it. Ask Messrs. Earl and Co., iron shipbuilders, of
Hull. They can tell you. Thu, iron shipbuilders
built one for them without the assistance of wooden
shipbuilders. And again. How many wooden ship-
builders worked on the Great Eastern while building?
None. In reference to smiths, iron shipbuilders have
their trade divided into three classes—viz.. rivetters,
Platers, and angle iron smiths; and it is by their being
brought up to it from boyhood they have advanced
from one branch to the other, that they thereby have
had a perfect knowledge of it throughout, and have
become smiths of no mean order. For there is scarcely
one amongst them that cannot take smith's work of any
description in hand, and complete it to the satisfaction
of their employers. There is not one of the wooden
Shipbuilders that can do the same. Again he says,
(who can blame a class of men when they see their
trade decreasing, and their numbers increasing, for
taking employment at atrade, that they say is so easily
Mastered, and highly renumerative). This I consider
is openly saying that robbery is no crime. And as to
the trade being easily mastered what I have said in a
previous part of this letter, and the following letter
will show

DOVER, November sth, 1862.—Dear Friend,—With
much pleasure I relply to yours of the 3rd instant, and
will try fi) give you?!every information I can in my
humble way concerning thatbulkhead, I made enquiries
again to-day, and am told that she was built at luessrs.
Wigram's yard, and that the wooden men put up the
said bulkhead. The name of the vessel is the
Sampphire, and when she came here, the mail
master would not pass her on account of the
bulkhead not being tight, therefore a party of
my shop-mates, J.E.' ' (iron shipbuilders) and myself
were ordered aboard of her to make good the defects,
and many a blessing we gave her; and I can assure
You, men never went to a job with more reluctance
than we did. I was ordered down below to look at the
lower plates that were joined to the kelson' and there
found such work that a rivet boy would have been
ashamed ef. The plates, instead of being rivetted,
they were bolted on with those coarse threaded bolts,
such as carpenters use for bolting woodwork together
with. They were all lengths, some with a half. dozen
washers on, filled up with badly made cement, and
what was worse, when I came to take the nuts off, I
could screw them off with my finger, and I reported
such to one of our head foremen, and he replied, What
could we expect from wooden shipbuilders? It was
then that I found out that the ship had been finished
by wooden shipbuilders; in three or four places I pulled
out lumps of tallow that had been stuffed in places that
they could not caulk, and in one place I found a
wooden plug, which I showed to the foreman; also the
tallow with it, and many more things connected with
it, confirmed the opinion of us all, that it was a most
scandalous job. The cross beams and shells were too
weak, in consequence of which we were obliged to
strengthen them before they would pass them. I
remain, yours, gm. T. W.,
Yours, &c.
Blackwall, Nov. 18th. J. J.

THE BOLTON JOINERS' STRIKE.
TO THE EDITOR OP THE BEEHIVE.
51z,-11aving been a constant subscriber to your
journal from the commencement, I have had. ample
opportunity of judging whether it is or not a fitting
Medium for the working classes generally to commu-
Ideate with their fellow toilers upon subjects of such
-vital importance as strikes or disputes in their respec-
tive trades and callings. I came to that conclusion,
Which, I think,
every real working man free from pre-
judice would do, that it is the only available organ
Open to them for such a purpose. Having formed that
Opinion I took the liberty of addressing a note to the
Bolton strike secretary, reminding him of the BEEHIVE'S
columns being open to them to state their case, and
Pointed out the advantages likely to follow in the
way of subscriptions, &c. In due course I received a
Polite note from the secretary thanking me for my
kind remarks, and stating, at the same time, that he
had received a communication from the Manager of the
pmuiy. upon the same subject, and promised for the
tere
fiescheei
(Nie
to send a report weekly for insertion. Since I
that assurance two papers have been pub-
ut
nothing concerning the dispute, which has
lasted' Something like twenty-two weeks, appears.
Now, Si;
I think there must be something wrong
either
:in the eauee or the management of it. If the
cause is a just one it cannot be too publicly known. If
the management is bad the sooner they reform the
better. I hope before you receive this that they have
seen the desirability oi communicating with you, by
which means they will still continue to receive the ,
support and good Wishes IL 11. I
Wrightington yours, &c. Hall of
—ov. 18, 1862.
The writer of the above letter sends us the follow-
ing balance-sbeet of the Bolton Joiners' Strike, for the
week ending November Bth, in which the committee
say : ‘Fellow-workmen,—In presenting this, our 21st
balance sheet, we feel it to be our bounden duty, at
this crisis, to offer a few remarks concerning our
strike. You are all aware, from the balance sheets
that have been issued weekly, that our present struggle
is for the small boon of what is termed the `half-holi-
day ' on Saturdays—a privilege which is enjoyed by
nearly all branches of trade; and those who do enjoy
it know well how to appreciate it, and they cannot
but for .a moment think, with a feeling of deep regret,
of their Bolton brothers, who have made so much sacri-
oe in their homes, and avoided the real necessaries
requisite for their families for the last twenty-one
Weeks, that they have shown themselves men worthy
of 'being called brothers, and deserving of that kind
and generous aid which we have solicited from you, .

and we entreat you still to make every effort that lies
in your power to SitV4 them from being crushed down
by a few unprincipled employers. The total income
Up to the present time has been £724 Is. Old., and the
total expenditure £BB9 is. Bd.

MEETING OF THE OPERATIVE BAKERS
OF BRISTOL.

On Saturday evening a public meeting of the opera-
tive bakers of Bristol was held at the Little Ship, Red-
cliffe-street, for the purpose of hearing from Mr.
Thompson and Mr. Rose, from London, an explanation
of the objects of the London Amalgamated Association
of Operative Bakers, and the twelve-hours system,
with a view to its adoption in Bristol. The chair was
taken by Mr. Durston.

The Chairman commenced the proceedings by ob-
serving that their object was to agitate the question of
the reduction of their hours of labour till they had
achieved their emancipation from the present injurious
system. Mr. Rose, corresponding secretary from the
central board ot management in London, and Mr.
Thompson, delegate of No. 1 branch, were present to
explain the advantages of the twelve-hour system, and
would answer any questions respecting their amalga-
mation with the London society. The journeymen
bakers present that ever ing were, he was sure, of
opinion that it was only by organisation that they
could accomplish their object. They should give
their moral and pecuniary support to the central
board of management of the London association,
who were labouring to eradicate that vile system
which deprived the journeymen bakers of their
social rights, and brought them to a premature
grave. The journeymen bakers of Bristol should
concentrate their individual and collective energy
to abolish the unnatural system of sleeping on
their employers' premises, and to reduce the hours of
labour, which were the great grievances of the trade.
Ile would invite the attention.of employers to one of
the rules of the association, which was that if any
member was convicted of robbing his employer, he
should be excluded from the association. He believed
that rule was the means of keeping many from joining
the association who neither cared for themselves nor
for their employers. (Hear, hear). He then called upon
Mr. Thompson to address the meeting. He said that
the present system of labour amongst the journeymen
bakers was one which he conceived to be a degradation
to the nation, and one which reduced men to mere
machines in business, and to mere animals in enjoyment.
The only way to raise themselves 'above that system
waa by organisation. The great evil in London was
night work. He did not deny that, in some instances,
night work, like Sunday work, was a necessity; but,
then, in other trades, night work was generally fol-
lowed by a diminution in daily labour, but no so with
the bakers. The second evil was the unlimited number
of hours they had to work—from 16 to 18 hours per
day. Then, again, the wages were low in proportion to
the number of hours. He urged upon themlto spread the
principles of the amalgamation, and he believed that not
only in Bristol but in other towns success would
ultimately crown their efforts. (Cheers).
Mr. Rose was the next speaker, and after some in-
troductory remarks, he said he had suffered much from
night work and from the system of working so many
hours per day. There was no trade that had the power
in their hands more than the bakers of ameliorating
their condition if they would only exert themselves,
and unite themselves into a strong association. The
journeymen bakers of London worked on the average
eighteen hours a day, and he contended that every
man who countenanced such a system was robbing his
fellow-workman, as well as his own wife and family,
to protect whom was his duty. (Hear, hear.) What,
then, was the object of the amalgamation? They
wished to raise themselves, and to get into such a posi-
tion as other tradesmen occupied: to assist their
fellow-workmen who were out of work; to protect the
widows and the orphans of deceased members, and
they hoped soon to be able to raise a fund to assist the
unemployed. A penny per week from each member
would insure at such member's death a sum of LiS to
bury him. In a very able speech he urged npon those
who had not yet joined the society to do so, and thus
do their duty to themselves, their wives, and families.
(Cheers.)
Mr. Hemmings counselled those present to tell their
shopmates what they had heard, and endeavour to get
them to join the society. If they would not do so then
they ought to work eighteen hours a day and submit
to the treatment they now received. (Hear, hear.)
Mr. J. Reybould then proposed, and Mr. W. Hem-
mings seconded the motion, and it was carried unani-
mously, That this meeting having heard the objects of
the Anndgamated Association of Operative Bakers
fully explained, pledges itself to support the same.'
Mr. James Pye proposed, and was seconded by Mr.
John Rippon, 'That the thanks of the Operative
Bakers of Bristol are due to Mr. John Rose and Mr.
Thomas Thompson, delegates from London, for their
able advocacy of the cause.'
_ _ _ _

The motion' was carried unanimously, and the meet-
ing separated.

THE TIN PLATE WORXERS.—The following appeal
has been issued by the London society on behalf of
the distressed operative tin plate workers of Lanca-
shire.:—We take the liberty of appealing to your
generous sympathy on behalf of the above, being fully
aware of the distressed condition in which they are
now placed, caused by the depression of trade in the
cotton districts, their condition having been laid before
the tin plate workers of London by Mr. Dunn, of
Manchester' at a meeting specially held for that pur-
pose, at the Sussex Hotel, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street,
on Wednesday, Nov. 12th, Mr. Dunn stating there
were totally out of employment 166, some having been so
from nine to fourteen months, and most of.whom have
wives and families suffering the greatest privations
and misery too heartrendiain- to be described; 220
were working from three to Zur days per week, only
about 100 making full time, but daily decreasing and
Adding to the number already out of work. At the
above meeting a committee was elected to sit at the
Bell Inn, Old Bailey, every Saturday evening, from
8 till 10 o'clock, to receive subscriptions. The
smallest donations will be thankfully received and
duly forwarded to the Manchester Committee, of
which Mr. Dunn is Secretary, to be by them distributed
where most needed.—We remain, yours faithfully,
J. Bawden (Chairman), F. Phillips, W. Thomas, F.
Corras, J. Hurst, and R. S. Provo (Secretary). N.B.
—The amount collected Nov. 14th, £6 4s. 4d. The
subscriptions will be acknowledged weekly in the
BEEHIVE.

THE GARMENT DYERS.—A general meeting of the
members of the London Journeymen Garment Dyers'
Trade Society was held on Monday night at the Fox,
Duke-street, Bloomsbury, for the purpose of consider-
ing the best means of co-operating in aid of the funds
now collecting for the relief of the distress in the
cotton pistricts. There was a full attendance. After
some discussion it was unanimously agreed that a
voluntary, weekly subscription be entered into
throughout the trade, and that subscription sheets
should for that purpose be issued to all the shops.
THE BRISTOL TAILORS.—The Trade Society have
voted £5 from the funds for the relief of the cotton
distress—£3 for Lancashire, and £2 for Bristol.
HOLE-LANE COLLIERY, NEAR BRISTOL.—The strike
of the colliers at this colliery, which took place about
five weeks ago, in consequence of the manager taking
on fresh hands while the old hands were only working
four days a week, has terminated, the proprietors
having conceded the demands of the men.
BRISTOL BOOT AND SHOE TRADE.—A strike has
taken place at two of the principal wholesale establish-
ments in this city, viz., Messrs. Derham and Messrs.
Waterman, caused by a proposition from the employers
to the men working in the rivet departments that they
should pay for their own gas. The men refused.
Ultimately the proposition was withdrawn, and conse-
quently the men have returned to their work.. We
believe the men have or are about to form a Riveters'
Society.'
AN EXAMPLE TO WORKING MEN. The following
notice of a Kidderminster man, now residing at
Wilton, where there are carpet manufactories, appears
in a Salisbury paper We have much pleasure in
recording the success, through study and perseverance,
of William Young, a weaver, in the employ of Mr. G.
F. Lapworth. Prom the Southern Counties Adult
Education Society, which holds annual examination
for the purpose of encouraging education among the
working classes, Mr. Young has obtained the follow-
ing certificates and prizes, viz. :—ln 1859, for an ex-
aminatin
w
a certificate of the second
degree, . in books; in 1861, a first

amination t

articles.title: CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-

GENCE.

RIPPONDEN AND DISTRICT SPINNING COMPANY,
LIMITED.—The contractors for the various works of the
new mill have done their work most satisfactorily both
to shareholders and themselves. Particularly so have
Messrs. Taylor and Hirst, engineers, Marsden, who
have furnished a 25-horse power beam condensing
steam engine, with preparation for another of the same
power, yoking thereto when the company's works are
extended according to present arrangements. The
engine was tried for the first time, on Saturday last,
and had a first-rate start. It was named Persever-
ance,' in the customary manner, by the President. It is
now standing ready for work, but two things are wanted
—more cotton, more money. The company make the
following appeal Friends of co-operation, the
former we shall have to patiently and hopefully wait
for. As Mr. Cobden says, "it may be released to us
to-morrow—we hope to God it may." The latter the
directors look to you for now, and trustyou will give your
prompt assistance in the shape of new shares, and the
payment of all arrears on old ones; that at the first
dawn of a revival of the trade, they may get the Mill
into full operation.'—Advt.

• Sr. VOTIIISERT, S Co-OPERATIVE ASSOCIATION.—A gene-
ral meeting of this association was held in Thornybank
School-room on Wednesday night, Mr. John Barrow-
man, president of the association, in the chair. The
report of the transactions of the society for the quarter
ending 27th October was laid on the table, from which
it appeared that during that period there had been
received from goods sold, &c., £543 ss. 9141.., and there
had been expended £517 is. Bd.; leaving a profit of
£26 4s. od., which, after deducting Cl. 18s. for inte-
rest on paid up capital, &c., left abalance of n 4 62.00.
for distribution amongst the members, who will
receive at the rate of lota. per pound sterling of
purchases. The report was approved of, and the
meeting proceeded to the election of office bearers for
the ensuing year, and to the disposal of other business
connected with the working of the association.
FORMATION OP A PROVIDENT CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY
AT PEEBLES.—On Monday evening, a meeting of
parties desirous of becoming members of a Co-operative
Society for trading in provisions and other articles was
held in the Chambers' Institution, Peebles. The com-
pany was constituted, thirty-six members having en-
tered, representing upwards of £lOO in small shares.
Thu following office-bearers were elected—s IZ., John
Bathgate, Esq., solicitor, president; Mr. Thomas
Anderson, treasurer; and Mr. d.. a Murray, secre-
tary; with a committee. The society intend to com-
mence business& immediately, and there is good
prospect that their scheme will meet with entire
success. The society is to be registered under the
provisions of the Friendly Societies' Act, 1862.

articles.title: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

FREEMASONS.

GRAND MASONIC CEREMONY AT HEREFORD.—An in-
teresting ceremony connected with the Masonic Grand
Lodge of Herefordshire took place at Hereford on
Monday. It consisted in the celebration of the cen-
tenary festival of the Palladian Lodge, No. 141, held
at the Green Dragon Hotel. The interest of the occa-
sion was considerably enhanced by the presentation of
a magnificent medal to the highly esteemed. Right
Worshipful the Provincial Grand Master, the Rev.
Dr. Bowles, of Staunton Lacy, Salop, and the delivery
of a brilliant oration on Masonry by the Right Wor-
shipful the Deputy Provincial Grand Master, the
Archdeacon of Hereford, Dr. Richard Lane Freer.

articles.title: ODD FELLOWS-11ANCIIESTER UNITY.
articles.text:
ODD FELLOWS-11ANCIIESTER UNITY.

The Sons of the Thames' Lodge held their dinner
on Monday last at the lodge-house, Mr. C. Penn's, the
Horselydown Inn, Fair •street, Horselydown. Mr. J.
W. Taylor, P.G., occupied the chair, and, after the
usual loyal toasts, proposed' Success to the Sons of the
Thames Lodge.' The toast was responded to by the
Secretary of the lodge, who mentioned that they had
met to rejoice at the lodge having been established 20
years, 18 of which he had had the honour of being their
secretary. He pointed out the early struggle which
the old members had to make the lodge a success, but
he was pleased to tell them that the lodge had now,
through the exertions of its members, outdistanced
17 other lodges of the district in strength, although those
lodges had been opened before the Sons of the
Thames.' He was proud to say that, although they
were increasing in numbers rapidly, they were not in-
creasing in age, but were getting younger. He called
attention to the lodge funds, and stated that, though
they had had the usual amount of deaths, sickness, and
distress for the year, yet the yearly contributions were
Ipirdly touched, the saving on the year having been
£lBO. The saved capital of the sick and funeral fund
of the lodge was over 4400, and the distress and
incidental funds were in an equally satisfactory. condi-
tion. The Manchester Unity and Board of Directors'
was responded to by Mr. V. R. Burgess, Deputy
Grand Master of the Order, who explained the objects
and constitution of the society, which was established
about the year 1812, and stated that on the Ist of
January last it numbered 335,000 members.
BRISTOL.—On Wednesday evening the Loyal Bene-
volent Ledge celebrated their 20th anniversary at their
lodge-room, the Pine Apple tavern, St. George's-road,
when about 60 members and their friends sat down to
a dinner liberally provided by the worthy hostess, Mrs.
Fear. The chair was taken by N. G. George David-
son. After the toasts of The Widow and Orphans' I
Fund,' Mr. J. P. M'Donald gave Prosperity to the
Benevolent Lodge.' (cheers). Secretary Bidgood, in
responding, congratulated the members on the pros-
perity of the lodge. During the last ten months, they
had paid for sick pay and funeral calls £166 6s. 6d.,
leaving a balance in favour of the lodge of
£62 I ls. 10d. ; and the total value of the lodge at the
present time was £1,'095 Ss. H.

ODD FELLOWS, K.U.
Hum..—On Tuesday the members of the Loyal St.
' George's Lodge, held their anniversary at Mrs. Wat-
kinson's Shakespeare Hotel, Humber-street, when
upwards of thirty sat down to an excellent supper.—
Dr. MacMillan, who occupied the chair, gave the usual
loyal and patriotic toasts, followed by the 'Loyal St.
George's Lodge.'—P. G. Wright, in responding to
the latter, stated :that since the rescue of the lodge
funds, held in abeyance by several seceders, and for
which great thanks were due to the registrar, Mr. Tidd
Pratt, the lodge had considerably increased in numbers
and in funds and on the whole was all that could be
desired.—The officers of the order and the district
officers were responded to by the grand master, Mr.
Rosenbaum, who especially alluded to the great
strength of the Hull district.—The Board of Direc-
tors' and Success to all Friendly Societies' were also
given, and responded to by P. G. Pinder and P.D.G.M.
Sissons.

articles.title: FORESTERS.
articles.text:
FORESTERS.

BRISTOL.—On Monday the Court Prince Edward,
No., 2,405, held their 11th anniversary at tho House of
Bro. Crocker, White Ladies Tavern. Upwards of 60
sat down to an excellent supper, which was prepared
in mine host's best style. An elegant timepiece was
presented to Bro. Newman by Courts Prince Edward
and Blaize Castle, as a token of the affection and
esteem in which he is held by the members of both
courts, and he made a feeling and appropriate reply.
The thirteenth anniversary dinner of Court Thomas
Chatterton, No. 1,944, was held at the house of Host
Harris, Punch Bowl, Radcliffe Back, on Monday.
The various loyal and patriotic toasts were ably given
and heartily responded to, and the financial condition
of the court was of the most satisfactory description, I
having netted more than £1 per week during the past '
year. The response on behalf of The District' and
'The Widows' and Orphan's Society' was most cheer-
ing, and after a very pleasantly spent evening the
company separated, gratified with the entertainment.
The Prince of Wales' Court, No. 1,697, celebrated.
their 12th anniversary on Monday evening. The pro-
ceedings opened with an excellent dinner, served by
Brother Host Pring, at the court house in the Old
Market. The meeting was presided over by Brother
Secretary Dell; vice C.R. Brother Edwin Burnett.
Some pleasing statistical accounts of the order were
laid before the meeting, showing that the financial
department is in a most flourishing condition, and had
been enabled in many interesting instances to carry
out with most happy results the benevolent principles
of the society. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts
were drunk.

_
At a meeting of the members of Court Edward Col-
ston (1,909) held on Monday at the Thatched House
Tavern, it was resolved that £5 should be given to the
relief fund for the Lancashire and Bristol cotton
weaver&

SHE HERDS.—On Tuesday the anniversary dinner of
lodge 'Princess of Prussia, No. 967 of the loyal order
of Ancient Shepherds, Ashton Unity, was held at the
Three Compasses, Jacob-street. About 60 brethren
sat down to an excellent repast, supplied in Host
Llewellin's best style. The room was neatly decorated
with devices incident to Shepherdry, several handsome
antlers being arranged ainund the walls. The chair
was taken by Brother Taylor.
- _

On Saturday afternocn the Hon. F. H. F. Berkeley,
M.P. for Bristol, was initiated a member of the ancient
order of Shepherds at the City of Bristol Lodge-room,
Coach and Horses Inn, Broadmead. Several gentle-
men of the city were present, and the ceremony was
performed by Bros. T. Thomas, G. Pitman, J. Clarke,
&e., Mr. J. Brookman and Mr. G. H. Sayers were also
initiated at the same time. The hon. member having
made a brief speech, in which he thanked the company
for their kindness, retired amid vociferous cheering.

articles.title: LAW INTELLIGENC
articles.text:
LAW INTELLIGENC

CHANCERY COURT.

(Before Vice-Chancellor KINDERSLE Y.)

FRIEND IN NEED £lOO EQUITABLE BENEFIT SOCIETY.

This case was again brought under the notice of this
eourt. As we ittated on a previous occasion, this was
a petition presented by some of the members of the
above-mentioned society, praying the court to wind up
the affairs, and the case had been ordered to stand over
with the yiew of enabling the society to collect the
contributions due to it, and wind up its affairs without
the intervention of the court. It appeared from the
statement of the learned counsel, that the peti-
tioners and the society had come to an arrangement
that the petitioners were willing to allow the society
to wind up its affairs with its own hands, and that the
costs of the present proceedings were to be paid out of
the society's funds. The Vice-Chancellor assented.

articles.title: COURT OF COMMON PLE&S.
articles.text:
COURT OF COMMON PLE&S.

TROTTER V. TREVOR.

In this case the question raised was whether a voter
was disqualified as a pauper, he paying is. 6d. a week
towards the support of his aged father to the parish, it
being contended that this amount did not support him,
and that therefore the voter received parochial relief.
—The. Chief Justice said, he was clearly of opinion
that the Revising Barrister was right in deciding that
the voter was not disqualified by receiving parochial
relief.—Judgment for the respondent, with costs.

. COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.
(Before Mr. Commissioner HOLROYD.)
IN RE PETER I,IORIIISON.—THE BANK OF DEPOSIT.

This was an application on the part ot the assignees
of the bankrupt Peter Morrison, described as. of Pall-
mall East and elsewhere, banker, but better known as
the manager of the unfortunate Bank of Deposit, to
expunge a claim of £5OO made by Mr. Bennett, of the
firm of Magnay and Bennett, wholesale stationers,
Thames-street. Mr. Bagley: The bankrupt is not in
England. Mr. Reed: I thought. so. Mr. Bagley:
We can't bring him, and I am not aware that this
court has any power to bring him to this country.
But I will give Mr. Reed his address. Mr. Reed asked
that as the matter stood the application should be dis-
missed with costs. Mr. Bagley: No; the costs will
abide by the result. The Commibsioner said he would
not proceed in the matter until the agreement was
produced, and dismissed the application, the costs to
abide the result of ulterior proceedings.
IN RE THE LONDON BUILDING COMPANY (LIMITED).
There being no appearance in this case, his Honour,
after waiting half an hour, directed the case to be
struck out of the paper.

MIDDLESEX SESSIONS, TUESDAY.
(Before Mr. BODKIN, Assistant-Judge).
EMBEZZLEHENT BY A TRADE SOCIETY'S SECRETARY.
William Pike, painter, aged 43, was indicted for
feloniously embezzling the NUM of £8 ss. id, 12s.
id., and Ll. Bs. Bd., moneys belonging to the London
Amalgamated Association of Operative Painters.
Mr. Orridge prosecuted; Mr. Bosley defended the
prisoner.

The counsel for the prosecution said: The prisoner
at the bar was elected general secretary to the Associ-
ation on the 25th of June, 1861, and continued to act
in that capacity until the 4th of April last, at which
time he was sent into the country on a special mission,
and he not returning to his duties on the Bth of April,
caused an application to be made at his house for the
books and papers of the Association, which his wife
gave up, and on examination it was proved that the
prisoner was a defaulter to the amounts specified in the
indictment, besides other monies.
Christopher Clinch said: I am secretary to the
Brighton branch of the association. On the 7th of
April last I sent a post-office order for £3 12s. Id. to
the prisoner, as general secretary to the association, for
which he never sent me a receipt.
William Chinnery said: On the 2nd of April last I
was secretary to the Kingston branch of the associa-
tion. On that date I gave the treasurer of the branch
instructions to forward to the prisoner, as general
secretary to the association, the eurn of Bs. Bd. in my
name, for which I never had a receipt.
Charles Toinkisson said: I am treasurer to the
Kingston branch of the association. On the 2nd of
April last I was instructed by the secretary of the
branch to take out a post-office order in his name for
Bs. Bd. and forward it to the prisoner, which I did.
Thomas Griffin Eliman said: I am clerk in the
Money Order Office at the General Post Office. I
produce two post office orders, one drawn at Brighton,
by Clinch, for £3 12s. Id., and payable at the Totten-
ham-,court-road Office, and the other drawn at
Kingston' in the name of Chinners, for Bs. Bd., and
payable at the Marylebatua-street Office, both orders
have been paid to the signature of William Pike.
George Carter said: I was treasurer to the Associa-
tion up to June last. The SUM of £8 ss. id. entered in
the book in my hand was never paid to me or I should
have signed for it in the same way as I have done for
every other sum that appears in the book.
Robert Shaw said: I am general secretary to the
association. The signatures on the two post-office
orders in my band are in the handwriting of the pri-
soner. The sums of £3 12s. id. and Bs. Bd. are not
entered in the ledger by the prisoner. They ought to
have been. It was the prisoner's duty to receive and
pay moneys on account of the association. He ab-
sconded on the Bth cf April last. A member of the
committee went to his house on that date and got the
books and papers from isis wife. A sub-committee was
appointed to examine the books. They delivered their
report on the 29th of April last. I was present at that
meeting; so was the prisoner. I asked him if he had
cashed the post-office order for £3 12s. id. on the day
that he absconded and made use of the money. He said
he had. He also said he had spent the Bs. Bd.
which came from Kingston by post-office order
I then asked him if it was true that the £8 ss. Id.
which was entered in the treasurer's cashbook had not
been paid to the treasurer, he said 'Yes.' I asked him
if he had made use of the money; he said he had been
very much pressed at the time. I asked him if he was
a defaulter to the amount stated by the sub-committee;
be said he thought not. I asked him why the ledger was
not posted during the last two months he had held
office; he said he had kept the cash account in a small
book. He never produced that book. He was asked
to produce a statement of his transactions for the last '
two months be was in office. He produced it on the
6th of May last. Thomas Adams and others are the
trustees; they were elected at a general meeting of the
association on the 2nd December, 1859.
George Lott said I am a constable in the Kent County
Constabulary. The prisoner was given into my cus-
tody by the witness, Shaw, at Patrixbourne, near
Canterbury, for embezzlement. I brought him to
London.
Mr. Besley then made a forcible appeal to the jury
in defence of the prisoner, and asked them to acquit
the prisoner of the charge of embezzlement, and
let the prosecutors sue him in a debtor's court for the
money.
His Lordship then summed up the case to the jury,
and left it in their hands to say whether the prisoner
was guilty of embezzlement in respect of the £8 ss. id.,
as the case was not so clear on that point as it was
with respect to the £3 12s. id. and Bs. Bd.
The jury acquitted the prisoner on the count for
£8 ss. Id., and found him guilty on the 2na. and 3rd
counts for £3 12s. Id. and Bs. Bd.
His Lordship then called the general 'secretary, who
said, from the fact of the prisoner not keeping any
account for the two months he was in office last the
committee were compelled to take his own statement,
which showed a deficiency of £l6 12s. Bd. The secre-
tary alio stated in answer to his Lordship, that the
objects of the association were to provide for the death
of members and their wives, and to assist each other in
getting work, and generally to assist the distressed
members of the trade. His Lordship said, he should
defer passing sentence until next session in order to
give the prisoner's friends ths opportunity of paying
the £8 ss. Id., which would make a difference in the
sentence.

SURREY SESSIONS.
EIIBEZZLEMF.NT By THE OFFICER OF A FRIENDLY

BOCIBTY,.

William George Hutchings, 22, pleaded guilty to
stealing several sums, the property of the trustees
of the Royal Liver Friendly Society, the Lon-
don branch of which was situated at 77, West-
minster-road. Mr. Robinson, who attended for the
prosecution, said that they had no wish to press for a
heavy punishment. All that the society required was
that the subscribers should be protected against 4is-
honest servants. Mr. Tilson observed that, although
the sums were small, considerable difficulty might be
thrown in the way of all subscribers by non-payment
of their subscriptions. He should sentence the prisoner
to six months' hard labour.

SOUTHWARK COUNTY COURT.
THURSDAY, Nov. 20.
(Before Mr. WHITMORE.)

AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF CARPENTERS V. JAMES

This case stood adjourned from the 6th instant. The
plaintiffs and defendant, with their counsel and wit-
nesses, were all in attendance at eleven o'clock, the time
arranged for the case to be called on. By some mis-
understanding of the clerk of the court, another ad-
journed case was taken first, which having lasted for
some hours without tiny prospect of its termination,
Mr. Joyce, the counsel for the defendant, applied to the
court to know whether his Honour would be able to
take the case that day. The whole of the witnesses,
all working men, had been in attendance for some

hours at considerable inconvenience, and if there was
no prospect of the case being called on, it was useless
either for himself, his learned friend on the opposite
side, or the witnesses, to be kept further waiting.—
Mr. Salter, counsel for the plaintiff, having made some
remarks to the same effect, his Honour said he regretted
that any inconvenience should have been experienced
by the mistakes of the clerk. The case now under
hearing would still occupy some time, and it would be
impossible to take the case in which the learned counsel
were engaged after that had terminated. He would,
therefore, appoint a special day for its bearing, and
with the consent of all parties would fix on Monday
next, the 24. th instant, at twelve o'clock.—This ar-
rangement having been agreed to by the respective
counsel, the case stood over accordingly.

LIVERPOOL COUNTY COURT.
(Before Mr. Sergeant Wheeler.)
MONDAY, NOVEMBER 17.
IMPORTANT TO THE BUILDING TRADE.

STEVENS V. RAY.—His Honour gave judgment in
this case which was tried on Friday. It was an action
to recover 4s. 4cl. alleged to be due to the plaintiff, a
journeyman joiner, late in the employ of the defen-
dant, a builder in Seel-street; but it involved the im-
portant question of the right of a master to discharge
his journeymen at the end of the working week, and
to compel him to attend either personally or by a
representative on the following day to receive his
wages. The facts of the case were as follows :—The
plaintiff, not having been paid his wages on the Friday
night, when discharged, went home, leaving his tools,
as before, in the lock-up house at the works, and on
the following morning (Saturday) returned to his
occupation as usual, took out his tools, and preplred to
begin his day's work. The foreman accosted him and
inquired what he was doing there. The plaintiff said
said he was there to proceed with his work. The fore-
man told him that he had been discharged on the
previous night. The plaintiff said he had not, for he
had not been paid his wages, and that his master had
no power to dismiss him in that summary way and for
no fault unless he paid his wages. After some further
conversation, the foreman told the plaintiff that it was
no use his beginning work, for that whatever he did he
would not be paid for. The plaintiff thereupon desisted
from work, and at half-past twelve o'clock on that
day presented himself at the pay-table for the purpose
of receiving his wages. The wages were reckoned
up to the Friday night, the plaintiff demanding,
if he was to be considered dismissed, the payment for
that day (Saturday) also. The payment was refased,
and he was again informed that he had been duly dis-
missed on the previous night, and that he was not
entitled to demand his wages due at that time until
that, the accustomed pay day. The plaintiff's place of
residence is Liverpool, and distant upwards of four
miles from the works.

On the part of the workman witnesses were called
to prove that when a man was summarily discharged,
it was customary in the trade to pay him at once;
whereas, on the part of the master, witnesses alleged
that there was no trade custom in this respect.
His Honour gave an elaborate judgment, and con-
sidered the weight of evidence as to the custom of the
trade strongly in favour of the plaintiff. He should
therefore decide that when a man, as in the present
instance, was summarily discharged, and was imme-
diately bereft of emolument, it was unjustifiable to
cause him to lose the wages of a future in order te
obtain the wages of a previous day.

ONE Or CARDINAL WISEMAN'S LIMBS. - Michael
Connor, who described himself as a labourer on the
Underground Railway, was charged before Mr. Barker
with being drunk and figiiting, and further with
assaulting a police-constable and tearing his coat, in
Somers-town. From the evidence of a police-constable
it appeared that on Monday he saw some drunken
men standing in the streets discussing the merits of
Garibaldi and the Pope. He dispersed tam, and shortly
afterwards he saw the prisoner strike a woman and knack
her against the railings, and then ask, with an oath,
what she had got to do with the Pope. He told him to go
away, on which be became very violent. He said the
constable was an enemy to the Pope, and wanted to
fight. He struck the constable a heavy blow on the
side of the head, which made his teeth clatter and for
a time hurt him very much. The prisoner tore the
constable's great coat, and said he would have every
rag off him. Mr. Barker said the conduct of the de-
fendant was disgraceful, and drunkenness was no
excuse for such outrages. He should order the
defendant to pay a fine of 205., and 40s. the damage
to the constable's coat, or in default of payment 14
days' iiriprisonment with hard labour in the House of
Correction. The prisoner, who said he had no money,
was locked up in default.

WORSHIP-STREET.

I A HOME' SERVANT.—Rhoda Peck, a respectably
attired and rather good-looking young woman, was
charged with robbing her master. Mr. Daniel King,
a corn dealer, resident at Dalston, and having a house
of business in the City, said that he engaged
the prisoner as a general servant from the
Home,' in Smithfield, and received an excellent
character with her. That was about six weeks
since, and on Sunday last she went out as usual,
but never returned. Suspicion was of course
aroused by her absence, and it was quickly ascer-
tained that two gold neck chains, a black silk dress, a
pair of boots, and a crinoline petticoat, all of which
articles belonged to his wife and daughter, were like-
wise absent. A little inquiry resulted in a great deal
of information. The Home' servant had on each
Sabbath indulgence dressed herself in the clothes
of her mistress and the jewellery of the younger
lady, covering the former with her own, left the house
in that condition, called upon a washing-woman in the
employ of his family (who, by the way, ought to have
been charged with her), left her own garments there for
several hours, then re-dressed and returned to her
place always at the given time, and with commendation
for her punctuality.—Clark, 223 N, a very acute
officer, who had been in quest of the runaway, stated
that he apprehended her at Chesterton, in Cambridge-
shire, while taking an airing with her sister in a 'fly.'
She yet wore the silk dress, crinoline, hoots,_ and one
of the gold chains, the other being pledged by her. A
shawl and purse containing 345. were also in her pos-
session.—Mr. King claimed these; and prisoner plead-
ingguilty, was sentenced to six months' hard labour in
the House of Correction.

THE MURDER NEAR BILSTON.—The four persons in
custody for the murder of Henry Swinnerton, at Bil-
ston, were on Tuesday fully committed for trial on the
charge of wilful murder.
ALDERMAN SALOMONS, M.P., AT DEFTFOED.—Mr.
Salmons, M.P. for Greenwich, addressed a crowded
meeting of the electors of the borough at the Literary
Institution, Deptford, on Tuesday night. Mr. Norfolk
presided. The worthy alderman explained his views
on various important public questions. He hoped the
time was at hand when a reduction in taxation might
be safely effected, and believed that when Parliament
re-assembled the question of
.the national expenditure
would be introduced. The civil war in America was
touched upon by the hon. gentleman. He saw no
prospect of the war coming tm close, unless the South
was completely vanquished, which was not likely to be
the case, or unless the North gave up the contest as
hopeless. After alluding to the prevailing distress in
Lancashire, and several matters of minor importance,
Mr. Salomons concluded a very lucid address. A vote
expressive of continued confidence in the hon. gentle.
man was unanimously adopted.
Loss OF LIFE IN THE LATE FOGEL—OH Monday,
Mr. H. Raffles Walthew, the deputy coroner, held
inquiries at the Black Horse Tavern, Poplar, respecting
the deaths of George Ricketts, aged 53, and George
Caul, aged 61, who lost their lives in the West India
Docks under the following circumstances. It appeared
that George Ricketts, a carrier, was proceeding, on
Thursday evening last, with a waggon and two horses
to the ship Reigate with provisions. The fog was
dense, and he was heard to hail, apparently to ascer-
tain where he was. A splash and a scream were heard
directly afterwards, and a boat put off to his rescue,
but owing to the fog he could not be seen. His body
was ultimately recovered dead. George Caul was a
ship minder on board the Minden, and as that ship was
leaving the dock he was suddenly missed. Owing to
the obscurity nothing could be done to save him, and
his body was recovered next morning. Verdicts of
Accidentally drowned during a fog' were returned by
the jury.
