THE EX7R4OI?DINARY CHARGE
AGAINST A SOLICITOR.

Mr. Edward Capel Whitehurst, the sectetary of the
Ballot Society, was again brought up at Bow-street on
Tuesday, to meet the charge tf inciting Mr. Rogers to
commit an unnatural offence. Mr. H. Berkeley, M.P.,
and Mr. Wyld, M.P., the chairman and deputy-chair-
man of the Ballot Society, were present.
Mr. J. Blyth, managing clerk to the defendant, pro-
duced a book in which Mr. Whitehurst's engagements
were entered. There was one for the 30th, viz.,
'6 CH, Rogers.' The figure would of course denote
the time at which the appointment was to be kept.
There were other entries of the same kind. On the
31st of October witness went to Constitution-hill,
about six o'clock, and waited about ten minutes or a
quarter of an hour. By Mr. Whitehurst's directions
he looked for a person with white kid gloves, smoking,
but no one came. The letters addressed to Mr. Rogers
were in the handwriting of Mr. Whitehurst, without
any attempt at disguise. They were posted in the
E.C. and S.W. districts. Mr. Whitehurst's offices
were in the E.C. district and his private residence in
S.W.

George Brown, of Beach-street, Barbican, clerk to a
public society, said he had known Mr. Whitehurst nine
years. Mr. Whitehurst was very much interested in
the society, and witness had been in the habit of seeing
him six or seven times a day sometimes, About the
24th or 25th of October witness saw a report in the
newspapers in which Mr. Rogers was the prosecutor
against a soldier. About that time Mr. Whitehurst
spoke to him about that case. He asked witness
whether be had seen the case in the papers, and
witness said be hal. He also said he would
endeavour to find out who was in the right, and that
he would write a letter or two to Mr. Rogers, and he
would try whether Mr. ItOgers would keep an appoint-
ment to a letter offering him what he desired. A day or
two afterwords Mr. Whitehurst said he had written a
letter to Mr. Rogers, but that he had not kept the
appointment. Witness advised him to drop it, and
upon this Mr. Whitehurst said he should like to get at
the bottom of it, and that he would try another letter
or two. He heard no more of the matter until after
Mr. Whitehurst's apprehension.
Mr. W. C. Russell, of 13, South Lambeth, articled
clerk to Mr. Whitchurst, said he remembered the case
of Mr. Rogers,—that of a charge against a soldier,—
appearing in the newspapers. The case was discussed
between himself and Mr. Whitehurst, during the week
immediately after the publication of the case. On
Monday, November 3rd, he left the office with Mr.
Whitehurst to watk home. He parted from Mr. White-
hurst in the Strand opposite to Bedford-street, about
half-past five. Mr. Whitehurst told him before leav-
ing 1 he City that he had an appointment at six o'clock,
but he did not remember that he meutioned where.
Mr. Whitehurst might have mentioned the place; if
so, he had forgotten it. Mr. Lewis was about to call
Miss Whitehurst, when
Mr. Corrie said Mr. Lewis had adduced sufficient
evidence to satisfy him that Mr. Whitehurst did not
intend to be a party to the horrible crime charged
against him.

-Mr. Lewis said that he had many witnesses, clergy-
men, officers, and gentlemen, whom he could call, but
after what had fallen front the magistrate he would
not call them. What he had already adduced would
therefore be the case for the defence.

Mr. Sleigh, in answer to an appeal from Mr. Lewis,
said. Le could not withdraw from the prosecution, and
characterised the expressions in Mr. Whitehurst's
letters as such as only could have proceeded from a
polluted mind, familiar with the detestable crime to the
commission of which be had invited the prosecutor..
He spoke of the defence as a concoction of the prisoner
himself, and got up by him, ou the flimsy pretext that
he was a philosopher or an amateur detective.
Mr. Corrie said he had already thrown out to a
certain extent the view he had taken of this case, but
it was of great importance that not another step
should be taken without his availing himself of the
opportunity of stating the course he intended to adopt.
With regard to the present case, he thought that the
letters written by Mr. Whitehurst had been properly
described by Mr. Sleigh as filthy. He (the magistrate)
had allowed evidence to be taken to show that there
was no intention on the part of Mr. Whi.ehurst to
commit the horrible crime which had been imputed to
him, and he had already expressed his opinion upon the
point. However foolish, and however wicked Mr.
Whitehurst's conduct might have been, he was still of
opinion that he did not intend to cwirnit the crime with
which he had been charged; still he considered that
some part of the charge urged by the prosecution had
been made out, for he thought that to write those letters
for the purpose of testing the objects and inclinations of
Mr. Rogers was in itself an offence. The young man, .
Rogers, had a right to catch Mr. Whitehurst, but Mr.
Whitehurst was not justified in writing such letters to
catch Mr. Rogers. He should therefore commit Mr.
Whitehurst for trial on the two cnarges—first, of
writing the letters; and secondly, for an obscene libel..
He would, however, admit him to bail, himself in
£3OO, and two sureties of £250 each.

Bail was immediately given, and Mr. Whitehurst
left with his friends.

THE HON. TFILLIAIf FREDERICK
BYAG AND HIS TAILOR.

-
A case of more than ordinary interest came before
Mr. Bailey, at the Westminster County Court, on
Wednesday. The plaintiff was Mr. Davi' Q the well-
known military tailor, of Regent-street, and the defen-
dant the Hon. William Frederick Byng, a brother of
the Hart of Strafford, and uncle of Lord Enfield, M.P.,
fur the county of Middlesex.

Mr. Best, in opening the case, said that the plaintiff
in this case was Mr. Tnomas Davis, army and military
tailor, Regent -streer. In the year 1841 the defendant was
a captain in the 13th Dragoon Guards, and quartered at
Canterbury. He was introduced to Mr. Davis, and
ordered one or two pairs of trousers from that gentleman.
He continued dealing with Mr. Davis at his shopfgiving
him orders—some of these orders being sent in letters.
He not only applied for clothes for himself, but ordered
them for a gentleman of the name of Clarke. In one of
the letters, dated June 5, 1841, he wrote to Mr. Davis,
',Please make the bearer a nice new coat.' (Laughter.)
He heard with some regret that his learned friend in-
tended to shield his client by pleading the statute of
limitations, which no honourable man would plead if
he could avoid it. If an honest man had incurred a
just debt, he submitted that he ought not to plead the
statute of limitations.—Mr. Lewis said the plaintiff
had had five days' notice of this plea, and ten years'
notice as far as Mr. Byng was concerned, for con-
tinual applications had been made to him during that
time for a debt which Mr. Byng conscientiously be-
lieved he had paid. In ordinary cases he admitted
that a gentleman should not put in such a
plea as this, but Mr. Byng believed he had
paid the money, and under such circumstances
it would be wrong not to set up the plea.—
Mr. Byng was then sworn, and said he resided at No.
33, St. George's-road, Eccleston-square. He was the
brother of the Earl of Strafford. He received goods in
1841 from Mr. Davis, to the amount of £4B 103., the
present claim—at least, he received goods, but he did
not remember the amount. He most firmly and
honestly and conscientiously believed that he had paid
for them. In August, 1841, he paid Mr. Davis £lOO
and upwards.—Mr. Blest: Had that payment of £lOO
anything on earth to do with the claim now before the
Court ?—Mr. Byng: I believe it had.—Mr. Blest: Had
not that £lOO reference to borrowed money ?
Byng: A portion of it perhaps, but not all.—Mr. Davis
said that if Mr. Byng meant to cheat him under the
statue of limitations he supposed he must submit, but
he shcald go from this court a much more gratified
man than he thought Mr. Byng would. Verdict for the
defendant

AMERICA.

• The New York Herald of the sth inst. contains the
following summary of military matters :
Our army is maleng rapid advances into the different
. Gaps of the Blue Ridge, heretofore held by the rebels,
and we are now in possession of all the Gaps as far as
Ashby's, our force being in front of that position.
Yesterday General Stahel, with a portion of Sigel's
ecmmand, drove the enemy out of Thorougfare Gap,
and General Carl Schurz immediately occupied it.
General Bayard's force meantime holds Aldee, and all
the country between that point and Sigel's front.
Buckland Mills is also in our possession. Thus the rebels
are pretty closely outflanked, hemmed in, and cut off
from Richmond. Gen. M`Clellan's army is 50 miles nearer
the rebel capital than General Lee's army, and a vigor-
ous movement—protected, of course, by a cautious
attention to his rear—may at any moment put him in
possession of that place. Amongst the most melancholy
portion of our war news to-day is the announcement of
the death of two of our brave generals—O. M. Mitchell
and J. B. Richardson. The former died at Beaufort of
yellow fever on the 31st ult., and General Richardson
died of wounds received at the battle of Antietam, at
Sharpsburg on Monday night.
Some of the rebel cavalry made an attack on our pickets
near Bolivar Heights yesterday, and captured three of
them, whom they sent to Charlestown and the river.
General Banks, in a few remarks which he made from
the platform of a railroad car in Boston on Saturday last,
said the approaching winter was not to be lost in inac-
tion. The government was determined now to put forth
its strength. Numerous expeditions were on foot that
could not, if vigorously pressed, but be fatal to the re-
volted states.
The second edition of the draft in Connecticut, which
was to have taken place to-day, has been postponed until
the 19th inst.
The following are the latest dispatches from the army
of General M'Clellan :
Headquarters of the army of the Potomac,
Bloomfield, Nov. 3.
The advance of the army of the Potomac up the valley
on the left side of the Blue-ridge is being pushed for-
ward with all dispatch.
General Pleasanton occupied Upperville this afternoon,
after a spirited engagement with the enemy for about
four hours.
We had none killed but several wounded. The rebels
left three of their dead on the field. Upperville is four
miles from Ashby's Gap, which the rebels are endeavour-
ing to hold. Our troops now hold all the gaps up to
Ashby's, with every prospect of having that to-morrow.
There was some force of the enemy to-day in front of
Snicker's Gap on the left bank of the Shenandoah, to '
dispute our passage at that point.
The rumours of the invasion by way of Downsville
are not believed at these headquarters. The last report
from the rear shows that these reports are unfounded.
The army is ready and prepared to fight a general
battle when the rebels may see proper to meet them.
The army is in better condition than it ever has been,
with the exception of the want of more cavalry—a want
that is greatly felt.
Harper's Ferry, Nov. 4.
About daylight this morning a squad of rebel cavalry
surprised and captured three of our pickets within two
miles of Bolivar Heights, near the railroad track, and
them carried off prisoners to Charlestown.
The rebels continue to show themselves in force in the
neighbourhood of Charleston.
Longetreet is at Paris. Jackson just passed through
Ashby's Gap, and Hill is close on him.
The general impression among the Feperal officers is
that the rebels are fast retreating to Gordonsville, and
all their movements are only feints to corer this move-
ment. They told thepeople of Purcellville several days
since, that they had no idea of wintering in the
Shenandoah Valley.
It has been beautiful Italian summer weather for the
laet three or four days, but this morning is cold and
cloudy, denoting rain. The Potomac is still low, but a
sudden and great rise is universally expected.
THE WAR IN THE SOUTH-WEST.
LOUSTILLE, Nov. 4.
It is reported that Bragg's army is at Murfreesboro''
Tennessee, and that 1,500 rebel cavalry are at Somerset,
Kentucky.
Four hundred sick and wounded Union soldiers from
the interior of the State arrived this evening, also some
forty rebel prisoners. General Bayle has ordered all
rebel prisoners at Harrodsburg and other hospitals suffi-
ciently well to be removed to come here for shipment to
Vicksburg.
The New York Times publishes the following dispatch
from its correspondent at Alexandria :
'ALEXANDRIA, VIRGINIA, Oct. 29.--The order re-
manding the old soldiers to their respective regiments
who have recently enlisted in the regular army has
produced the greatest satisfaction. Many of the oldest
and best regiments in the service were rapidly becoming
decimated from the effects of the order granting
soldiers in the volunteer corps the privilege of the re-
enlisting as regulars. Hundreds are daily rushing to
the recruiting stations for that purpose about
Alexandria, and discipline was ridiculed under the
plea of intentions to " enlist in the regulars."
Many of the regiments wore rapidly reduced to
shadows, and the effect in a few days would have
been the complete disorganize ion of the very flower
of many of the peninsular conneands and the muster-
ing out of service of many of our ablest and most valu-
able officers. Vast storehouses for army purposes are in
the course of erection in this place, and subsistence
supplies are rapidly pouring into them as fast as the work
will permit. Forage in prodigious quantities is also
being piled up on the wharves, and all supplies pertain-
ing to the quartermaster's and commissary's departments
are being landed in the most vigorous manner at all the
government wharves. Thousands of stores are being
forwarded to the troops occupying the defences of Wash-
ington on this side the river, and busy preparation is
making in all the camps, under the probability of a per-
manent residence here for the winter, and the regular
supplies of fuel are being conveyedto the encampments.
Still these preparations do not positively determine that
the troops are to remain here for the winter; but the
fact that these preparations are permitted to pro-
gress without interruption, or orders to the contrary,
conforms so materially with the programme of last fall,
that the troops justly infer that they will not be dis-
turbed in the occupation of their winter quarters here.
s Such has been the demand for lumber for this purpose,
that the supply in Alexandria has been swept away, and
the supplies arriving are insufficient to meet the neces-
sary wants of the official departments. This want will
be remedied in a few days, however as a large number
of vessels laden with building material are known to be
on their way hither from eastern ports. But the soldiers
meanwhile are by no means allowed to remain in idle-
ness. The old fortifications are being materially
strengthened, bridges are being built, old roads repaired,
and new ones constructed, while new and important
lines of breastworks are being thrown up, and the entire
line of defence rendered as impregnable as skilful en-
gineering and indefatigable labour can make it.'
The elections, which took place yesterday at New
York, are thus described by the New York Herald of to-
day:—
The elections, notwithstanding all the dreadful fore•
bodiiags that were entertained to the contrary, passed off
yesterday with a degree of quietude truly remarkable,
considering the intense excitement existing among the
friends of the opposing candidates. There was not a
single disturbance worthy of record from the time the
polls opened until sunset. Of course there were num-
berless small affairs resulting from a diversity of opinion
regarding the claims of Seymour and Wadsworth,
Walbridge and Ben Wood, Conkling and Chainer, &c.;
but, as a rule, these rows were promptly quelled before
the intervention of the police was called for, and
resulte • in no more extensive bodily injuries than a
bloody nose, a blackened eye, or a contused cranium.
The weather was clear and bright, the atmosphere
pleasantly cool, and everything favourable to the
developement of a large vote. So far as could be
ascertained by a single person taking a flying glance
through the various districts, the number of votes cast
was very heavy, and the democratic gains proportion-
ally large. Seymour's strength was undoubtedly far
away and beyond that of his republican opponent, and
the democratic nominees for surrogate, supervisors,
Congress and Assembly seemed to run with wonderful
success in all the districts.
The New York Times sums up the elections as
follows :—The election in the City and State of New
York yesterday resulted in a complete revolution in the
ascendaney of parties as far as the State and Congressional
tickets are concerned. The Democrats carried the city
by over 30,000, King's County by 5,500, and the State
by a majority not yet ascertained in its extent, though
Ihere is no present reason to doubt that it will be
decided. The Congressional delegation will stand 16 or
18 Democrats to 13 or 15 Republicans. The Legislature
is Republican in the Senate, elected for two years in
1861, and probably Republican in the Assembly. The
returns from Massachusetts are very full, and insure
the re-election of Governor Andrew by a very large
majority.
The New York Times of the sth inst. attributes the
victory obtained by the democrats to the failure of the
government to prosecute the war with vigour, energy,
and success which the vast resources at its command
warranted the country in expecting at ;ts hands, and
adds: What is the use of trying to sustain an adminis-
tration which lags so far behind the country, and seems
so indifferent and incompetent to the dreadful task com-
mitted to its hands ? If the government had given the
people victories—if it had even shown any just appre-
ciation of the need of victories, and had taken the most
ordinary means of exacting them at the hands of its
generals in the field, the people would have rallied as one
ina!l to its support. They would have spurned with
iudignation the base attempts of demagogues to ma

their faith in the administration, and to array
them in hostility against it. The vote in this
State, as in Pennsylvania and the West, indicates
a profound dissatisfaction with the method of the
administration in carrying on this war, and a peremp-
tory demand for the adoption of one better adapted to
the awful emergencies of the ease. The President must
not hesitate an hour to respond to this demand. Let the
popular verdict just pronounced dispel whatever of
hesitation or timidity may have hampered his move-
ments. There must be an end of apologies and delays.
The country will no longer tolerate half-hearted coun-
sels in the cabinet, or half-hearted leadership in the
field. The fate of the nation niust no longer be com-
mitted to generals who, like Essex in the English revo-
lution, next to a great defeat dread a great victory. The
government must no longer be content with deftnding
itself against a rebellion. It must act upon the offen-
sive—and act with the vigour and determination that
insure a victory. If the recent elections shall inspire
the administration with this spirit and prompt it to
such action, they will be of more service than results
which might have betrayed it into a delusive and fatal
canfidence in the fruitless policy it has hitherto pursued.
The New York Tribune partly ascribes the defeat of
the Republicans to the absence of 100,000 voters at the
seat of war, two thirds of whom it estimates are ardent
Republicans.

Litt the cause of defeat on which the Tribune lays
most stress is the general dissatisfaction with the slow
progress, or no progress, of our armies, and a wide-spread
feeling that, through the incapacity, inefficiency, or in-
sincerity of our military leaders, the blood and treasures
of the loyal millions are sacrificed in vain.
The Tribune concludes by saying :
We tell the administration most earnestly that the
country cannot endure another month's inaction of our
armies—that a Fernando-Wood dictatorship at the
North in thorough sympathy, ,if not in open alliance
with the Jeff. Davis rebellion at the south, will
inevitably result from such inaction. The war for the
Union must be fought out speedily and resolutely, or it
will die out. Defeat would be calamity, but delay is
ruin.

The New York Herald considers the triumph of
the Democratic party as most complete and. over-
whelming, but states that this popular demonstration
does not mean that the war shall be ended in an
ignominious and ruinous peace, involving a division of
the Union into two independent confederacies, but that
the war shall be prosecuted for the maintenance of the
Union, and for nothing else; that the malign abolition
influences have brought defeats and disasters to our
armies where we should otherwise have been crowned
with victory, and that the radical Marplots who in Con-
gress and in the Cabinet have caused the squandering
of hundreds of millions of money, and the neddless
sacrifice of thousands of our brave soldiers, shall be
henceforth repudiated by President Lincoln.

But as the new Congress cannot, unless specially con-
vened, meet until December, 1863, the Herald suggests
that to enable the new representatives, fresh from the
people,' to give their counsels to the President, they
should hold an informal meeting, after the fashion of
the late Altoona conference, of the governors of the loyal
states, in order that they may agree upon a series of
recommendations and declarations of the general policy
which they believe would meet the cordial support of
our loyal people.'
Let a meeting of this character, continues the New
York Herald, be held in this city before the reassembling
of Congress, and it may contribute much to aid the Pre-
sident in the recommendation of his annual message,
and in the important work of a reconstruction of his
cabinet.

articles.title: P.RIVATIONS AND _RESOURCES OF TEE COTTON TRADE FOR IVEXT YEAR.
articles.text:
P.RIVATIONS AND _RESOURCES OF
TEE COTTON TRADE FOR
IVEXT YEAR.

(From the Economist.)

We are very much inclined to take a less gloomy
view of the prospects of Lancashire operatives than
that accepted by most of our contemporaries. We do
not mean that the coming winter will not necessarily
be one of scanty wages, interrupted employment, and
consequent severe pressure both upon the endurance
of the poor and the resources of the rich. We do not
mean that there will not be ample scope and need
for the utmest liberality and charitable effort
on the part of all classes. We du not mean
that many hundred thousands of the popula-
tion in the manufacturing districts will not have
to be supported, wholly or in a great measure, by their
own former employers, by Boards of Guardians, or by
the Central,:Relief Committee, or by charity in some
form or other. We are disposed to think that by the
beginning of 1863 the worst will be over, even though
all hopes of an early termination of the war in America
should have to be abandoned. We ground our opinion
on the following facts—which, as being future, are, of
course, in some degree uncertain, but which at the
same time may be as confidently counted upon as most
of the contingencies and estimates on which prudent
men are content to base their plans and their commer-
cial ventures.

The present price of cotton is so high, and the
present price of goods and yarn are so disproportion-
ately low, that few cautious manufacturers dare either
to buy or to work. More mills are stopped every day.
For a little while, probably, this process must continue.
But the effect of its continuance is that the stock of
cotton in this country is increasing every week, while
the stock of goods and yarns is diminishing. The
price of the former, therefore, must fall, and the price
of the latter must rise; till before long it will become,
not exactly profitable to begin manufacturing again,
but neither ruinous nor unsafe. As soon as the loss by
working ceases to be considerable, most men of capital,
out of regard for their operatives and machinery, will be
glad to start their mills again cautiously no doubt and
tentatively, but enough to relieve the population from
actual idleness and destitution. Independently of the
American crop—which in our calculations we put en-
tirely out of consideration—it is now pretty certain
that for the coming year 1863 we can count upon a
supply of cotton sufficient to keep our mills at work for
four days a week; and four days' work a week will
suffice to keep the manufacturing operatives in tolerable
comfort as far as food and clothing are concerned—if
only it be equally distributed among them. We beg
attention to the following figures, which are procured
from the best sources, and may be relied upon as care-
fully and moderately framed.
A short time ago the stock of cotton in Liverpool
had fallen below 70,000 bales, and prices were very
wild in consequence. Exports were checked and pur-
chases for home consumption almost ceased. Cargoes
began also to arrive from India and elsewhere. The
stock gradually augmented under the combined opera-
tion of these influences till it reached at the end of
October 350,000. It is now pretty certain that, calcu-
lating on what has yet to arrive, and making liberal
allowance for probable purchase and export, the stock
at the end of the year will reach nearly, if not quite,
400,000 bales. The supply which we shall obtain from
India is still no doubt to a considerable extent obscure,
but the best informed merchants count on decidedly
more than last year, and in our expectations from
Brazil and Egypt we cannot be very far wrong. The
demand for export next year will, it is anticipated, be
large. The Continent will have to draw almost its
entire supply from this country, instead of a portion
only, as in ordinary years when much American cotton
goes direct to Havre, and not a little Egyptian cotton
direct to Trieste. Tho estimate for 1363 will then
stand thus :

The amount required for four days' work a week we
have calculated on the standard of 1861. But with
the economy which has since been enforced in every
mill and in every process, a less quantity might perhaps
suffice, The result, however, is in any case encourag.
ing ; since it shows that, even without a single bale
arriving from America, there would still be cotton
enough to afford our operatives about two-thirds their
ordinary work and wages, and still leave a stock of
upwards of 100,000 bales at the end of 1363.

PRINCE'S-STREET AT NIGHT.—The Edinburgh Cor-
respondent of the Glasgow Citizen, in describing the
November attractions of our Scottish capital, thus
adverts to one of its most striking sights Prince's-
street is pretty enough in summer, when the trees are ih
foliage and flower-beds are gorgeous, and the military
band is playing at the foot of the Castle; but in these
wintry nights, when all the lamps are lit and the old
town is illuminated, the sight is perfectly wonderful;
and, in its own way, perhaps cannot be paralleled in
Europe. All this nocturnal splendour the wandering
Cockney misses, and it is just probable that the ordinary
Edinburgh man never thinks of it. People, in point of'
fact, never see that which is constantly before their eyes.
The night side of Edinburgh is really a thing once seen
to be remembered. It is like what we might expect to
meet with in books of enchantment. It is as if a mighty
victory was being celebrated nightly—it is a perpetual
feast of lanterns.'

articles.title: PRINCE OF WALES AT NAPLES.
articles.text:
THE PRINCE OF WALES AT NAPLES.

NAPLES, Nov. 9.—lt is one great advantage of an
incognito that a Royal Prince is not deprived by his
rank of those pleasures which every private gentleman
enjoys, and under cover of this mantle our Princes have
been walking and driving about during their•short visit.
The people have been astonished at their early and un-
ceremonious habits, for as soon as half-past eight or nine
o'clock in the morning they have been recognised visit-
ing the various coral shops and studios and other places
of interest, just as you or T might have done. Palchetti
and Bolton had the honour of an inspection, as also the
celebrated photographist Grillet. A German artist, too,
M. Gutzloff, received the honour of a visit and of com-
missions.

On Saturday the Royal party started in eight car-
riages for Pompeii, where they arrived at midday, and
entered the silent city by the street of the Tombs. After
exploring the house of Diomede and the whole of the in-
teresting locality they proceeded to the house of 'the
Tragic poet, the public baths, the street so called of:the
Two Fountains, and then entered the Forum. The
Strada Olconio was next visited for the sake of the
house No. 4, which is remarkably well preserved, and
the house of Cornelio Rufo, in which is a very beauti-
ful Impluviunz, and a bust of the proprietor. On the
left of this street is the singularly interesting house
where at the threshold you are mat by the inscription
in mosaic, "Salve lucrum I" By this time it was two
o'clock, and an excavation was made at the back of the
Lupinari, and Bernourd, a French artist, photographed
the party as they sat around looking down on the novel
and exciting scene. The results, however, were not
great, as nothing was found except some bronze hinges
and nails, tolerably well preserved, and which the Prince
appropriated, with much glee. The Princess, too, ap-
peared greatly interested with the operations. Thence
the party proceeded to the Bagni Nuovi,' where lun-
cheon was provided, and Bernourd again photographed
them, two or three of the ladies in waiting being sum-
moned to take their part in the group. After reposing
a short time the Princes were conducted to the western
part of the Stra.da Stabiana, and a very successful ex-
cavation was made. An Oa of bronze, another ef clay,
and three little lucernce of the same material were
turned up, as also the skeletons of three fowls and
the remains of some egg-shells, which the Princess
took possession of. In the corner of the room, too, was
found a cameo with an engraving.
The next visit was to the amphitheatre, which lies at
a short distance from the city, and after examining the
lower part the distinguished visitors mounted the seats
which run round the ruin, the Prince of Wales being
especially active and jumping from block to block with
all the gaiety active,
befere leaving Bernourd took
another phoio,graph of the party as they sat or stood
about, with the western sun shining full upon them, and
as the points chosen were admirable, I doubt not but
that these three photographs will prove to be worthy
reminiscences of our Prince's visit to Pompeii. The
carriages were waiting at the Porta Stabiana, and now
that they are safely shut in let us leave them to talk
over their impressions of this very agreeable day.
On Sunday the Prince of Wales attained his majority,
and at eight o'clock in the morning all the British ves-
sels of war dressed, except the Osborne, each mast of
which, however, was surmounted by a crown of ever-
greens. No salutes were fired, the incognito of the
Prince being preserved, and an obvious respect being
paid to the wishes and feelings of Her Majesty. At
twelve o'clock the Princes and the Princess of Prussia
honoured the London and the Doris with a visit, and
the usual pretty spectacle was presented of manning
yards. After the return of the Prince to the Osborne
salutes were fired as a matter of course. On Sunday
afternoons our great promenade, the Villa Reale, is al-
ways crowded with a mixed company of persons
whose occupations prevent them from enjoying them-
selves during the week, and it used to be the rule
of the aristocratic ignebile vulgus' to abstain from
breathing the same air with them. Our Royal
family must have other ideas of infection, for in the'
afternoon they mingled in the crowd, and walked up to
the jetty, returning afterwards to the spot where the
band plays, and occupying some of the many hundred
chairs which are placed there at two or three grani a
head. An English lady who sat near, on seeing the
Princes, gave the master of the band a hint, and the
Royal Anthem was struck up, but, unaccustomed and
unprepared, the performers only got half-way through
it. Meantime the crowd formed in a half-circle around
to gaze at Royal Princes who actually could condescend
to walk and sit among them, and even pay for their
seats. In the evening there was a dinner on board the
Osborne which was given by the Prince of Prussia,
covers being laid for twenty-four. Besides the Prince
and Princess of Leiningen and the Royal suite, Captain
Chads, of the London, Captain Sir L. M'Clintock, of
the Doris, General La Marmora, Mr. Bonham and Mr.
Stolti, the British and Prussian Consuls, had the honour
of being invited. At the close of the dinner the health
of her Majesty was given, and was received with much
enthusiasm, and then General Knollys, all the guests
rising, proposed the health of the Prince of Wales.
Briefly, but in a very feeling manner, he intimated that
but for the great loss which the Royal family and the
nation had sustained the Prince would not have been
here that evening, and then, alluding to the great future
which lay before him he pointed to and eulogised the
bright example of the deeply to be regretted Prince
Albert. The Princesses were much affected, and, as
the guests raised their glasses to drink the toast, the
Princess of Prussia, who stood next to his Royal High-
ness, turned towards and kissed her brother. I fear to
have committed an indelicacy in thus violating the
privacy of the Royal party, yet I am much mistaken
in the character of the sons and daughters of old Erg-
land, if they will not love their Princes all the more for
those little touches of affection which unite them to us
by the bonds of a common humanity. A rocket an-
nounced that the toast of the evening had been drunk,
and in a moment the -London, the Doris, and the
Magicienne were blazing with blue lights; they ran
along the yards and peered out of the portholes, while
rockets were sent up from each vessel, and the silence
of the evening was broken by the cheers of the crews as
they drank the health of the Prince of Wales.

Yesterday, like all last days, was occupied in driving
about and visiting studios and making purchases. To-
wards the evening the Princes took a drive in the Strada
Nuova, and spent the evening on board, as San Carlo,
which, it had been announced, would be opened on the
10th, was still shut up, because the scenery was not ready.
Ap I am writing the Doris is getting up her steam, and
she, together with the Magicienne, will accompany the
Osborne round to Baive. The Royal party go round
by land to Pozzuoli, Cumm, and Baim, and, getting on
board, will proceed to Civita Vecchia in the afternoon,
and so on to Rome by rail. There the Princess will
spend her birthday, which comes off on the 21st, and
about the Ist of December the whole party will leave
Italy for the North. Thus ends my journal of our
Prince's doings in the Bay of Naples. Everything has
passed off well, and nothing could have exceeded the
calm beauty of the weather, which has shed jades
cribable loveliness on the natural attractions of this
neighbourhood.

NEW INVENTIONS.—The Garteactube of Leipzig
publishes a highly interesting article on a numerous
series of inventions, either executed or projected, by a
clever German engineer named William Bailer, for whom
a national subscription is now in progress throughout
Germany, to enav,le him to carry out a plan for raising
sunken ships from the bottom of a river, harbour, &c.
During the late war with Russia, Herr Bauer offered the
Government of that country an invention which, if
realised, might have done incalculable mischief. The in-
vention consisted of a submarine corvette, carrying
twenty-four guns, a model of which on a scale of one-
twelfth was executed by order of the Grand Duke Con-
stantine. She was calculated for a crew of eighty men,
for whom an atmosphere of 28,800 cubic feet of air was
provided. The vess Iwas to sink as soon as she came within
sight of the enemy's fleet, every porthole :and aperture
of any kind being previously hermetically closed in an
instant. Having got close to the enemy's ships, she was
to emerge suddenly from the deep, pour her broadside
into the vessel nearest hand, and then sink again, her
short stay above water having been employed in turn-
ing off the vitiated air. Another contrivance of the same
inventor, viz., an ice-cutting vessel, is now used. in the
Baltic; it is a flat-bottomed boat, carrying two circular
saws at her bows, which cut their way through the ice,
while by another device the blocks cut out are cast on one
side. Herr Bauer also invented a floating revolving
battery, which was received with but little favour until
the Monitor broke the quiet slumbers of official wisdom,
and led to an investigation of his plan. His battery
consists of a floating wooden platform, crowned with an
earthen parapet, slightly protected by a thin coat of
tinfoil. Behind the parapet rises a bomb-proof tower
revolving round an axis, the guns being fired by an
electric battery. Another invention, not easy to describe,
is one by which Herr Bauer gets up submarine electric
cables, in order to subject them to the necessary repairs.
This has not yet been tried.
A MODEST EPITAPH.—The following unique inscrip-
tion is from a stone in Hampstead parish church :
Here lie the ashes of Mr. John Hindly, of Stanhope-
street, Mayfair, London, and formerly of King-street,
Liverpool, who, under peculiar disadvantages, which to
common minds would have been a bar to any exertions,
raised himself from an obscure station of birth to fortune,
and, by his own industry and frugality, to the enjoyment
of a moderate competency. He attained to peculiar
excellence in penmanship and drawing without the in-
structions of a master, and to eminence in arithmetic, and
in the higher branches of mathematics, by going to school
only a year and eight months. He died a bachelor on the
24th day of October, 1807, in the fifty-fifth year of his
age; and, without forgttting relations, friends, or
acquaintances, bequeathed one-fifth of his property to
public charities. Reader; the world is open to thee, go
thou and do likewise

articles.title: SINGULAR TirIAL.
articles.text:
SINGULAR TirIAL.

The Assize Court at Paris, writes a correspondent
was crowded on Thursday morning, the
.13th, by a
well-dressed audience, among whom were several
actors and actresses, to hear a singularly dramatic trial
for an attempted murder. The prisoner, a young man
of 19, but looking younger, was a jeune premier (player
of lover's characters) at the little theatre ot Mont
Parnasse. His name is Dumont. He appears to have
been a sort of Cherubino, sighing after every lady
within his ken. The actress to whom he made love
laughed at him and treated him as a child, and their
husbands or protectors never considered.him as a rival
worth notice. In the course of the summer he became
very seriously in love with the wife of a brother actor,
named Demongeot, with whom he was on terms of
intimacy. He wrote her several amatory epistles,
which she never answered; but she gave him no
encouragement, reproved him when they met, and al-
though she did not show the love letters to her hus-
band, only abstained, as it seems, in mercy to her
youthful admirer. On July 5, while Demongeot was
on the stage in ch iracter at the Mont ParnassAheatre,
Dumont went to his dressing-room, took the key of his
apartments from the pocket of the ordinary clothes
which he found there, returned to the body of the
theatre, where he vehemently applauded his friend,
and then stealthily making use of the key, got into his
lodgings. There he partly undressed himself, and,
armed with a poniard and a carving knife, took up an
expectant position under Madame Demongeot's bed.
There he was when the unsuspecting husband came home
at midnight. The wife, who had been playing at the
Island theatre, in the Bois de Boulogne, d id not get home
till half-an-hour later. The couple took their supper
together leisurely, and it was about two in the morn-
ing before they retired to rest—in separate beds.
Dumont waited quietly till they were well asleep, and
must have remained in his hiding place for nearly four
hours. At three in the morning he got up and made a
murderous attack on M. Demongeot in his bed, inflict-
ing no less than fifteen wounds, none of which, how-
ever, happily, proved fatal or even dangerous. The
wife, awakened by her husband's screams, ran down
stairs in her night dress, crying for help. A police-
sergeant and a neighbour quicklyj came to herjassist-
tance, and Dumont was secured while struggling with
his victim, with whom he was rolling over and over on
the floor. Under these circumstances Dumont is in-
dicted on the capital charge of having, with premedita-
tion and gmet ci pens (lying in wait), • attempted to
murder Demongeot. From the depositions and the
examination of the prisoner in court, it is to be
collected that his intention was to murder the hus-
band, and then, if possible, possess the wife; or, in case
of her resistance, to murder her and kill himself. As
soon as the examination of witnesses was concluded,
the Imperial Procnreur moved the court that, inas-
much as some of the prisoner's witnesses spoke of him
as reputed insane, the trial should be postponed to
another session, in order to afford time for medical
examination. This motion was energetically opposed
by the prisoner's counsel, M. Algernon Jones (a French
barrister of English birth), who contended that during
the three months which his client had been in prison
the public prosecutor liad had plenty of time to inquire
into the state of his mind, and abundant notice that
the question would be raised for the defence. The
court, however, to the great disappointment of the
audience, acceded to the Imperial Procureur's demand,
and so the trial stands adjourned.
In his letter on Saturday a correspondent says :
'The condensed report of the extraordinary trial at
the Assize Court yesterday, which I gave from memory,
was substantially correct as far as it went, but I was
too fax off to hear all the witnesses said, and I find in
the legal journals two or three additionals fatts which
are worth noticing. I mentioned that the prisoner
Dumont obtained access to his friend Demongeot's
lodgings by taking the key from the pocket of his
trousers while the latter vas on the stage performing
in costume. The question may occur to your readers
how did Demangeot get into his own room when he
left the theatre? I should have said that Dumont
found a second key in the lodgings, harming up in a
place which he knew of. Taking this, he went back
to the theatre, restored a key to the pocket of
the trousers from which he had taken one,
went into the body of the theatre, made himself
conspicuous by vehemently applauding his friend
and intended victim, and then sneaked back to his
home to lie in wait for him under his bed. Calculating
that he would want light to strike a deadly blow,
Dumont provided himself with some lucifer matches.
When, rightly judging that the husband, and wife
must be asleep, he came out from his lurking place, he
drew a lucifer match along the floor, to light it.
Demongeot, who fortunately for himself slept lightly,
was awakened by the slight noise, which he mistook
for the scratching of a cat, and when his half-opened
eyes saw a phosphoric light he felt confirmed in the
supposition, for he fancied it proceeded from the eyes
of the cat- He jumped out of bed, and. at once felt the
gash of a knife. Then he struggled in the dark with
his assailant, as before described, and received fifteen
wounds. The wife, who ran for assistance, was not
conscious of the presence of an assassin, but fancied
that her husband was in a raving fit.
'On the occasion of this trial, it has been remarked
that the proportion of crimes committed by members
of the theatrical profession is less than in any other
class of society. I rather think that English statistics
show an analogous fact.'

articles.title: TEE RUSH FOR GOLD.
articles.text:
TEE RUSH FOR GOLD.

We have experienced a perfect paroxysm of excite-
ment since my last. About the middle of last month
two men suddenly made their appearance in:te.wn laden
with a tag containing no, less than 871bs. weight of
fine gold. As soon as the fact became known the place
was in a hubbub of excitement; and when, as the
result of a negociation with the provincial government,
by which the discoverers were to receive £2,000, pro-
vided 16,000 ounces of gold were produced in three
months, the locality was made known, a rush cora-
tnenced, and continued for several days unparalleled in
the annals of Dunedin. Hundreds of ill provided, in-
experienced men started off with little or no acquaint-
ance of the route most easy and practicable, only to meet
with sufferings and privations of the most appalling kind.
Lucrative employments were rashly abandoned, situa-
tions thrown up, and the most reckless determination
manifested to seek at all hazards an early claim at the
new El Dorado. Fora season apprehensions were enter-
tainedlest numbers who had started without preparation
would actually die of starvation. It was known that
supplies could not be obtained within anything like a
reasonable distance of the field, and that the road to
it was all but impracticable for loaded drays. And
the first tidings that reached Dunedin from the spot
went far towards confirming these fears. No actual
deaths from destitution were reported, but it was said
that swarms of half famished men were daily arriving,
and that the various stations on the route were actually
besieged by men imploring for morsels of food, while,
to crown all, the most unfavourable representations as
to the value of the discovery were in circulation. It
was said that the richness of the ground had been
grossly exaggerated, and that very few of those en-
gaged in digging were making enough to procure food.
This had a tendency to sober down the excitement
and restore the remaining population to a frame of
mind more rational than had been exhibited. Tera-
puka and the old established fields were all but
deserted, the miners having dwindled down in less
than a fortnight from thousands to hundreds.—
Otago correspondent of the Nezv Zealand Examiner.

THE ARMY.—Necessarily restricted as was the batch
of honours conferred on the army on the occasion of the
attainment of his majority by the Prince of Wales, the
Extraordinary Gazette announcing them was, neverthe-
less, read with much satisfaction throughout the service.
The two gallant veterans, Blakeney and Gough, will
fitly clse their long and brilliant career with the baton
of . Field-Marshal in their grasp. His Royal birth,
gallant service in the field, arid unquestionable devotion
to the interests of the service at the head of which he

placed, all make up a claim on the part of the Duke
of Cambridge which is far beyond that implied in the
conventional usage that lifts a Royal Duke easily to
such a position. The gift of none of the four batons
will bo more generally ratified by the service than
that awarded to Lord Clyde. To him the debt long due
by the country has at last been paid, and the national
con,cience need be no longer troubled with the reflection
that one of her most devoted and chivalrous sons has not
obtained his fair reward. The Prince of Wales's
eltvation to the rank of General will, of course, be felt
as an honour by the army, inasmuch as it more
prominently marks his connexion with the service. We
believe that his Royal Highness will only occupy the
position honorarily, as he has hitherto occupied that of
colonel, without pay, and not stopping one of the
promotions consequent on the creation of the four Field-
Marshals. Th, se promotions will quite make a small
brevet, and, with the distribution of the Bath, will cause
no inconsiderable change in some of the pages of the nest
Army List.—Army and.Aravy Gazette.

The painful duty devolves on us to announce the
death of one of our most prominent public men, and
one of the most patriotic of our resident proprietors—
the Honourable Bertle E. Jarvis, senior member of the
legislative council, who died on board the royal mail
steamer Seine, on his outward voyage from England,
two days before reaching St. Thomas. Mr. and Mrs.
Jervis left this island on a visit to England, in spring
last, and they were on their return when the hon.
gentleman's life terminated,—.Antigua Wk4t Rvister.

RESPITE OF SAMUEL G ARDNER.

On Saturday morning, about twelve o'clock, Mr.
Jonas, the Governor of Newgate, received a communi-
cation from the Home Office respiting, during her Ma-
jesty's pleasure, the sweep, Samuel Gardner, who was
to have suffered the last penalty of the law on Moil-
ing for the murder of his wife. Mr. Ribton, the
counsel for the prisoner, who was strongly impressed
with the conviction that the evidence was insufficient
to support the charge, wrote to the Home Secretary,
and, at his earnest request, Sir G. Grey had an inter-
view with the learned counsel on Friday afternoon,
when the latter most strongly urged the same points
that he addressed to the jury on behalf of the prisoner,
which were, it will be remembered, that no marks
of blood were seen upon the prisoner—that there
had been no quarrel, that it was quite as probable
the girl Elizabeth Humbler should have committed
murder as the prisoner, and that if the scream
that was heard at six o'clock on the morning of the
murder proceeded from the deceased, and the murder
was committed at that time, the prisoner could not have
been the guilty party, as he was clearly proved to have
been elsewhere at the time. The learned counsel, it
is understood, also urged upon the attention of the
Home Secretary the facts that the coroner's jury had
returned a verdict of wilful murder against the girl
Humbler as well as the prisoner; that the grand jury
also returned a true bill against both, and he said that
he was taken completely by surprise, when both
prisoners had been given in charge to the jury, by the
course that was taken by the counsel for the prosecu-
tion of abandoning the charge against the woman and
calling her as a witness for the crown. Sir G. Grey
listened attentively to all the arguments that were
used by Mr. Ribton, but at this time he declined to
alter the decision he had previously arrived at, stating
that all the circumstances referred to had been care-
fully considered by the jury before they returned their
verdict, and the case was of such a character that he
did not think he ought to interfere, but he at the same
time said that he should be ready to give his most
anxious attention to any fresh matter that might be
brought before him, and should be ready to recommend
the prisoner to the merciful consideration of the crown
if any fresh facts were brought forward which he con-
sidered would justify him in taking that course. It
appears that alter this Mr. Ribton had an interview
with the Lord Chief Baron, who tried the prisoner,
when be again urged the insufficiency of the evidence
and after a long interview it is understood that the
learned judge expresspd an opinion that some of the
points in the case were not quite so conclusive as they
should have been, and at the same time said that if
the Home Secretary thought there was any doubt in
the case, he should offer no opposition to his giving
effect to such an impression by respiting the prisoner,
and upon this intimation being conveyed to Sir
G. Grey, added to the earnest solicitations of the
counsel for the prisoner, he consented to respite
the culprit. The result was so little anticipated by
the gaol officials, that the culprit only on Thursday had
been earnestly exhorted not to entertain any hopes,
which, from the nature of the ease, would almost cerh-
tainly turn out fallacious, and in the course of that day
he had a final interview with his two children, both
girls, one of whom is aged nine and the other three ;
and the latter, it will be remembered, was asleep in the
same bed with the unhappy deceased woman at the
time she met her death. The culprit has exhibited ex-
traordinary fortitude ever since his conviction, and he
evinced very little emotion even when taking, what
was no doubt considered to be at the time, a last fare-
well of his children in this world, and he appeared
more affected when the announcement was made to
him that his life would be spared, as. he had evidently
made up his mind that there was no hope for him.

articles.title: EXTENSIVE COMIERCIAL FRAUDS.
articles.text:
EXTENSIVE COMIERCIAL FRAUDS.

Hugo Duliens, a German, who, it is supposed, has
been for several years pursuing an extensive system of
frauds upon the commercial community of the City, by
tarrying on business under fictitious names, was placed
at the bar of the Mansion-house, on the 15th, before the
Lord Mayor, to undergo a final examination upon a
charge of obtaining, by means of false pretences, a
quantity of woollen goods, to the value of about £l2O,
from Messrs. Thackralm and Co., of 20, Lawrence-lane;
and a quantity of carpet, &c., to the araout of £26 odd,
from Alessrs. Taplin and Co., of Gresham-street, carpet
manufacturers.

Mr. George Lewis again appeared to conduct the pro-
secution; and Mr. Murray attended on behalf of the
prisoner.

On the former occasion Mr. Lewis's statement was to
the effect that the prisoner had for several years carried
on business of various kinds in London. In 1859 he
became bankrupt, and did not obtain his discharge till
January in the present year. He then, took an office in
Little Britain, and carried on busines& under the name
of Teel, Lester, and Co. In June he again went through
the Bankruptcy Court, and he was confined in White-
cross street Prison, where he remained until August,
when he obtained his certificate, a third-class one, and
was at the same time released. He then appeared to
have commenced business at his office in Little Britain
under the name of Walter Berthold and Co.) which name
he had painted on the door, as well as Teed, Lester, and
Co., and again he set up a firm as Hugo, Dullens, and
Co. He obtained goods from different houses under
these names, he himself being the party who constituted
the three firms. He appeared to have been in the habit
of ordering goods at different warehouses, promising to
pay cash on delivery, and on the goods being sent to his
office he gave a cheque in payment, which on being
presented was returned unpaid, and marked no effects.
In nearly every case he postdated the cheques appa-
rently under the impression that by so doing he would
evade the law. A cheque book was found upon him
containing the counterfeits of a number of cheques to
the amount of upwards of £7OO, which were made
payable to different persons in the City—nearly all of
which were payable on the 10th November, which was
a day or two subsequent to his apprehension, and before
which day he no doubt intended to make a grand coup,
and at the same time make himself scarce.' Thii later
supposition was more apparent from a Lumber of bills
of exchange which were found upon the prisoner—
amounting in the aggregate to a considerable sum—and
some of which were drawn by himself upon Teed and
Lester, and Walter Berthold, and Teeds, Lester, and
Walter Berthold upon himself, and which were in readi-
ness for circulation.

It will be remembered that witnesses were called by
whose evidence it appeared that in October last the
prisoner went to the house of Messrs. Taplin and Co.,
and selected some carpets and rugs, to the amount of
£26, for which he promised to pay cash. The goods
were sent to his office by the porter, to whom the pri-
soner gave a cheque upon Messrs. Jones and Webster,
bankers, in Newington. Upon the porter taking the
cheque back it was discovered that it was postdated. It
was, however, presented on the day it was male
payable, and was returned unpaid. On the 4th of Novem-
ber the prisoner went to the warehouse of Messrs. Thack-
rah, of Lawrence-lane, and there selected cloth goods
to the amount of £ll4, Ihe agreement being that he
was to pay £5O of the £ll4 at the time the goods were
delivered. The prisoner directed the goods to be sent
home that day, and said he would pay the £;)0 to Mr.
Thackrah if he went with them. The goods were
accordingly sent in the course of the afternoon of the
4th, and Mr. Thackrah went for the money. The pri-
soner wrote him a cheque for £5O on Messrs. Jones and
Webster, which he at first dated the 10th November,
but which, at the request of Mr. Thackrah, he altered
to the sth, at the same time asking him not to present it
until the after part of the day. The cheque was presen t€ d
on the sth, and was returned unpaid.
On Saturday Mr. Lewis said although there were a
great many cases similar to that of Messrs. Thackrah's
and Messrs. Taplin's against the prisoner, he did not
intend to go into them, but merely to complete the two
cases which had been already gone into, but he thought
it righE to mention that besides the office at 13, Little
Britain, where the prisoner carried on business under
the names of Teed, Lester, Walter Berthold and Co., and
Hugo Dullens, he,had offices in Bury-street, St. Mary-axe,
andin Joiner-street, Bermondsey, and carried on business
atthelatterplace in the name of Murray. While in Bury-
court, he had obtained watches to the amount of upwards of
£2,000 from Messrs. Lecoutre and Soubet, a firm at St.
Croix, in Switzerland, in the name of Hugo Dullens.
Mr. Pollaky, the foreign agent, had been in communi-
cation with those gentlemen; and, since the last ex-
amination, he had received a letter from them which
was in the prisoner's handwriting, and signed Hugo
Dullens, and in which he acknowledges the receipt of
the watches, but Mr. Pollaky unfortunately received
the information too late, and was unable to discover any
trace of the goods and the prisoner, owing to the number
of names under which he traded, had many facilities of
making away with them, or at leastdestroying any trace
of them. Witnesses having been called, the prisoner
was committed for trial.

The workmen e—mplOyed in the alterations and decora
tions of Marlborough House, in preparation for the resi-
dence of the Prince and the future Princess of Wales,
have not yet cleared out of the building, therefore it
will be some time ere it is fit for occupation.
Accounts from Toulon state that the reports current
on the subject of a fleet of iron-coated frigates being
fitted out for sea have completely ceased, and if the
Government ever intended anything of the sort, it has
been indefinitely adjourned, for the Gloire is about to be
laid up in ordinary, and the Invincible to be placed on
the reserved list. The expedition to Mexico having
dipped deeply into the budget of the Marine, it has
been found necessary to postpone various experiments
which the Minister had proposed to make with iron.

articles.title: TIZE YANEEE COMMANDER WILKES.
articles.text:
TIZE YANEEE COMMANDER
WILKES.

The secret of the extraordinary antipathy exhibited
towards England by brave Commander Wilkes of the
Federal navy is not generally known in this country.
An intelligent gentleman, a native of Virginia, who ie
now in London aseisting in the promotion of a public
undertaking of great importance, which is to be brought
out when the war is over, has however, given me a
satisfactory solution a the mystery. On expressing my
surprise at the unnecessary display of antipathy ex-
hibited by the valiant Wilkes, this gentleman said,
'And do you not know the cause ? ' I protested my igno-
rance. Why,' added he, have you never heard
about Wilkes and Sir John Ross?' Never; I replied.
Well,' continued my Transatlantic friend, 'l'll tell
you, and let it be a caution to you for the future.'
He then told me that Wilkes was the commander of
the United States expedition, fitted out, in common
with similar expeditions by England and Russia, some
years ago, to discover the North-West passage. The
American expedition went first and Sir John Ross fol-
lowed a few months afterwards. The United States
party was met on its return by Sir John Ross, when
Captain Wilkes gave all the information he had acquired
(or, as my Yankee friend said, all he chose to give') to
the British expedition. He also gave them a chart of
his progress. This was carefully preserved by Sir
John Ross but subsequent experience proved that it
was altogether fallacious, as Sir John Roses ships
actually sailed over places which were described as
mountains in the chart of Captain Wilkes The infer-
ence left on the mind of Sir John Ross was, naturally
enough, that the Yankee commander had drawn upon
his imagination for his facts. Be this as it may, he was
obliged to state in his official report to the Government,
that Commander Wilkes was not quite as reliable an.
Arctic traveller as some of his predecessors; and that,
in fact, the Yankee report was, in some respects, a
romance. Hence the bitter antagonism of the valourous
Wilke, and hence his extraordinary anxiety to insUl,t
the British flag.—arrespondent of Belfast News Letter.

articles.text:
THE CIVIL IVAI AHERICA.-TIIE
PROPOSED MEDIATION:

The 1011471, Gazette of Friday contains the follow

FOREIGN OFFICE, Nov. 14, 1562,

The folio wing dispatch has been addressed by Earl

Foreign Office, Nov. 13, 1862.
My Lon-The Count de Flahault came to the
Foreign Office by appointment on Monday, the 10th
inst., and read to me a dispatch from M. Drouyn de
Lhuys, relating to the civil war in North Ameriea :
In this dispatch the Minister for Foreign Affairs
states that Europe has followed with p iinful interest
the struggle which has now been going on for more
than a year on the American Continent. Ile does jua-
tice to the energy and perseverance which have been
displayed by both sides, but he observes that these
proofs of their costrage have been given at the expense
of innumerable calamities and immense bloodshed.
To these accompaniments of civil conflict is to-
be added the apprehension of a servile war, which
If these calamities affected America only, these sufferings
would be the climax of so many irreparable misfortunes.
of a friendly nation would be enough to excite the
anxiety and sympathy of the Emperor. But Europe also
has suffered in one of the principal branches of her in-
dustry, and her artisans have been subjected to the most
cruel trials. France and the maritime Powers have
during this struggle maintained the strictest neutrality;
but the sentiments by which they are animated, far
from imposing on them anything like indifference, seem,
on the contrary, to require that they should assist the
two belligerent parties in an endeavour to escape from a
position which appears to have no issue. The forces of
the two sides have hitherto fought with balanced success,
and the latest accounts de not show any prospect of a
speedy termination of the war. These circum-
stances, taken together, would seem to favour the
adoption of measure l which might bring about a
truce. The Emperor of the French, therefore, is
of opinion that there is now an opportunity of
offering to the belligerents the good offices of the
maritime Powers. He, therefore, proposes to her
Majesty, as well as to the Emperor of Russia, that the
three Courts should endeavour, both at Washington
and in communication with the Confederate States, to
bring about a suspension of arms of six months, during
which every act of hostility, direct or indirect, should
cease, at sea as well as on land. This armistice might,
if necessary, be renewed for a further period. This
proposal, M. Drouyn de Lhuys proceeds to say, would
not imply on the part of the three Powers any judg-
ment on the origin of the war, or any pressure on the
negotiations for peace which it is hoped would take
place during the armistice. The three Powers would
only interfere to smooth obstacles, and only within
limits which the two interested parties would prescribe.
The French Government is of opinion that, even in the
event of failure of immediate success, these overtures
might be useful in turning the minds of men, heated by
passion, to consider the advantages of conciliation and of
peace. Such is, in substance, the proposal of the Govern-
ment of the Emperor of the French, and I need hardly say
that it has attracted the serious attention of her
Majesty's Government. Her Majesty is desirous of
acting in concurrence with France upon the great
questions now agitating the world, and upon none more
than on the contingencies connected with the great
struggle now going on in North America. Neither her
Majesty the Queen nor the British nation will ever
forget the noble and emphatic manner in which the Em-
peror of the French vindicated the law of nations, and
assisted the cause of peace in the instance of the seizure
of the Confederate Commissioners on board the Trent.
Her Majesty's Government recognise with pleasure in the
design of arresting the progress of war by friendly mea-
sures the benevolent views and humane intentions of the
Emperor. They are also of opinion that if the steps
proposed were to be taken the concurrence of Russia
would be extremely desirable. Her Majesty's Govern-
ment have, however, not been informed up to the pre-
sent time that the Russian Government have agreed to
co-operate with England and France on this occasion,
although that Government may support the endeavours
of England and France to attain the end proposed. But is
the end proposed attainable at the present moment by
the course suggested by the Government of France?
Such is the question which has been anxiously and
carefully examined by her Majesty's Government.
After weighing all the information which has
been received from America, her Majesty's Go-
vernment are led to the conclusion that there is
no ground at the present moment to hope that
the Federal Government would accept the proposal
suggested, and a refusal from Washington at present

STUDENT INTERPRETERS IN CHINA. AND Sum.--
Lord Russell has addressed a letter to the Duke of
Devonshire, Chancellor a the University of Cambridge,
intimating that he proposes to nominate a certain number
ef candidates to compete before the Civil Service Com-
missioners for the appointments of student interpreters
in China and Siam. The candidates selected are to be
between 18 and 24 years of age, and Lord Russell
adds :—‘ The object for which such appointments are
made is that the persons on' whom they are conferred
should, in the first place, devote themselves to the study
of the Chinese or Siamese language, as the case may be,
and, in the next place,
China or Siam, so
generally for the should
in ld qualify themselves
public services
that Her Majesty's Government may always have at
their disposal persons competent to discharge the duties
entrusted to Her Majesty's consular offices in those
countries. The salary which is assigned to the office of
student interpreter in either counfin,
is at
,the rate of
£2OO a year, to commence from the date of departure
from this country, the passage from England to the place
of destination being, moreover, provided at the public
expense. . • • As the climates of China and of Siam
are considered to be more or less trying to English con-
stitutions, the probability that the health of the can-
didates will be such as to bear a residence in those
climates will be taken into consideration by the Civil
Service Commissioners Candidates must clearly under-
stand that if they succeed in obtaining one of the vacant
appointments— of which as regards China there are four,
•and as regards Siam two, to be filled up on the present
occasion—their retention in the public service and their
future advancement in it will depend entirely upon the
ability which they may show after their arrival at their
destination' and on their general steadiness and good'good'conduct.' The !examination is to take place on Thurs-
day, December so, and the heads of the examination
are—' General intelligence, _Precis, orthography, hand-
writing, first four rules of arithmetic first four books of
Euclid, translation from Latin into English, translation
from French into English, general knowledge of ramlern
geography.'

articles.title: AXR.RICA.
articles.text:
AXR.RICA.

8 (Morning).--It is semi-officially NEw YORK, Noi
=pounced that th 'report of a protest from the French
Minister against the acts of General Butler is apocry-
phal. The draft will take place in the city of New
York on the 10th instant. There will be no draft in
Boston. The Richmond Whig says the order of the
Secretary of War to enrol conscripts between 18 and 45
years of age is unpopular, if not odious, among a large
class of Southern people. A letter from the captain of
the Federal steamer Huntsville has been published,
stating that the Blanche was burnt by her own crew
when run ashore near Havana. Horatio Seymour was
elected Governor of New York by a majority of 10,000 votes.
The Democrats have carried the elections in Illinois by
a majority of 15,000. It is reported that General
Hunter will replace General Mitchell in South Caro-
lina. The Philadelphia Inquirer contains a letter,
stating that 3,000 Confederates had surrendered uncon-
ditionally to General Foster's expedition at Plymouth,
North Carolina. It is officially announced that Cana-
dian duties on American goods will be calculated
according to the depreciation of American paper
currency as compared with gold on the date of the
invoice of the goods. Several suggestions are being
put forward to send from New York voluntary contri-
butions in cargoes of grain for the relief of the distress
in Lancashire. . _

NEW YORK,Nov. 7 (Evening).—General M'Clellan's
army has oocupied Ashby 's Gap. No Confederates
could be seen from the heights commanding Shenandoah
Valley. Another portion of General M‘Clellan's army)
after a successful skirmish with General Stuart's cavalry,
has occupied Barbour, near the mouth of Chester Gap,
where General Stonewall Jackson has taken up a posi-
tion. All the approaches to Manassas on the left of the
Blue Ridge are in possession of the Federals. They
also. occupy Warrentown. No information has been
recessed of the position or movements of General Lee's
army. An expedition, consisting of 12,000 men and
several gunboats, has left Newbern, North Carolina.
Its destination is unknown. The owners of the cargo
of the barque Laurietta, which was burned by the Con-
federate steamer Alabama, have protested before the
British and Portuguese Consuls, on the ground that.
their British and Portuguese nationality was certified by
the Consul's certificates, which were shown to Captain
Semmes. The New York Chamber of Commerce has ap-
pointed a committee to take measures for capturing the
Alabama. During the discussion on this subject, Mr.
Prosper Wentmore said that the Liverpool Chamber of
Commerce lately held a meeting, at which every.encou-
ragement was given to the fitting out of other piratical
vessels in England. A letter from Mr. Seward was read,
acknowledging the receipt of the resolutions of the
Chamber of Commerce, concerning the destruction of
American vessels. by pirates, who, he says, are sent from
the shores of a friendly nation in violation of the restric-
tions of municipal and international laws. Mr. Seward
further says, that he has directed the attention of the
American Minister in London to this subject, and noti-
fied all American consuls. It is reported that the
French Minister at Washington has protested against
several acts of General Butler towards Frenchmen at
New Orleans, and has demanded the release and indem-
nification for Mr. Heidsick, now confined in Fort
Jackson.

articles.title: NEW' FIELD-MARSHALS.
articles.text:
THE NEW' FIELD-MARSHALS.

The following is a recapitulation of the services of
the recently gazetted Field-Marshals :
His Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge entered
the army in 1837, with the nominal rank of colonel,
and did duty with the 12th and 17th Dragoons, and
33rd Foot, and subsequently commanded the Dublin
district. In 1852 he became Colonel of the Scots
Fusilier Guards. At the outbreak of the Russian
war he proceeded with the Guards to Scutari, and
subsequently commanded the Ist Division of the army.
He was in the thickest of the fight at the battles
of Alma and Inkerman, and in the latter his horse
was killed under him. He was also present at Balak-
lava, and during a great portion of the siege of Sebas-
topol. On the death of Lord Hardinge his royal high-
ness was appointed Commander-in-Chief, a post which
he has filled with the hearty approbation of the army,
and entire satisfaction to the public.
Viscount Gough commenced his military career in
1794, and served at the Cape of Good Hope against the
Dutch in that year. Next year he was again fighting
in the West Indies. In the Peninsular war he com-
manded the 86th Regiipent at Talavera (where he was
seriously wounded), at Barossa, Nivelle (wounded a
second time), at Vittoria, and at the defence of Cadiz,
where he was once more wounded. The 86th was for-
tunate enough to capture an eagle at Barossa, and the
baton of Marshal Jourdain at Vittoria. After a long pe-
riod of comparative ipaction, he was appointed to com-
mand the forces in China in 1842, and at the termina-
tion of hostilities he was made a baronet and G.C.B.
From 1843 to 1846 he was actively engaged against the
Mahrattas and Sikhs; and the battles. of Moodkee,
Ferozeshah, Sobraon, and Goojerat will always be iden-
tified with his name. It was after the last-named battle
that this gallant officer was created a peer. His lordship
was appointed to the coloneley of the Royal Horse
Guards in 1855, and specially proceeded to Sebastopol
to distribute the honours so hardly won by the army.
Sir Edward Blakeney also entered the army in 1791
as cornet, but he speedily changed into the infantry, and
commenced an active career in 1796 in the West Indies.
In 1807 he was present atthe capture of the Danish fleet
and:surrender of Copenhagen, and in 1809 he served at the
capture of Martinique. In 1811 he commanded the 7th
Foot, and was present at the battle of Busaco, Albuera
(in the latter of which he was severely wounded), sieges
of Ciudad Rodigo and Badajoz (wounded asccond time) ;
and he was also engaged at Vittoria, Pampeluna, the
Pyrenees, and Nivelle. In 1814 he served at New
Orleans, and next year joined the Duke of Wellington's
army in Belgium. He was commander of the forces in
Ireland for some time, and on being made Lieutenant-
Governor of the Royal Hospital, at Chelsea, was suc-
ceeded by Lord Seaton. Sir Edward was appointed to
the eolonelcy of the Ist Foot in 1854.
Lord Clyde commencedhis military career in 1808, and
with the 9th Foot, was engaged at Vimiera and Corunna,
Vittoria, St. Sebastian, passage of the Bidassoa, and was
three times severely wounded. In 1814 he served in
America with the 60th Rifles. In 1842 he served under
Lord Gough in China, commanding the 98th Regiment.
In 1848 he commanded a division of the army of the Pun-
jaub, under Sir Charles Napier, and was wounded at
Chillianwallan ;he was also present at Goojerat. In
1851 and 1852 he was actively employed against the
hill tribes, and returned to England only to proceed
once more on active service in command of the High-
land Brigade, with which he remained during the Crimean
wax. He had not been long at home before the Indian
mutiny broke out. and Lord Panmure, then Secretary of
State for war, decided upon placing the appointment of
Commander- is, Chief in India in his hands. The gallant Gld
soldier made his decision at once. We believe the offer
was made and accepted one afternoon in the private walk
which leads from the office in Pall-mall to the Mall in

tinguished services during the mutiny, for which he was
raised to the peerage, need not be enlarged upon. Lord
Clyde was appointed to the colonelcy of the Coldstream
Guards in 1880.
