articles.title: DESTRUCTION OF A MILL BY FIRE,T THE INTERNATIONAL .EXHIBITION. NEAR TORIIORDEN.
articles.text:
DESTRUCTION OF A MILL BY FIRE,T THE INTERNATIONAL .EXHIBITION.
NEAR TORIIORDEN.

At about ten minutes past eleven o'clock on Tues-
day evening, a fire broke out in the large flour mill
at Wood-mill, near Todmorden, belonging to the
Messrs. Thompson and Sons, of Wakefield. The fire
was discovered by policeman Swithenbank, of the
West Riding police force, who was on duty near the
place at the time. The mill is about forty yards
in length, four storeys in height, and was replete
with all tha newest improvements considerable
alterations having been going forward for a long
time. The fire originated in the third storey, in which
room there was a fan that is supposed to have struck
fire. There was only one person, named Crabtree,
working in the mill, and he was in the bottom room,
and ignorant of the existence of fire until informed by
a person named Dawson, the night watchman of the
railway station adjoining. By this time,the fire had
gained so much power, that the feeble efforts to extin-
guish it which could be put forth by the few persons
present, were of no avail. A messenger was dispatched
for the Hebden-bridge fire brigade, and the books in
the office, and the few sacks of flour in the lower storey,
were got out of the place. The fire brigade arrived about
twelve o'clock, but by that time the place was entirely
gutted, with the exception of a small portion of the
west end, which was stored with grain. To the pre-
servation of this section of the buildings the efforts of
the fire brigade were at once directed, and to some ex
text they succeeded, though not till the roof had been
consumed. An immense quantity of flour has been
destroyed, several hundred sacks being stowed in one
of the rooms above. Mr. Inspector Tucker, of the
West Riding force, and his staff of men, deserve great
praise for the efficient services they rendered. The
damage has not yet been ascertained, but probably it
will exceed £20,000, a large portion, if not the whole,
of which is covered by insurance.

The work of dismantling the interior of the building
has at last really commenced, and is being prosecuted
with a vigour which bids fair to leave nothing but the
empty walls in the course of another fortnight or three
weeks. All the minor articles were got rid of during
the days of sale, and the great trophy articles, which
no one in his senses ever contemplated buying—such
as obelisks of pickles or granite, colossal telescopes or
Armstrong guns—are in process of disintegration,
and the floor of the nave is either cumbered
with them or obstructed with the little scaffold-
ings required to help the masses down. On every
side a thousand hammers are going; side courts and
formerly thronged byways are littered ankle deep
with shavings, hay, and reams of crumpled paper;
and the long vista of galleries, stripped a their many
coloured draperies, show only the skeleton framework
of rough timbers on which they hung, and have a
weird, cold, forlorn aspect, suggestive of anything but
festivity. The great jewelry cases are all black and
empty as so many hearses, and the long range of stalls
where the English cut-glass vied in brilliancy and sur-
passed in art any diamonds shown, have scarcely even
the rough deal tables left to show where once this
beautiful collection stood. Appearances are still Ifiept
up to a certain extent in the Porcelain Court by some
specimens of Worcester china, with a few of the master-
pieces of Minton and Copeland, which remain, not
because they are unsold, but because th ir great value
renders extra care in their removal requisite. Beyond a
few such isolated samples here and there, almost every-
thing which could be removed by hand has been taken
from the English side of the building, including
nearly all the pianos and most of the decorative
furniture. The colonies, too, are getting very forward
in their preparation to be gone, though, from the nature
of the packing their goods require, this is a slower
process. Arnngements sire also making with many
colonies—a kind of system of exchange—by which the
most curious of their native products may be left in this
country in return for similar contributions here to the
various colonial museums. Victoria is especially likely
to tio well in this arrangement, and from this source, as
also from the liberality of various wealthy colonists here,
their commissioners are likely to take back the nucleus
of a very valuable museum. From the Indian collection
not much of consequence has yet been taken—a fact
which is rather in favour of the settlement of some
disputes which have arisen as to certain coveted objects
having been sold to two or more purchasers. The Indian
collection is almost the only department on the English
side where complaints of this nature have arisen.
The foreign side is ;lot so forward in dismantling as
the English. Austria only, which, thanks to the care
and pains bestowed by her chief commissioner, Chevalier
Schwartz, has throughout set an example, is ready to
go. The final arrangements have, however, been very
much facilitated by the fact that she has sold almost
every single article she brought, and has very little to
to take back but her machinery. Austria was the first
foreign court ready after the opening, and she will be
the first to return her space to the disposal of the com-
missioners. The various States of the Zollvereiri,
Belgium, Saxony, and Russia are also all well forward
in their ariangements, and day by day the goods leave
quietly, without the least hurry, and consequently
without damage. Much of this is due to the admirable
arrangements of the exhibitors themselves, though we
should not be doing justice to one of the most indefati-
gable members of the executive if we did not also state
that the exhibitors, on their part, ascribe these facilities
entirely to the care of their chief superintendent, Mr.
Owen whose general management of the foreign side of
the building deserves the highest praise. The French,
who were the last to come, are likely to be the last to
go, for they have to take back with them a very large
proportion of the goods they brought, and which, even
during the sale days, when visitors spent almost reck-
lessly and without inquiry, did not find purchasers at
the fabulous sums they demanded. We are sorry that
this should be so, but our neighbours have no one to thank
but themselves, and we hope the lesson thus taught, that
an Englishman is not always willing to pay double the
prices that would be asked of anybody else, will not be
altogether lost upon them.
Minton's fountain still remains intact under the east
dome. It is to be hoped that some effort will be made
to retain this magnificent work either for the building
itself or the conservatory of the Horticultural Gardens.
From the arrangements now making for lighting the
building with gas it would seem to be definitely decided
that the distribution of prize medals by his Royal High-
ness the Prince of Wales will take place, if not at night,
yet, at least, late in the afternoon, and either during the
last week in January or the first in February. The
warming as well as the lightinc, arrangements should,
at such a season of the year, be also an important item
in the arrangements to be considered for the festivity.

articles.title: DEBBYSEIRE BURGLARY.
articles.text:
THE DEBBYSEIRE BURGLARY.

The police have succeeded in arresting two men be-
lieved to be concerned in the daring burglary at the
residence of Mr. Norman, at Whaley, Derbyshire, on
Wednesday last, when one of the gang, it is supposed,
was dangerously wounded by. a shot from a revolver,
levelled at his head by Mrs. Norman. The prisoners
were brought before two of the county justices on Mon-
day last, when the only evidence taken was that of
Mrs. Mary Norman, who said: I am the wife of Cecil
George Norman, and reside at Whaley. At about a
quarter past three o'clock in the morning of 12th inst.,
while I was feeding the baby in bed, I heard a crash of
glass in the window of the room on the ground floor
under our bed-room. My husband was in bed asleep.
I did not awake him, because he was ill. I got out of
bed, and took a revolver off a table in the room, and
went downstairs. I did not take a light, as I could not
find the matches. On opening the door of the front
sitting-room I saw a man standing beside the cup-
board near the window. He was looking in the direc-
tion of the door where I stood. He had what appeared
'o be a short iron bar in his hand. He had also a
lighted candle in the other. I tried to discharge the
pistol at him, but the cap missed fire, and I immediately
fired the next barrel. All the barrels were loaded with
ball. The man clapped his hand to his shoulder, and
in a tone of pain exclaimed, 'Oh G-1 Bill—Dick!'
The lower sash of the wihdow was up, and he threw
one leg out of the window, and a man seized him by
the collar and dragged him out. It was a fine moon-
light night. There were a man and lad, apparently 17
or 18 years of age, outside the window. I can't identify
any of the prisoners, because the faces of the men who
committed the burglary were covered with handker-
chiefs, and the youngest, who had no handkerchief
over his face, had his back turned to me. The youngest
prisoner seems to be of the same size as one of the
men who stood outside the window, and the colour of
his coat corresponds with that of the same man. The
prisoners were then remanded.

EGYPTIAN COTTON.—Of the three kinds of cotton
which are produced in Egypt, the Indian alone is
maintaining its ground; the others are disappearing by
degrees, being usuited to commercial purposes. The
soil is particularly favourable to the cultivation of
Indian cotton, and the quantity of land devoted to it is
constantly on the increase. Every part of Egypt is
favourable to the growth of cotton, but especially those
soils which retain moisture, although there may be an
excess of humidity. The cotton plants retain their
vigour for three years; but after that their productive
power diminishes, and they require to be renewed. At
present cotton is grown only in Lower Egypt, and
chiefly in the five provinces of Kallioub, Charkieh, Da-
kalieh, Garbieh, and Menouf. There is great room
therefore, for the development of its cultivation, should
this be justified by the state of the market, and the re-
quirements of commerce.—lfoniteur.
The Sleds of yesterday says :—There has been a good
deal of talk the last day or two of a new work, by M.
Michelet, The Sorciere'—a villainous word, but a
touching thing. This book, full of eloquent, ingenious,
and profound passages, is, to describe it briefly, a fine
and admirable history of the devil, certainly the best
and most veracious that has ever been written of that
personage, who has, nevertheless, not been without
historians. M. Michelet has followed him from the
middle ages to the present day, upon desert land, in the
palace, in convents, at the confessional. He snatches
from him all his old masks, and the last one which he
has worn, that of M. Tartuffe. That worthy man will
doubtless utter loud cries in reading The Sorciere.'
He will cry, as in the case of Les Pretres et les
Femmes,' that it is impiety, irreligion, immorality, and
so on. He may calumniate at his leisure, and every-
body will read this powerful study, going %-) the very
foundations of history, of psychology, and of the human
heart.

KIDNAPPING A BRITISH SUBJECT.—The last mail
from Canada has brought intelligence of a case of kid-
napping, which occurred at Bedford, a frontier village
in Lower or Eastern Canada. A resident 'writes to the
Montreal Gazette the following particulars: A man of
wealth in the State of Connecticut was drafted, and
must necessarily fight for his cherished flag, unless a
substitute could be procured; and, by making an offer
of 300 dols , he procured that substitute, in the person of a
young man named George Baxter, for many years a
resident of this village. The engagement was made,
and the agreement signed ; but instead of fulfilling his
engagement he only paid Baxter 50 dols., refusing to pay
him any further sum of money. Baxter was hurried
off to camp, but embraced the first favourable opportu-
nity, and left the gallant Connecticut 25th and came to
Canada. On the night of the 25th of the present
month, a party from the town of S wanton, in the State
of Vermont, wearing the uniform of the American
soldier, came to this village, and, having procured the
aid of some low, disreputable loafers, entered the'
house where Baxter boarded, took him forcibly from
his bed, and carried him in irons to Swanton.
This great outrage has, as a matter of course, created
much excitement. One of the guilty parties has
been arrested, and his examination will commence
this morning. Parties are on the look out for the
others. I may add, also, that the matter will be repre-
sented to the Government in order that the retarn of
Baxter may be claimed from the United States autho-
rities.'

SERIOUS CRINOLINE ACCIDENT TO MDLLE. EMMA
L/TRY.—An alarming accident occurred lately at the
Grand Opera during a rehearsal of La lifuette de Partici.
Mae. Livry, who was to play the part of Fenella,

In her terror she rushed across the stage, when she was

i

Livry was then conveyed to her dressing-room, and her
burns having been dressed by the two doctors on service,

given to iniouiries made was that Mdlle. Livry was far
more injured than was at first supposed. On Monday, the
Countess Walewski paid a visit to the distinguished

burns are not very itleep, but
.they extend over a third
part of the body. She is in a high fever, the pulse beat-
ing 160. The doctors say they must wait three days
before they can pronounce her out of danger.

articles.title: FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE CALE. DONLAN .RAILWAY.
articles.text:
FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE CALE-
. DONLAN .RAILWAY.

An accident, attended with fatal' consequences,
occurred to the mail train which left Glasgow at 9.10
p.m. on Saturday evening. The train proceeded in
safety until about twelve o'clock, when it approached
the Beattock incline, about 45 miles from Carlisle, and
60 miles from Glasgow. As it proceeded down the
incline the tire of one of the leading wheels broke, and
the train ran between 500 and 600 yards off the rails.
The engine then swerved, and took to the right hand
across the down line of rails, dragging the guard's van
and one of the carriages after it. Four carriages and
the post-office van, which had become disconnected
from the foremost part of the train, ran to the left side
of the line, and went over an embankment to a depth
of between 15 and 20 feet. Several carriages at the end
of the train remained upon the line. The carriages
which went over the embankment fell on their sides,
and we regret to state that one of the passengers, named
Captain James Bridie, who occupied a third-class car-
riage, was killed on the spot, his neck being dislocated.
His wife and child, the latter aged four and a-half
years, were in the same compartment, but we are happy
to say that the mother escaped with no further injury
than a cut on the forehead and a bruise on the nose,
while the child escaped scathless, and did
,not even
appear frightened. A gentleman belonging to Lon-
don, named Percival, received a very severe scalp
wound; and a young man named Morrison, a draper's
assistant, who was on his way to London to fill a
situation, was much shaken, although there was no
appearance of any external injury. The carriages
were more or less damaged. The injured prssengers
were conveyed to the Beattock Hotel, where they were
attended by Drs. Memo and Kerr, who were sum-
moned from Moffat. The engine-driver received a cut
on the thigh, and the fireman was also injured; they
were removed to Carlisle, and placed in the infirmary.
Other carriages were procured without loss of time, ana
the uninjured passengers proceeded on their journey.
On the accident becoming known, the general manager
of the line and other officials of the company has-
tened to the spot without loss of time, anci
made the necessary arrangements for the clearing
of the line. Captain Bridie had left Greenock on
Saturday for the purpose of joining his ship, the Rob
Roy, at London. The engine, we are informed, hact
only been at work a month, after having undergone
thorough overhaul. The tires of the engine were new,
and made of the best iron. The rails at the spot where
the accident occurred were in perfect condition, ane
were fish-jointed, and the road was well ballasted and
in excellent order. The other passengers who wer,
carried over the embankment were severely shaken and
frightened, but sustained no serious injuries, and after
a detention of little more than half an hour proceeded
south. The limited train which left Londcn on Satur-
day evening was detained at Carlisle for some time
from some unexplained cause, and arrived late in
Glasgow on Sunday morning. The ordinary train from
London was fully an hour behind time in arriving io
Glasgow.

articles.title: ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT IVICHLING.
articles.text:
ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT
IVICHLING.

Mr. Major Murton, farmer, was brought up on re-
mand on the 19th, in the custody of Superintendent
Maloney, and charged before D. Scratton, Esq., and
Captain Robinson, at the magistrates' clerk's office,
Maidstone, with ill-treating his wife, who subsequently
died.

The two principal witnesses were Mrs. Walter, a
married daughter of the accused, and Harriet Russell,
a servant, from whose eviuence it appeared that on
Thursday night., October 23, prisoner returned home
with two women of loose character, ordering his wife
and daughter to prepare supper and to get the best
bedroom ready. One of the women, named Whit-
bread, said that if she had known that Mrs. Mur-
ton was at home she would not have come, and
expressed her intention to go away. Thereupon
Murton threw himself into a violent passion, and going
into the kitchen, where his wife was, struck her a
severe blow across the head with his hunting-whip, at
the same time ordering her, with an oath, to get out of
the house or he would kick her out. He then pulled
her out of the chair, and threw her violently on to the
brick kitchen floor. Not content with this, he attacked
his unfortunate wife with the tongs, and beat her
severely about the head and body till she was almost
insensible, in which state her daughter managed to get
her to bed. The servant, who was so frightened by
the prisoner's violence that she ran out of the house and
hid, returned about two o'clock, when she was admitted
by her unfortunate mistress, who pointed out to her a
large bruise on the thigh, and said, See what that vil-
lain has done to me.' The two prostitutes remained in
the house all night. On the following Sunday Mrs.
Murton took refuge at a neighbouring farmer's, and
died a weelr afterwards, saying several times before
her death, That villain has broken my heart—h‘, has
been the cause of my death.' In addition to his
evidence before the coroner's jury, Mr. Robinson, the
medical gentleman who attended the deceased, made
the important statement that in his opinion the fall on
the brick kitchen floor had accelerated the deceased's
death.

Prisoner was again remanded till Thursday next,
bail being refused, and it is probable that he will then
be committed for manslaughter.
As he was being taken away in custody he handed
over his watch and all the money in his possession to
one of the loose women who had accompanied him
home, and they were seized by her with avidity. We
are also informed that, by Murton's authority, they
remain the only occupants of his house at the present
t ime.—Maidstone Journal.

articles.title: DETTBUCTION OF,'THE LAFAYETTE BY T.HE ALABAMA.
articles.text:
THE DETTBUCTION OF,'THE
LAFAYETTE BY T.HE ALABAMA.

Immediately on the arrival of the Captain of the
Lafayette at Boston, 'he lodged a protest with the
notary public against the destruction of his ship by
Captain Semmes, of the Alabama. The Lafayette was
laden with corn, wheat, &c., and sailed from New
York for Belfast on the 20th of October. Nothing
unusual happened until the afternoon of the 23rd of
October, about four o'clock, when (to quote Captain
Small's statement) : wind north, north-west and
squally, ship under full sail, made a sail about two
points off the weather bow, which they took to be a
topsail schooner, bound to the westward by the wind.
Being headed directly for them, they did not discover
that the sail was other than they supposed her to be
until within a mile of them, when she sheered off,
showing her broadside, and they discovered that she
was a steamer, having the British flag, the cross of
St. George flying at the mizen peak. This was imme-
diately hauled down, the Confederate flag hoisted, and
a shot fired across the bows of the Lafayette. Deeming
it impossible to get out of her way, they were
obliged to haul to, and considering that the cargo was
the property of British subjects, protected by a eertid-
cate to that effect, they supposed that they would be
allowed to proceed without molestation. A boat's
crew then boarded the Lafayette, and Captain Small
was ordered on board the steamer with his papers. On
reaching the steamer, Captain Small was shown into
the cabin, when an officer came in, who, he sub,e-
quently learned, was Captain Semmes, of the Confede-
rate steamer Alabama. The ship's papers were then
examined, and on Captain Small's calling Semmes'
attention to the fact that the property had been sworn
to before a notary public as the property of British
subjects, and a consular certificate attached to each bill
of lading to that effect, he observed that the people of
New York were getting very sharp; but that this
would not save me; it was all a damned hatched-up
mess, and unless I had other proof than that he should
burn the vessel.' Captain Small then replied that
he had no further proof. Semmes then called his
first lieutenant—Kale—and ordered him to have the
appearer put on board his vessel, giving him liberty to
take one trunk, and the crew a bag of clothes each, and
then to return to the steamer and the ship to be set on
fire immediately, all of which was accordingly done.
As soon as the ship was well on fire the steamer stood
to the north-east under sail. The ship was soon in
flames, and the last seen of her was about ten o'clock
p.m. The steamer took all the nautical instruments,
books, charts, &c., together with such live stock as was
on board. On arrival on board the steamer, the
entire crew were put in irons, officers included, where
they remained till the evening of the 29th of October,
when they were removed on board the brig Baron de
Castine, which vessel had been taken a prize by the
Alabama, but was ransomed and released, and on
board of which they arrived at Boston on the 2nd of
November.

articles.title: ROME FOR POOR FACTORY GIRLS.
articles.text:
ROME FOR POOR FACTORY GIRLS.

Our readers will be glad to hear that Mrs. W. E.
Gladstone, who so kindly, with Miss Burdett Coutts,
paid Blackburn a vi-it the other day, has established a
home at Hawarden Castle for orphan girls, or factory
girls, wishing for situations in gentlemen's families, or
girls whose parents in this trying time find it difficult to
provide for their children. It arose, we believe, out of
correspondence with Mrs. Gerald Potter, with reference
to her benevolent plans of placing unemployed girls
in temporary service and finding others a home where
they should be fed and clothed. Indeed, to some ex-
tent it is a combination of both of Mrs. Potter's
schemes, retaining the excellencies of both, and at the
same time avoiding many of the defects which attach
to them separately. Instead of untutored girls being
sent at once to situations in gentlemen's families,
for which they are manifestly unfitted, and where
there is but little opportunity for careful indi-
vidual training, they are placed in a home close to the
Castle, in the care of an experienced matron, and
immediately under Mrs. Gladstone's own inspection.
They are then in turns admitted into the Castle for a
week at a time, and properly instructed in the duties
which appertain to the domestics of a large establish-
ment. After this, if they wish it, they are drafted off
into situations which Mrs. Gladstone and her friends
are enabled to provide for them. Already several girls
have gone from Blackburn, who have expressed, in
letters to their friends, their gratitude for their comfort-
able home and kind treatment they have met with.
There are now vacancies for four, and it is likely, from
the interest whish is taken in the Home, and the com-
missions which are given by Mrs. Gladstone's friends,
that others will continually occur. The Rev. Dr.
Robinson has undertaken to receive applications for
admission, and to pay the fare and forward any girls
who may be suitable; and he authorises us to say that
he will be glad to give any further information (and
arrange for their conveyance to Hawarden if they are
selected) to such candidites as will call at Holy Trinity
Parsonage from eight until nine in the morning, or from
five until six in the evei ing. We ought to add that the
home at Ha warden is visit. d almost every day by the
clergyman of thb parish, and is conducted on strictly
religious principles.—Blackburn Standard.

THE COSELY 11JaDER. —The adjourned inquest upon
the body of Henry Swinnerton, a shingler, aged 33,
was on Friday concluded near Cosely, a small town in
the black country,' near to Wolverhampton. By a
reference to the evidence given upon a previous occa-
sion it is shown that the deceased, on Tuesday night,
the 4th inst., went away from a public-house near, to
Cci,ely in company with four persons, two men and
two women, the latter prostitutes. They proceeded to
a lonely spot on the bank of a canal in the neighbour-
hood. There the deceased was attacked and robbed
by one or more of his companions. After beating him
with a large gutta-percha stick, and trying to throttle
him, they finally threw him over some rails into an
adjacent field, atter which they ran away. The man
sustained injuries which resulted in his death early on
the following Monday morning. Before he died, how-
ever, he identified four persons as his assailants. Their
names are respectively William Henshaw, Jesse
Watts, Hannah Simms, and Mary Downing. The
statements of the accused were taken. They were all
of the same nature, and tended to show that S winner-
ton had while at the public-house threatened to fight
Henshaw an 1 Watts. The latter, accompanied by a
man named Kelsey, went away, but were followed by
him along
.the c nat. bank. Watts knocked down the
deceased two or three times. The latter still con-
tinued to so follow them. Kelsey then suggested that
he should be thrown irqo the canal. Ait- r some de-

SUICIDE OF A. FEENCII COUNTESS.

An Irish contemporary, the _Limerick Chronicle, is
responsible for the following sensation story, which
if not true at least does credit to the invention of the
writer :

The sudden death of one of the leading stars of the
fashionable world of Paris is announced, and rumour
states in rather a singular manner. At the Eaux of
Ems, the Countess de - had formed a liaison with a
young Russian, which caused her to protract her stay
there longer than usual, till, in short, a pressing letter
from her husbana induced her to return to Paris. Along
with her Russian lover she returned the very evening
before the husband, who was also absent from
Paris, had announced his arrival, so that not only
were appearances saved, but a laudable alacrity ex-
hil,ited. By her companion's advice, the lady alighted
at her own hotel in the Rue de Grenelle ; thus prov-
ing, by the acte de presence, that she had obeyed
the injunctions of the Count, her husband; but, as it
had been agreed upon beforehand, the lovers were re-
solved to spend this last evening together before part-
ing, as it were for ever. The great gulf of etiquette,
propriety, and the prudence of Paris life once between
them, they knew well enough that they would hence-
forth become as much separated as though by the whole
breadth of the universe. With this reflection they
agreed to meet at a cafe at the angle of the Boulevard
des Italiens and a street called by the grandins La Vance
des Lames (d'autrui), and here the mystery of the
suicide begins. Arriving together, they ordered a cabi-
net part iculier, which was furnished them in the series
overlooking the boulevard. The lady appeared over-
come with grief and trouble. A dinner de premier qualite
was served, and during its consumption both attendants
appointed to wait observed the striking contrast
exhibited in the behaviour of the two guests. While the
lady grew more and more desponding as the dinner pro-
ceeded, the spirits of the gentleman rose higher. He
had already drunk largely during dinner, taking nothing
but champagne, according to Russian taste; and when
the dessert was placed upon the table, and the waiters
withdrew, both of them observed that the gentleman
seemed to have had as much as was good for him.'
After the exit of the waiters a silence of more than an
hour took place in the room occupied by the pair, when
suddenly there burst forth from that room the wildest
shriek ever uttered in mortal agony. The door flew
open, and the young Russian, pale as death, with totter-
ing steps, and a countenance frightfully distorted,
rushed along the galley, calling aloud for help. The
whole establishrntnt was aroused on the instant; and the
lady was beheld lying back upon the sofa a corpse, the
blood streaming in a torrent from her throat, and flowing
slowly through the rich lace trimmings of her dress, to
form a ghastly pool, in which her violet coloured boots
were soaking, with horrible contrast to the gay scene
around. A doctor was immediately sent for (Dr. -,
of the Rue de hider), and he pronounced life extinct,
death having been immediate from the stab in the neck,
which had severed the jugular vein. The police were,
of course, on the alert -Instantly.
What had taken place in the hour after the waiters
had left can only be learnt from the young Russian's
own account. He declares that through the haze of
wine and cigars he can but remember having arrived,
amid the tears and regrets of his companion, to the
second bottle of champagne, which stood in the wine
cooler, and his hand was on the bell to summon the
waiter to draw the cork, when the lady, who had been
weeping violently, implored him to abstain from calling
any one who might be able to bear testimony to her
emotion. Accordingly, willing to accede to her request,
he drew from his pocket, a knife of curious manufacture,
which he purchased in England some little time ago, and
which had already accompanied him on his travels, and
which contained a spring corkscrew as well as several
blades of various sizes which he opened one after
another to show to his companion, in order to create some
little diversion to her grief. The last one of all was a
kind of broad priming blade, sharp, bright, and powerful,
such as England alone produces, and, although at the
time under the influence of the wine he had been drink-
ing to an incredible extent, he fancies that he can
remember the very words of the conversation which took
place upon the occasion. He remembers, too, perfectly
having placed the corkscrew in the cork, hearing the
creaking, hissing sound which accompanied its yielding
to the pressure of the fixed air within, and after that
shock, a fearful shriek, and nothing more. A hand was
extended to the knife, and the Countess snatched it from
where it was placed, open: the idea of suicide was
suggested by the temptation, and she plunged it into her
neck. The Russian is so completely under the effect of
the shock that he is about to quit Paris for ever, and to
retire to his own estates; and the husband of the
Countess, regarding the affair as a just retribution of
Heaven, refuses to challenge the paramour, though urged
to do so by good-natured friends.

• COURT OF PROBATE, NOVEMBER 18.
It will probably be within the recollection of the
public that a Mrs. Ityves, who claimed to be the
daughter of Mrs. Serres, made an application before Sir
Creswell Cresswell some time back for the purpose of
establishing her legitimacy, which the Court allowed.
The claim was that Mrs. Serres had been the legitimate
child of his Royal Highness the late Duke of Cumber-
land, and it was deducible therefrom that, if Mrs.
Ryves was the legitimate daughter of Mrs Serres, then
she would be entitled to inherit any property to which
her mother would have been ent,tled. Mrs. Serres had
propounded the will of his Maji sty King George the
Third, in which his Royal brother, the late Duke of
Cumberland, had been appointed sole legatee, but the
Prerogative Court of Canterbury refused to grant her
probate of the will on the ground that the will in ques-
tion, being the will of a Royal sovereign, the Preroga-
tive Court had not any jurisdiction.
This morning Mr. Gibbons moved that his Grace the
Duke ot Wellington and her Majesty's Attorney-
General should be cited before the Court, in order to
enable the petitioner to establish the validity of the will
in question. The late Duke of Wellington had been
appointed executor to his Majesty King George the
Fourth, who inherited his father's estate, and the pre-
sent Duke of Wellington was his representative.
The Judge Ordinary said that the question of this
will had been already decided by Sir John Nichol', the
late learned judge of the Prerogative Court of Canter-
bury. He (the Judge Ordinary) felt very much disin-
clined to set aside the decision arrived at by that
learned judge. He considered the Court had not any
jurisdiction in the present case. The motion would
therefore he di4missed.

The motion of Mr. Gibbons was dismissed.
We give the alleged testamentary paper itself; it
was in the following terms :
George R. _ St. ,Tames's.

In case of oiir royal demise, we give and Ve-J.Lth
to Olive, our brother of Cumberland's daughter, the
sum of £15,000; commanding our heir and successor to
pay the same privately to our said niece for her use, as a
recompense for the misfortunes she may have known
through her father. June 2, 1774.
Witnesses—J. Dunning, Chatham, Warwick.'

THE FEMALE STUDENT QUESTION.—The Senatus Aca-
demicus of St. Andrew's have decided, in the case of
Niss Garrett, who matriculated at the University, and
then applied tor admission to the chemistry and anatomy
classes, in accordance with the opinion of Mr. A. R.
Clark, the counsel whom they consulted. They hold
the matriculation null and of no effect, and 'seeing that
it is incompetent to any professor to issue a ticket confer-
ring academical privileges to a student not legally
matriculated, resolve that the tickets of the anatomy and
chemistry clas-es, issued to Miss Gdrrett, are void and of
no effect, and that the fees be teturned.' Miss Garrett,
on her part, laid a memorial
.narrating the facts before
the Lord Advocate, whose opinion entirely supports the
resolution of the Senatus. Miss Garrett may appeal to
the University Court against the decision of the Senatus,
and if that decision is confirmed she will be excluded
from the college classes. As she does not care for
damages, and has little prospect of being successful in
an action for specific performance of the contract, there
does not appear to be any practical solution of the
iemale student que-tion, except what may come from
the University Commission, which exists until January,
or from the Leg'slature.
PERTHSHME. WHITE HARE AND PARTRIDGE
SHOOTING.—On most of the shooting quarters in this
county the sport has now been commenced, and the low
covers are much better stocked than was anticipated.
White hare shooting on the northern moors has been
very successful, and from 1,500 to 2,000 have been
bagged on several estates within the past three weeks.
They are very numerous on the Grampian ranges, and
on sonic of the passes from 60 to SO may be shot in a few
hours. Roe deer are very numerous and in fine condi-
tion. A large number have been shot on the best
wooded estates. Brown hares and rabbits are plentiful
on the low covers. Partridges and pheasants are scarce,
but healthy and well-conditioned. In Strathearn, the
covers are extensively stocked. At Strathallan Lord
Strathallan, the Master of Strathallan, and Captain
Greenhill have enjoyed excellent sport, and have killed
from 500 to 600 head of game. Lord Dupplin, Lord
Charles Ker, Sir Thomas Moncreiffe, and party bagged
upwards of 1,000 head of game in four days' sh,oting
on the Dupplin preserves. On the Inchbrakie, Trinity-
Gail:, •Monereiffe, and Mansfield estates, several hun-
'red head of game have been bagged ri')ring the week.

PUNCH'S PRISON DISCIPLINE.

Confinement and low diet are the punishment of
paupers in the workhouse. The workhouse system is
said to work well in the prevention, to some extent, of
pauperism. What if convicts and paupers were made
to change places? It is probable that pauperism would
increase enormously, and that crime would greatly

The treatment of criminals in gaols appears to be
based on the humane theory that crime is the
result of moral disease. Tho heads of the patients, or
prisoners, are closely cropped, they are kept upon a
wholesome and nutritious, though not stimulating, diet,
and made to perform an amount of labour not exceeding
the bounds of healthy exercise.
All this would be very well, provided that it
answered that the effect of prison discipline was in
general the cure of criminals, and the prevention of
crime. In that case the benevolent system .of treating
offenders might be carried further; the eonvaleseent
might be allowed fight and savoury soups,',-broths,
jellies, and made dishes, with wine and beckin_modera-
tion. They might be encouraged to amuse themselves
with music and dancing, to get up private theatricals,
and practise sundry other elegant and innocent
recreations. The only limit to improvement in this di-
rection would be that of the expense which it might ne-
cessitate.

But the regimen to which convicts are now subjected,
unfortunately does by no means operate in curing
thieves of roguery and felony, thereby deterring their
associates from following their example. Is it, then,
advisable to punish them with the same severity as that
which paupers are punished with? If they are to be
reduced to workhouse-diet, their exercise musthe dis-
continued, lest it should kill them. The .cheaper and
more merciful plan would be to hang them at once.
The present keep of convicts is so dear that the Go-
vernment, for economy's sake, lets them out of gaol long
before their sentences have expired. As soon as they
have been turned loose with tickets of leave, they go
about the streets knocking passengers down, garotting
them, and rifling their pockets.
How to avoid the expense of keeping a felon com-
fortably, correct the (offender himself, and constitute
him a caution to other villains P That is the ,question.
There seems at present to be only one answer to it.
Imprison him on pauper's allowance, and whip him.
Tie him up and flog him, as you flog a bad soldier. If
it is right to flog a soldier it cannot be wrong to flog a
ruffian. Does flogging in the Army answer its purpose?
Is the power of inflicting it necessary to be retained at
least in the face of an enemy? If the fear of
flogging will control soldiers, it will restrain civilian
scoundrels. The lash is not too bad for the back of the
miscreant who cracks your skull. Robberies accom.
panied with violence, and all brutal assaults, at any
rate, might deservedly be rendered punishable by whip-
ping. That chastisement the convicted savage might
undergo upon a public scaffold, or it might be inflicted
on him in the prison-yard; and tickets of leave for
admission to see it might be distributed by the police
amongst the frequenters of thieves' lodging-houses and
taverns. The spectacle of one sound flogging adminis-
tered to a garotte-robber' would prevent many; a .fero-
cious outrage and cruel murder. Benevolence might
accept the execution as an economy of pain. • it would
not, probably, have to be repeated very soon.

REVISION OF VEdDICTS.—A woman condemned to be
hanged for murder, contrives to get a respite by accusing
an innocent old man of having committed the crime.
Therefoie her sentence has been commuted to penal
servitude for life. But is this justice? Ay, marry, is
it; Home-Secretary's justice. There ought to be a
Court of Criminal Appeal (for culprits only) as many
persons have said, besides Punch. Mr. Punch only adds
the suggestion that the appellant to such a Court ought
to be sajected to judicial examination. The old English
course of criminal procedure would thus be combined
with all that is advantageous, and nothing that is
objectionable, in the French ; the accused would get all
the law that is now given them, and justice into the
bargain.

MISERABLE STATE OF THE CROPS Is THE lIIGH-
LARES.—Never did the close of harvest present a more
threatening and ruinous aspect in the Highlands than
it does at the present time. On most farms which are
favourably situated the crop is well secured, but on late
places and in high glens, where the soil is cold and
heavy, comparatively little has been done to the in-
gathering of the grain—so little, that on some farms in
this neighbourhood only two and three stacks have
appeared in the stack yards, and the fields present a
miserable aspect. So little of the crop had been
gathered in, that gatting ' had to be resorted to. This
is done by binding the sheaves below the ears, and
spreading out the lower part of them, so that every
sheaf is made to stand by itself—a process which has
failed in giving satisfaction this year, as snow has
naw covered the ground to the depth of . five or six
itches, which has broken down the gate and lodged
them among the snow, like bushes of mountain heath
in the middle of winter. The only cheering feature we
have under these disheartening•circumstances is the fact
that most farriers in this district depend chiefly on their
sheep and cattle for the wherewithal to pay their rents;
and if a sufficient quantity of straw cou.cl be secured
for the wintering of cattle most parties might Come
pretty well out of it a; all.—Thincito Advertiser. .

PARIS Permanent Universal xhi
TO BE OPENED IN 1863.
. -•
For many years National Exhibitions have beeen held
in various cities, with universal success in stimulating
industry and developing trade between the countries
represented by the Exhibitions.
The central position of Paris, and the vast nnmber of
visitors passing through the city every year, have sug-
gested there the establi%hment there of a Permanent
Exhibition: where specimens of the manufactures and
products of every country will be collected together in
one spacious building, in order that dealers and con-
sumers from all parts of the world may see them; and
base their orders upon the quality and cost of the arti-
cles exhinited.
The project has met with the entire approval of the
Emperor Napoleon 111. and a special license has been
granted by the Ministers of Finance and Commerce for
admission to the Permanent Universal Exhibition,
dating the entire period that it is open, of all Foreign
Products, Free of Duty, ssith liberty to re-export them
without payment of duties, or to sell them on the spot,
on paying the duties imposed by the new International
Tariff.
The whole of the capital, amounting to £600,000, has
been subscribed in France, and the Palace (now in
course of construction) will be opened early in the slim-
mer of 1863.
The amount of space allotted to France and several
other continental countries has al:eady been taken up.
Admission will be gratuitous on at least five days of
the week.
The British Exhibitors will be reyresented by a Com-
mittee of twenty members, who, with those appointed by
other countries will form a General Committee, to
organise the distribution of space, and frame a code of
rules for general observance; and agencies will be esta-
bashed in Paris to receive orders.
All products and manufactures will be classified, so
that those of the sante nature from different countri, s,
being placed in juxta-position, may be easily compared.
Two rates of rental (payable annually In advance)
will be charged, the space being tak,m for six years:
The first rate (.£2 per square metre per annum) will
apply to all products and manufactures.
The second rate (£1 per square metre per annum)
will apply to wall surface for advertisements.
N.B.—Five square metres are equal to six square
yards.
Drawings of the Building can be seen at the principal
Railway Stations and Exchanges in London and the
country; in the Refreshment-rooms of the present
London Exhibition: and at the Offices of Messrs. J.
STUDDY LEIGH &CG., 27. Leadenhall-street, London.
Agents for Great Britain. Ireland, and the Colonies, from
whom forms of agreement and full information may be
obtained.

TLONDON OPERATIVE
HOPE3fAKERS' Appeal to the Metropolitan
Trades, and Trades of the United Kingdom.
BROTHER WORKING MEN: It is with a feelin Of
reluctance that we, the Loudon Operative Hopemakers,
venture to draw your attention to our present position,
knowing as we do the great depression of trade in
almost every degartment of manufacture, and yet we
feel encouraged to lay our cases before you, soliciting
your sympathy and aid, by the conviction that we are
well known by the London trades, and to many trades
in the country, for our willingness to assist others in
times of difficulty. We will therefore simply state our
case to you, hoping that you will deem it worthy of
your kind consideration
On the 11th of June last one of our employers offered
a reduction of sevenpence per day, or three and six-
pence per week, from our wages, and we, having a
well organised trade society, could not submit to any
reduction of wages, recognising, as fair workmen should
do that a fair day's work is entitled to a fair day's pay,
and having enjoyed the present rate of wages for the
last seven years, and there being no reasonable plea
given why such reduction should take place.
Having sent deputations to the employers to reason
the matter with them and used every effort to pre-
vent a strike, but finding that the employers were
determined if possible to effect a general reduction of
wages throughout the trade, there was no other course
left us but to withdraw the whole of the journeymen
from the firm, viz.—Messrs. J. H. Baker, Bermond-
sey. This is the eighth week of the strike, and our
men are firm and in good spirits, being convinced of the
justness of their claims and ultimate success, for al-
though the firm has resorted to all kinds of misrepre-
sentation to obtain men their shop is stud empty, for
as fast as the men come up from the country through
their agents and advertisements in the country local
papers, they (the men) after having the 'question of
dispute explained to them, leave their work, and by
our assistance leave London again, which creates a
large expense over the actual cost of keeping our own
members on strike. We have expended over £l5O, a
large sum for only one firm, but then we are fighting
for the whole trade, for some of the other employers
have already given notice to their men, that as soon
As Messrs. Baker and Brothers 0 supplied with men
at the reduction that they will give no more for their
work than the Messrs. Baker's, and if we are com-
pelled to submit to this reduction we shall lose
£1,500 per year in wages (then leaving a large surplus
of men out of work), a sum you will admit woe&
struggling for.
Having thus briefly stated our !present position we
earnestly appeal to the sympathy of our fellow workmen
another trades, soliciting their assistance to enable us to
defend successfully our right of wages and trade against
these grasping employers. In appealing to our fellow
working men, we may say that we have had always a
willing heart, and ready hand to assist other trades
placed in similar circnmstances ; indeed, since 1853 there
has not been a question affecting the interest of the
working classes, or a dispute in any other trade, but
what we have supported and sustained to our utmost
ability. We therefore make this appeal ' with some
ciegree of confidene, that you will readily respond to us
ia our present difficulties, and show to the employing
classes that there is a spirit of union and brotherhood
amongst the working men of England, that will' enable
them to rally round their fellow bat oppressed brother
Workmen.
We beg to rennin yours very respectfully, on behalf of
the trade. Thomas Hay, Charles Howe, William Matthews,
Charles Terdre, Robert Still, committee; Richard Bur
ridge, treasurer; Daniel Smith, secretary.

quired, or forward any information on the question of
dispute, by applying to
